That several Lodges hold their property through a board of trustees, and in some
lnst11nces these trustees are elected yearly. In consequence, the property is not In
the hands of any legitimate head, and much trouble is and may be experienced in
transferring it:
That in one district a diminution of membership is reported, although with an
increase of population and an unusual production of the mines. The explanation
is had in the fact of the establishment of various societies which, assisted by can·
vassers, attracted large numbers by the inducements offered of cheap fees and flattering promises of le.rge benefits; especially to young men were the attractions
seemingly too great for resistance:
That a Master elect was unable to qualify, Three years ago he was elected but
failed to learn the work. The Lodge in excessive amiability elected him for the
ser,ond time, but the inability to Require the work was chronic, and now it is proposed
to elect some one who can' quality:
That the Lodges flnanclaliy were flouri~hlng, yet that little work had been done,
owing to a determination to use only good material. It would be better if this
determination to accept only good material applied to aome of the other districts:
That a Lodge had a debt of $1800, with many members in arrears for dues from
one to two years who are quite able to pay, but that it was not the practice to suspend
members for the non-payment of dues.
Notice is made of the exhausted condition of Dibble Lodge, No.109, with a recommendation that the charter be surrendered by its members. A petition for it. surrender has been received.
From another report I quote : "The Lodge Is in good working order and In a
prosperous condition financially,' but I am sorry to say we are not living so harmonl·
ously as we have heretofore, owing to a couple of turbulent members who have not
yet learued to submit to the will of the majority or the meaning of charity." This
reminds me of the words of a Persian philosopher; "By the means of one disorderly
person in a company, the hearts of many wise men become afflicted. It' you fill a
cistern with rose water and a dog should fall Into It, it would thereby become
impure."
'fhe fifteenth General Regulation require& an Inspector to visit annually each
Lodge In his dlsb'ict. A resolution adopted last year (see 'Proceedings, page 621.),
makes the necessity for visiting Lodges to be determined by the Inspectors, and
"that a Lodge should only be required to pay the expense of an Inspector's visit,
when made at its request." Another resolution (page 587) of last year, requires
every Jnspoctor to report annually to the Grand Master'' the condition of every
Lodge under his snpervlsion, in the matter of working, keeping of books, etc.,
together with such observations and suggestions as may be of interest to the Grand
Lodge." The Grand Lodge cannot expect an Inspector to defray the cost incideni
to Lodge visitations, and while making it imperative that every Lodge should be
visited, it has resolved that the Lodge should !lot be required to pay the expense of
said visitation unless the same is made ai Its request. As a result a conflict has
already arisen between an Inspector and certain I,odges. Another Inspectol', not
being ab!e'to visit Lodges at his own cost, called their attention to the resolution and
requested them to notify him if a visit was desired. No Invitations were re.oeived,
no visits were made, and no report Is had. At present, unless the Lodges desire a
visitation, the chief duty of an Inspector will be to qualify Masters. The necessity
of inspecting a Lodge may properly be left to the discretion of the Inspector. I do
not think such a radical change was contemplated by the committee who framed
the resolutions.
The Inconsistency of the requirement is apparent, It is an
example of what not unfrequently happens as the result of too much or too rapidly
considered legislation. It is recommended that the matter be referred to a special
committee.

The follnwing telegram was received: "Has Hermann Lodge the right to bnry e.
defaulter and suicide?" I replied, "Bermann Lodge will determine If the suicide
was an act of insanity and as to the propriety of interring the deceased defaulter
and suicide with Masonic ho11ors." The Lodge buried its deceased membt>r, who
had confessed the defalcation anD. whose suicide, it is presumed, was the result of
the criminal act, an.d not of insanity. In this c11se I cannot think the unfortunate brother
was entitled to a Masonic burial. His self-accusation made him a criminal, and as
such he would have been subjected to Ma~onlc censure and punishment. His death
did not weaken the fact. The rights of the Frater11lty are to be resp~cted equally
with those of the individual. The compact between the Lodge and the member is
binding, and the guilty ought not to receive thl' respectful consideration awarded to
the innocent. The public wonders at the eqnal distribution of funeral honors, which
H had supposed was the reward of a life of integrity. Falling to comprehend the
apparent inconsistenoy between profession and practice, It oondemns-Iiow unchnrl·
tably, you well know. You have decided" that in the case of a suicide by a Master
Mason In this jurisdiction, the Lodge to which he belonged sh111l determine as to his
inS!Lnity, and as to the propriety of interring him with.Masonic honors." Will It not
be just to prohibit the Masonic Interment of a suicide, which presum·ably wa• occa·
sloned by, or at least associated with, a criminal act ? I leave the subject for you1"
deliberation, asking for it a careful and charitable attentioD~

Stiint Mark's Lodge, No. 85, resolved to change its place of meeting from Oleta
to Plymouth. This was objected to by ])rytowr; Lodge, No. 174 , since Plymouth,
being situate only three miles from Drytown, its proximity would, by a restriction of
jurisdiction, lessen the amount of material , occasion the dimission of some inem hers,
and seriously impair the condition of I>rytown Lodge, whose existence at present is an
effort. As in the formation of a new Lodge it fa a prerequisite to have a recommendation from the nearest or most convenient chartered Lodge, so in equity the principle
should apply to the removal of a Lodge from one town to another ; consequently tho
proposed removal did not receive an approval.
A few days since it was brought to my notice that a Master elect failed to qualify,
was not Installed, and th e Lodge has been directed by the Master of the past year.
Such carelessness, indilference , or cnlpability ought to have future prevention by
legislative enactment. It is therefore recommended that the Constitution be amended
so as to require a Master elect to procure a certificate of qualification and be installed
within sixty days, failing iu which the Lodge shall be r equired to ask for a dispensa·
tion to bold an election for Master.
Union S tar Lodge, No. 320, in New York, wished to confer the degrees u11on an
applicant w.ho did not have the required time of residence, but who could receive the
same provided it had the consent of the Lodge within whose jurisdiction the appll·
cant last resided, it being in accordance with the law of New York. Our Live Oak
Lodge, No. 61, within whose jurisdiction the applicant had resliled, refused consent
on the ground that our Constitution gave no right to grant the request. The :Master
of Union Star Lodge then asked my permission to confer the degrees. In replying,
I stated that our Const:tution requires the applicant for the degrees to have resided
in the State for one year-a prerequisite without qualification, except In the cnee of n.
person belonging to the army or navy; thn.t Lfoe Oak Lodge was right In consider·
ing that it had no power to grant permission, nor was any such power vested in mo
as Grand :Master; and that If Union S tar Lodge wns satisfied to confer the degrees,
1 could have no objection, but I could not grant a permission which Is not enter·
tained nor contemplated In our laws.
Arizona Lodge, U. D., at Phrenix, Arizona Territory, asked if petitions for the
degrees might be received from those who had lived In the Territory only seven or
eight months, but who came from California, where they had resided at the time of
removal. I answered that when the Constitution was adopted the jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge was limited to the State; that had a territorial jurisdiction been
contemplated, doubtless the wording of Sec. 2, A rt. III, Part III, of the Constitution
would have been "a resident within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge," Instead
of "a resident within the State;" and that the intent of the statute is carried out,
if this construction be given, and conseqnently the petitions were authorized to be
receiv ed.
In a case where the petitioner for the degreea was going from place to place, in
each having a temporary residence, the question of jurisdiction arose. It was decided
that it should be determined by citizenship. The place s~lected for his home,
where he intended to vote, 11nd for the period of six months he not having voted else·
where, should ha\•e jurisdiction.

Question. Must not an objection by a member to a visiting brother sitting in a
Lodge come directly from the party raising the objection to the Master of the Lodge,
and not by hearsay ?
.Answer. The Master alone decides as to the validity of the objection. Under
ordinary circumstances no Master should deprive a brother of the right of visitation
upon merely a hearsay objection. The whole matter Is left to the judgment of the
·
Master.
Question. Has a member of a Lodge the right to objeot to a brother visiting
the Lodge, by filing such objection with the Master, without giving his reasons therefor, although the one to whom the objection is made is a member In good standing of
another Lodge ln the same place? Has the brother to whom the objection is made
no redress? Is he not entitled to know why snch objection is made, or must he be
barred from visiting such Lodge, so long as the objection stands, no matter how
unjust, simply to gratify some petty spite or personal grievance?
Answer. A member can object to a brother visiting a Lodge, and give no reasons
for the objection, but the Master to whom the objection is made alone determines
its validity. The Master has to preserve the peace and harmony of his Lodge, and
therefore it is his will that admits or rejects. One ought to believe that no Master
would refuse a brother the privilege of visiting upon an objection made by a member
who declines to give reasons therefor. In support of this assertion, I refer to a subdivision of an ancient landmark, from whloh I quote: "but when admission is refused to 11 Mason in good standing, who knocks at the door of a Lodge as a visitor,
it is to be expected that some good and sufficient reason shall be furnished for thla
violation of what Is, in general, a Masonic right founded on the Landmarks of the
Order."
Question. A brother Mason is arrested, charged with the crime of embezzlement
or grand larceny, and Is acquitted, or the Grand Jury Ml to indict, and he is discharged. Charges are then preferred against him, specifying, as grounds, t11e identical embezzlement or grand hi.rceny for which he was acquitted or discharged. Is not
the record of his acqnittal. or discharge a complete defense ? Can a .Masonic commission fine} a brother guilty of a crime against the State, for which he has been
acqnltted or discharged In a criminal prosecution f Does not the promise that every
Mason has made to obey the Jaws of the land and be a good citizen, estop him from
asserting that a person acquitted 01· discharged by Jaw is gullt7? In an action for
slander or libel, in accusing a person of larceny, tlte defendant Is not allowed by the
laws of this State or of the United States, to go behind the records of the Oourts; can a
M11sonic commission do so?
.An•wer. Ii:t Masonic law It is a settled axiom that every offense committed is an
injury to the Fraternity, inasmuoh that It, at least, reflects discredit on the institution;
hence, an acquittal by a civil court does not prevent the Lodge from investigating the
olfense. T~e accused may be acquitted through some technicality of Jaw, where
release from legal punishment follows, but the " sb11me upon the craft " la not
removed, nor h he free from guilt in the opinion of the community.

Bro. AARON DAVIS PARK, Grand Senior Warden in 1857, and Grand King of the
Grand Chapter In 1869, died at Truckee, In January last. He was also a Past Comma.oder. He was a mechanic; industrious and honest, geni11l In manners, with unaf·
fected kindness of heart, exceeding in generosity, and in nature gentle, charitable,
and humane. As a Mason he w11s essentially zealous and energetic, direct In purpose , untiring in execution, and always ready to assume any post of labor. He held
the respect of the communities in which he lived: and in death is honored for his
loyalty as a Mason and his ·uprightness 11s a citizen.
Bro. JouN R.1.NDOLPH MoCoNN&LL, Past Junior Grand Warden in 1852, died
recently at Denver. He wns a pioneer, a charter memb er of Ne:oada Lodge , No. 18,
an Attorney General of the State, and at one t ime the Democratic n ominee for
Governor. His talents were substantial, he was a cl ose reaRoner, logical, intellect·
ually cultivated and given to research. In temper stern, fixed, fearless , and unyield·
ing, pronounced in his social relations, a good friend, and a devoted husband and
father. His epitaph might be," he was firm, faithful , and true."
A. few words. in conclusion. In the retr ospect of my administration the memories
of social and official Intercourse with the Fraternity throughout the jurisdiction are
laden with kindness, hospitality, and zealous co-operation, and for these exhibition&
of regard, courtesy, and assistance, I tender a grateful recognition. During t he long
tenure of my honorable and responsible office I h11ve ever endeavored to discharge
its duties in a manner oommensumte with the high and Important trusts committed to
my keeping; and for the distinguished honors yun have conferred upon me in the years
·gone by, words are inadequate to express a suitable acknowledgment. If in the
performance of duty ther e was a something too much of expectation, a hope too
highly placed, resultiug from your partial favor, yet I have given to the work my
earnest efforts, with best motives for your Interests, and thus have had a sweetness
of labor and the satisfaction of fulf\lled claims.
In certain decisions I me.y have oocaaioned disappointment, even vexation , but I
have had no intention to wound the feelings of the most sensitive, and these deci·
sions have been arrived at without prejudice and Irrespective of sympathy, by adher·
ing to that which was considered right and equitable; and therefore, the retrospect
occasion& no regret for acts which are yet believed to be for the benefit of the Craft.
Many of my reoommende.tlons have been adopted, as I think, with advantage. For
those which were rejected I have still the a:utbor's desire and hope, with unvarying
respect for the opinions that prevented their realization. In having no temporizing
or evasive pollcy,il have set forth unpleasant facts-facts not beclouded, but rigidly
stated, in order that their real validity 11nd weight might be fully considered, and
that great utility might result. My labors are nearly over, and In their review, see·
ing how they could have bee~ greater aud more effective, I thoroughly realize the
saying that "our deeds are always poorer than our wills."
·
And now I have t o thank the various Inspectors and Grand Officers, who \Jave
been associated with me from time to t ime, for their appreciated aid In facilitating the
execution of the duties of my office, and for the interest evinced In the discharge of
their own peculiar duties.
I specially recognize the important services rendered by the Grand Lecturer. In
making visitations throughout this large jurisdiction he has usually been my travel·
Ing companion, and an intimate relationship thus formed has enabled me to fully

In addif.ion to the foregoing opinions of Inspector W1110HT, I desire to add my
views upon this subject of visitation, in conneC'tion with the resolution of the l118t
Oommnnication-providing that a Lodge should only be required to pay the expenses
of an Inspector's visit, •·when made at its request." I believe the proviso mentioned
to be unnecessary, and not prodootive of good results ; and that the last paragraph
of the resolution virtually nullifies the first-that " the necessity for visiting Lodges
within their respective districts shoul<l be left to the sound discretion of ~e Inspectors." He~e I believe that our legislation should have left it. Most of our Inspectors are brethren of long residence in their respective districts, and of extensive
Masonic· experience. '.!'hey are the best judges of the necessity for visiting the
Lodges placed under their charge; and if, in their " sound discretion," they believe
the necessity exists, the visit should be made with or without the r equest of the
Lodge; and, if made, most certainly the Inspector's expenses should be paid. In
accordance with the oft-expressed wish of the Grand L odge, that our system of inspection should be protected and perpetuated, I most earnestly recommend tile revision of the resolution referred to, an,d that the proviso which leaves the subject to
the wiII er discretion of the Lodges be stricken out.
Inspector JOHN Q. ADAMS reports, in detail , the condition o' the t.en Lodges comprising the Sixteenth District. He says that the officers generally are proficient in
their duties, and work well together. Everything ap:riears to run smoothly in bis
district. One Lodge, which had conferred but one degree during the year, and that
in a creditable mann~r, appears to be la.boring under great disadvantages. It appears
that m ost of the members reside on the line of the railroad which conveys them to
the plo.ce where the Lodge is located. The train usually arrives a t hall-past eigM
o'clock, P. v . Nothing can be done until its arrival, which makes it nearly nine
o'clock before they get to work; and, as m ost of the members reside a t a. distanoe of
from three to seven miles, the result is that by the time the Lodge is engaged in
work, it is time for tliem to return home. He says it is difficult at limes to get
enough members together to open the Lodge, and he fears that unless some change
is made soon, the Lodge will be compelled to surrender its charter.
Inapector TnoMAS 0. PocxHAN, of the Seventeent!J, District, reports having visited most of the Lodges under his supervision. Great improvement had been made
in the work, and harmony prevailed. He especially compliments Baoramer•to Lodge,
No. 40, for the masterly manner in which the thirddegreewae oonferredon the evening
of his visit.

Inspector EDWAllD R. HEDGES reports having visited all the Lodges in the Twentieth District, except two. Those located in the midst of large and permanen~ populations are steadily increMing in numbers. The others are not. The officers of

fication of the work in several Lodges, and W118 plea.."6d with the manner in which it

ALABAMA.
The fifty-eighth Aunual Communication of the Grand Lodge of this jurisdiction
was commenced in the city of Montgomery, on the secC'nd day of December,
1878, -the M.". w.-. HENRY CLAY ARMSTRONG, Grand Master, presiding, and tbe R.-.
W.'. j)ANIEL SAYRE being Grand Secretary. '.l'wo hundred and sixteen Lodges were
repr.es"nted.
The Address of Grand Master .ARMSTHONG is well written, of very reasonable
length, and full of good advice and sound Masonic doctJ:ine. Thanks are appropriately
rendered to a merciful Providence for general exemption from the plague that
almost decimated parts of neighboring jurisdictions. Brethren of Alabama bad, bow·
ever, generously and heroically volunteered themselves as helps to their nftlicted
brotherhood elsewhere, and bad been faithful in their work, even unto death.
Masonry ln the jurisdiction was prosperous, peace and harmony everywhere prevailing. He bad declined a request to call a special Communication o'r the Grand
Lodge to entertain a measure intended to "provide an endowment .to the Master
Mason's degree, to he paid to the heirs of all Master Masons who pattlcipated in the
scheme." He approved of the law, but thought it could be as well considered at the
.Annual Communication. The matter was referred to a seleot committee, who had
leave to report thereon at the n~xt Communication.
We note several of the decisions of the Grand Master. One was that "not less
than seven Master Masons can hold a Lodge. " What will our" three Master Mason"
friends say to this?
.Again: "General worthlessness and the repulalion of a common liar is good
cause for preferring charges, and If sustained, the brother is unworthy of Masonic
protection and should be expelled.'' We should think as much.
Again: "Anything that contravenes the moral law is unmasonic. Habitual
drunkenness being immoral, Is therefore unmesonic . Temperance is oue of t he car·
dinal virtues of our institution, and its observance ought to be rigidly enforced by the
subordinate Lodge." The Grand Master's bead is level on that point.
He denounced, in just and severe terms, the atbeistical course of the Grand
Orient of France. He says: "This action on tbe part of the Grnnd Orient of ~'ranee I
firmly believe to be subversive of many principles which, from the earliest period of
Masonry to the present time, have been the beauty and glory of the Order, end I must
say that I am appalled at the evils which may result from it unless it everywhere
receive the unqualified disapprobation It so well deserves.''
The name of " High-log Lodge," was changed to "Hopewell Lodge." What's in
a'Dame?
The Committee on " suspensions, appeals etc.," reported on several cases before
them, al¥1 then gave some plain advice as to tile prevalence of drunkenness and pro·
fanity among the ~aft. They recommended "that it be considered and held to be a
su11lcient cause for arresting the charter. of any subordinate Lodge, that the said

Grand Lodge was calied on again, the M.-. W.-. JOHN F. HILL, Grand Master, presld·
Ing, and the R.-. W.-. LUKE E. BillBER being Grand Secretary. One hundred and
twenty Lodges were represented.
The Address of the Grand Master was short and to the point. While the two
political parties had been engaged in earnest contest, no ill feelings therefrom had
orept into the Lodges. Although the jurisdiction had been abundantly blessed with
health, yet death bad summoned away some prominent members of the Craft. Bros.
JoNATH.lN W. JORDAN, Past D. D. Grand Master,and WILLIAM H. BUTTON, Past Grand
Lecturer, had passed to the unseen world. The Grand Master, on his own authority,
had forwarded four hundred dollars of the Grand Lodge funds for the relief of the yellow
fever sufferers in Memphis. St. J obn's College was reported in a prosperous condi·
tion. It was educating some tw~nty-llve benellciaries, children of deceased brethren,
who had been appointed there by the Grand Master. There was a debt hanging over
the College, whicl1 he recommended the Grand Lodge to pay. Ht! had granted dispensations for the establishment of fifteen new Lodges. The relations with all the
Grand Lodges of the United States and Territories were pleasant. "We hail them,''
says the Grand Master," as brethren, North, Sontb, East and West, and greet them
a Happy New Year, and may the God of Heaven bless their charities extended to the
yellow fever sufferers of the United States "-to all which we say Amen.
Past Grand Master ENGLISH, President of the Board of Trustees of St. John's
College, submitted a detailed report of its operations during the year. It had been
no charg~ upon the Grand Lodge, the Board of Trusteeij being happy to report that
"from the resources of the corporation they were able to support the institution for
the ensuing collegiate yea,r, pay all the current expenses, carry the usual number of
free students, meet the interest upon the c9llege debt promptly as it matured, and
pay $1,000 of tho prlaclpal." Be adds the following paragraph, which approaches
sarcasm:. And now, since the Grand J,odge has decided no longer to donate lte surplus
revenue to the College, but to appropriate It to other purpoaes, It Is to be hoped,
as the Colle11:e costs the Grand Lodge nothing and is Oil burden upon It, the Grand
Mast~r and Grand Orators will cease to speak dolefully of it, and no more call it an
" eleJJhant," but that all Masonic Bodies, und all Masons, as well BB friends of education, will cheerfully award to it moral encouragement and support; aud may the
time come when t.he whole Craft will join with multltudlnons people In clapping
their hands and hailing it as a shining light In the field of education.
This College has always been a pet of Bro. ENGLISH, and we offer him our congratulations that it still lives and grows, giving good promise of a vigorous and longlived manhood.
Bro. HENKY HEMPSTE.lD delivered a fine oration, in which he discussed the qnestion
of "the strength of voluntary associations." He maintained, and successfully as
well as eloquently, these two positions :Fi,.st.-That to make voluntary associations successful, it is necessary tbat the
individuals comprising them should enter into the oause with their utmost zeal.
s~cond.-That to keep them stroi..g, it is necessary that the members thereof
should be actuated by high and pure principles.
We' give the clo~lng paragraph of this line address, as follows:Masonry has come down to us with certain ancient forms which we must ever
keep in view, certain ancient landmarks which we must constantlv run bHck to, to
guide our walk. Let us not transmit it to our successors lowered and belittled from
its objects and in its usurances, because of .our want of wutchrulness as to who
enters, and our want of zeal in its behalf. Let us support it with an earnest warmth,
and let us see that none enter but those whose characters will prove a guaranty that
they will do Hkewlse ; anii we will prove ourselves worthy links to knit the generations past and to come, and worthy to have basked.in "that hieroglyphic light that
none but Craftsmen ever saw."
One of the Past District Deputy Grand Masters, a certain Bro. ARMSTRONG, bad
"gone to Texas," owing the Grand Lodge over two hundred dollars which he bad

[Oct. 14,

collected from Lodges in his district and appropriated to his own use. Charges of
unmasonic conduct were made against him, and he was summoned to stand trial i.t
the next Annual Communication.
A certain brother, FLA vrus C. HARVEY by name, asked redress from the action or
his Lodge, which had sentenced him to a three years suspension for "raising a fuss
with Bro. WILLIAM CRIBBS, and nearly pnshing him otf a bridge in anger." They do
occasionally have some queer trials in our sister jurisdictions, and perhap.! also in
California.
Bro. R. L. DODGE, who for many yeare, and until his health failed, had been an
active and energetic Mason, and for twenty-five years Grand Treasurer of the Grand
Lodge, was by an unanimous vote constir.uted an honorary member of that body.
The Report of the Committee on Correspondence was submitted by Bro. GEORGE
E. DODGE. It covers nearly ninety pages of the proceedings and is well and
tersely written, though our brother felt and half complained that he was working in
a strait jacket. California for 1877 receives a liberal notice. He compliments Grand
Master BROWNE in high terms, quoting largely from his Address and remarking that
he had marked twelve other places for comment, but" lack of space" forbade, Bro.
DODGE rather likes that idea llf the "clam-bake," and more than hint~ that he would
·like to have been there. He thinks that" all were happy as clams, except the olams
themselves."

The Grand Master, in his Address, after rendering due thanks to Almighty God
for his mercies during the year, announced the death of Past Grand Master ROBERT
BURNABY, in England, whither he had gone in the hope that his failing health
might be re-established. "His life," says the Grand Master, " had been devoted to the happiness of his fellow men, end he died, as he had lived, an honored
member of the Order wbich he loved." The four Lodges in Victoria had been consolidated into two; 11 wise act, in his opinion. Steps had been taken towards, and a
contract made, for the erection of a Masonic Temple in Victoria, the estimated cost
to be $8 ,500.
The Deputy Grand Master also submitted a report of considerable length, mainly
devoted to his efforts to secure subscriptions for the new 'femple, in which he had
been eminently successful.
The salary of the Grand Secretary was fixed at $150 per annum. We hope the
afflicted brother is not compelled to devote his whole time to the affairs of the Craft.
The M.-. w... ELI HARBISON was elected Grand Master and the R ... w... ELI
HARRISON, Jr., was re-elected Grand Secretary. A rare spectacle. this of fatlfer and
son holding these principal offices at the same time.

A Special Communication was held in Victoria. on the twenty-second day of April

twenty-eighth day of October, to consecrate the building. Our Columbia brethren,
it is evident, did not permit .much grass to grow under their feet dnring
the progress of this work. The Temple cost about $2,000 more than the estimate
as given in the Grand Master's Address.

CANADA.

The twenty-third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Canada was held
in the city of Toronto on the eleventh day of September, 1878,-the M.·. W.·, W. H.
WELLE!!., Grand Master, "on the throne," and the
JOHN J. MASON being
Grand Secretary. Two hundred and thirty-four Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master, in his Address, stated that eleven Special Communications had
been held during the year, four of which were called to lay the corner-stones or
churches, four to constitute new Lodges, and three to dedicate new halls. He had
Issued dispensations for the formation of eight new Lodges. The finances or the
Grand Lodiie were in a satisfactory condition, the receipts having exceeded the
expenditures by more than twelve hundred dollars, and there being a reserve fund
to the amount of $60,000. He regretted that difficulties had arisen between the
Grand Lodges of Quebec and Scotlaud. He hpped that the breach would soon be
closed, and did not think it best for the Grand Lodge of Canada to intel'fere.
The Grand Lodges of Spain, Egypt, and Cuba had asked for formal recognition and
exchange of representatives. The first two were thus favored, but action on the
rival claims in Cuba was postponed until more definite information could be
obtained. The Grand Master pointedly condemned the atheistical action of the
Grand Orient of France, and had withdrawn the credentials of lh.e representative
near that body.

The Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence take issue with the Grand Master as to

specifically granted them by their particular Grand Lodge, or extended to them by

Alluding to the suffering among brethren In other jurisdictions on account of the
yellow fever, the Grand Master stated that he had advanced $400 from the Grand
Lodge funds, and regretted that owing to the financial state of the treasury he
oould not have advanced more. He discusses at some length the matters at variance
between the Grand Lodges of Quebec and Scotland, and is not clear In bis own mind
whether the latter had not the strict right to do what it has done, as it occopled the
territory of the Province of Quebec before the Grand Lodge of Quebec was formed.
We hardly think that this will hold water when fairly tested, but, like the Grand'
Master, we express the hope that the "matter may receive careful and deliberate
consideration" from ell the Grand Lodges. He recommends that the Grand Lodge
of the Indian Territory should be recognized, and that the Lodge therein, still bold·
Ing allegiance to Kansas, be advised to transfer the same to the new Grand Lodge.
This view was concurred in by the Grand Lodge, and thus that little speck of war
11 removed from that part of the horizon. He pays glowing tributes to the memory
of Past Deputy Grand Master JOHN W. S111ITH and Past Grand Master ANDREW J.
WHEELER, of Tennessee, who had fallen at his post while laboring to allevide the
ravages of the yellow fever at Memphis.

eloquence, replete with beautifol Imagery and instruction In the hidden meanings of
the Mystic Art." We can well believe that, for we remember on one occasion liitenlng to that illustrious brother in an address of three hours' length, and no one wished

In 1870 the north wing of the building was completed and dedicated by the Grand
Lodge. All the available room "was soon filled by the widows and orphans for
whose benefit it was intended." The Fraternity, and especially those in Louisville,
Immediately went to work to insure the completion of the whole building, and the
ladies, by their efforts, contributed many thousands to that noble work. In June,
1875, a tornado nearly destroyed the whole work, but the Masons of the city and
State were equal to the emergency, and the completed structure was solemnly
dedicated on this day. The address, asking for the dedication, gives the history of
the work and what has been done, so fully, that we clip the major po.rt thereof:On the nineteenth day of October, 1869, the corner-stone of this building was
laid by the Grand Lodge of Kentucky, Grand Master E. S. FITCH officiating. One
year later, on the eighteenth of October, 1870, the north wing of the building, having
been completed, was dedicated by the Grand Lodge, Grand Master CHARLES EGIN·
TON officiating; since which time sunshine and shower have marked the Home's
career.
It bad been determined, as soon as one wing was finished, to rapidly push forward
the work to completion, and satisfactory progress was making in tha~ dire?ti?n until
the second day of June, 1875, when, during a severe storm, the me.m butldrng "'.as
blown down and the magnificent towers damaged to such an exlent as to requtre
them to be taken down.
'.rhat was indeed a trying hour in our history. On the morning of June third, ~he
directors, with many friends of the Home, w.ire gathered here go.zing npon the rums
with sad hearts. The board was convened for consultation, and the first thing done
was to offer pre.ver to the Almighty God, led by the venerable Dr. HELM. Supplication w•s made to our Heavenly Father to direct and connsel those intrusted with the
management. Thus inspired, the board began a.new its labors, and a ge~erou~ J<'ra·
ternity nobly responding, the entire structl!re has been completed, standm~ with its
splendid proport10ns before you to-day. Su, we feel grateful to God for this result,
and thankrul for the liberality of the Fraternity and our friends.
Much good bas already been accomplished. Two hundred and twenty.four wid·
owed and orphaned ones have been thus far admitted, of whom one hundred and
twenty-three remain to-day. Much greater results awe.it the future history of the
Home, as it will accommodate, when furnished and sufficiently endowed, from four
to five hundred widows and orphans.
•
This is a. great and glorious work, but one that can only succeed as it shoul~, by a
united effort upon the po.rt of the entire Fraternity of the State, While calling to
mind the princely liberality of the Grand Lodge toward the Institution, onr hearts
11re saddened by the recollection that some of the veterans in the cause have been
co.lied away. Among these we recall the noble SWIGERT, McCoRKLE and others, and
but recently our beloved associate 0. HENRY FINCK. They have gone from labor
to reward; but the work must not cease. We pray God to raise up others who may
ever be ready to plead for the widow and orphan.
Sir, I perceive that this reference and these surroundings deeply stir your feelings.
It is ri,,ht and proper that it be so, as you are interested in an institution that bas caused
a wid;w to say: " I thank God for the Home. I will never cease to pray to Him to
bless the Masons of Kentucky for providing such a home for my child-so much bet·
ter one than I could provide for her myself." Or, as upon another occasion, when
death's shadows were gathering over a dear Christian mother, and gloomy fo~ebod·
lngs and anxiety filled her mind as to the future of her three interesting clnldren,
and her fears had well-nigh yielded to despair, it was said to her: "Be of good cheer;
your little ones will find a welcome In the Me.sonic Widows' and Orphans' Home at
Louisville." That message irradiated her countenance and dispelled her fears. She
was a. Mason's widow, and it was the privilege of a. brother Mason to calm and make
tranquil her dying moment by these word~ of love. If angelic ones a.re permitted to
blend with us in our rejoicings, perchance that mother, in company with the beloved
MoCoRKLE and others, is about us now in our exultation at the fe.ct'that the templed
Home of widowhood and orphanage ls completed.
For ages po.st Masonic tledications of public buildings have been customary., Th~
honored Fraternity you represent has often performed this work; and to-day It he.1
been delegated to me by my associate directors, who for the time being are intrusted
with the management and control of one of the greatest charities of the age., to pre·
sent to you, in their no.me, and through you to the Me.sons of Kentucky, this large
edifice, erected by their liberalit7, for consecration to God and the sacred co.use of
charity. Our brothers in other Jurisdictions have reared grand and imposing str.u~­
tures. The magnificent temples of New York, Philadelphia, and elsewhere, ehc1t
the admiration of the beholder while gazing upon their stately columns, tall towers
and domes-standing as prond monuments of architectural glory and beauty.

MANITOBA.
Our brethren of this "Frozen North" jurisdiction send us their compliments, in
the shape of the proceedings of the third Annual Communication or this Grand
Lodge held in the oity of Winnipeg on the twelfth day or June, 1878,-the M.·. W.·,
GEORGE F. NEWCOMB, Grand :Master, pl'esldlng, and the R.·. W:. JOHN H. BELL being

The Address of the Grand Master Is very long and quite unique as to its com po"
1ltion. He congratulates the Craft upon the harmony that prevailed throughout the .
Jurisdiction, and hoped that the disturbing elements that had developeiJ themselves
at previous Communications might not again present themselves. He gives a brief
history of the establishment of Freemasonry and uf the Grand Lodge in this
remote section of the Dominion of Canada. A Lodge we.s first iastltuted in 186i, by
the Grand Lodge of :Minnesota, but that Lodge ceased to work a short time prior to
the " Red River Rebellion," and loaned or gave its regalia and jewels to a new Lodge
at Lower Fort Garry. When the Hudson Bay Company, in 1877, transferred its
territory to the Dominion of Canada, the "Red River Settlement," as it was called,
wa s constituted into a Province, to be called Manitoba, and the Grand Lodge of
Canada assuming jurisdiction, soon after issued charters to Prince Rupert and Li$·
gar Lodges. When the N orthern Light Lodge-chartered by Minnesota-became
extinct it" numbered twenty-three members, who have since scattered In various
directions. Some have gone to break the bread of life to perishing and weary souls
In connection with the Church of England ; others to legislate for the Province in
the House of Commons, and some have gone the way of all the earth, to that undiscovered country from whose bourne no weary traveler returns." He alluded to the
difficulties that had prevented some of the Lodges from being as bright and useful
as they might and should be. These difficulties OI' evils were t.11e following:First. Unintelligent voting upon the application of cand idates.

The duties of my vocation, together with the compulsory amount of attention

We have also'reoeived a pamphlet purporting to contain the proceedings of the
Grand Lodge of Manitoba at its third and fourth Annual Communications. But upon
'examination we find the same to be only the version of the recent difficulties in that
Grand Lodge, as given by the expelled malcontents. We are too far off to judge of
the fairness or truth of the complaints made by these brethren, but as we have only
official intercourse with the Grand Lodge of Manitoba, we can, of course, hold none
with those it denounces as unworthy' and as having been expelled from its association. We can therefore take no further notice of this pamphlet, except to express
the earnest wish that these unfortunate quarrels may be soon ended and that peace
and harmony may again prevail among these semi-arctic brethren.
Since writing the above we have received from our Grand Secretary the annexed official proclamation from the Grand Master of Manitoba, which conveys to us
the pleasing intelligence that all is once more quiet and serene among our hyperborean brethren. So mote it be:-

and obligatftms which those vows imposed upon them; viz.: the "Order of Dru id-, "

Jesuits ," which was founded to fight for the glory of God against all infidels, etc., etc.
The various classes of Roman Catholics, grouped into separnte eooletles, under differ·

from all classes of society, and the assumption of its vows does not require se para·

NEW JERSEY.
The ninety-second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of New Jersey
was held in the city of Trenton on the twenty-second day of January, 1879,-the
M.-. W.-. MARSHALL B. SMITH, Grand ~hster, presiding, 11nd the R.·. W.-. JOSEPH H.
Hoi;an being Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from one hundred
and thirty-t.wo Lodges.

The Grand Master and Junior Grand W11rden of the jurisdiction of Pennsylvania,
being present, were formally Introduced and received with the usual Grand honors.
Grand Master SMITH read an able and well written Address. Grateful for the
honor conferred upon him, by an election for three successive years, be had striven
to the best of his ability to discharge the duties of the office faitbfnlly, and, as be
hoped, to the satisfaction of the Craft. Dispensation had been granted for the
esta blisbment of one new Lodge. On the one hundredth anniversary of ·t he battle
of Monmouth, (June 28, 1878,) he bad 6ffi.ciated at the laying of the corner-stone of
a monument to be erected to the memory of the " heroic Craftsmen who under the
burning sun of a June day, one hundred ye11rs ago, struck a decisive blow in
defense of colonial rights and human liberty." From a casual notice in the Grand
Master's Address, we infer that this latter day was about as hot a~ its predecessor,
for he complained of the undue length of the march, made the more fatiguing from
the intense heat. Dut he tritely remarks that " two of my predecessors "in the
office of Grand Master having borne the beat and burdens of the day, in defense of
our liberties, on June 28th, 1778, It was a privilege to assist in paying even this tardy
tribute to their wisdom and Masonic worth aft.er the lapse of a hundred years."
In the addre~s delivered by the Grand Master, at the laying of the corner stone, we
also find these items, which we give for the benefit of our own readers:Especially as Masons have we a right to honor this day and its associations. Our
institution, planted on the soil of New Jersey fn 1730, has, for ne11rly one hundred and
fifty years , embraced within its number great and brave and good men of this Commonwealth. Every General (so far B• kuown) in the bbtorio battle at Monmouth
Court House was a Craftsman ti'ied and true ; one of them wa• afterward Governor
of New Jersey and !;rand Me.ster of Masons, and ~wo others were also Grand Ma•ters of New Jersey. Of the twenty-seven Governors New Jersey has bad, fourteen
have been or are members of our Fraternity, and seven of them, beginning with
Governor RICHARD HowstL, uotive officers or members of our Grand Lodge. The
first Gr11nd Master of New .Jersey after the Re volution was the Hon. D.1.vm BnlilAR·
LEY, UWef Justice of the State, who, with distinguished abilfty, governed the Craft
as !;rand Master for four years (from 1786to1790 inclusive.) In Olive Branch Lodge,
St. J ohn's Lodge, and in many other old bistorio Lodges of this jurisdiotion, soldiers
and otliceu of the Revolntlon held the gavel and ruled the labors of the Craft.
Thus the history of Freemasonry in New JerseJ' is linked with the patriotic record
of the Commonwealth ; and to-day we weld another llnk as, in the presence of our
honored Chief Magistrate and hi• immediate predecessors-true Craftsmen all-we
symbolize our loyalty to the State and our reverence for the heroic dead, In this perfe ct asl1lar that, bedded In the courses laid by the hands of operative Mason~. shall
be a memorial, to the centuries yet unborn, of the undimmed p11trlotlsm of New
Jersey, and of the loyalty of our time-honored institution. Amid the bo()mlng of
arti1lery, the measured trend of soldiery, and the gathering host of bistorlo a111pcia·
tions, we of the great Masonic Brotherhood c11n he11r the voice of the God who tules
In the camp as by the fireside, in the State as in the family, proclaiming "Pe~ on
earth;" and even at this boar, on this old historic battle-field, we look forwtWll joyously to the day
"Wh~n forever
War's dread banners shall be furled,
And the angel Peace be welcomed
As Regent of the world."

OREGON.
The Grand Lodge of Oregon-Bro. CHADWICK objects to the title," webfoot"

The Gran<l Master submitted 'an Address, well written and of moderate dimensions.
During the year he had visited about two-thirds of the Lodges in the jurisdiction, and.
with few exception•, found them enjoying a degree of prosperity that would
compare favorably with any former year of the existence of the Grand Lodge. He
recommended that the •ea! of condemnation by the Grand J.odge be placed upon
the atheistic revolutionists of the Grand Orient of France. Dispensations had been
granted for the formation of two new Lodges. We note two of his decisions, the
first of which arose out of a novel state of things, and we give it In full:In December, 1875, A. petitioned for the degrees; hi• petition took the usual
course and he was duly elected. On presenting himself for initiation It wns ascertained that" his faith was not .well founded," and he was refused the deJ?reeP. In
July, 1877, he again petitioned the Lodge. The question arose," What Is his statue,
and is it nece"sary to again spread the ballot?"
An.~wer. In this jurisdiction the law requires one year to elapse bP.foro a rejected
candidate can renew his petition. It r~quires him to s11bmlt his petition in the UPUlll
form , and it most take the regular course as tr no previous petition had heen before
the Lodge from the same person. Now, the law will not step In and di•crlminate
between one who had been rejected by ballot and one who had been rejected by
force of law, by granting the latter an immunity from an ordeal through which it
says the former must pass. A. Is, to all Intent~ and purposes, a rejected candidate.
Hence, I am clearly of the opinion the ballot should be spread.
In the second decision the ruling Is different from our praotice In California, and,
wlt.h all due respect to our brethren of the North, we believe our own practice to be
the best:An unfavorable report by a minority or majority of the committee does not of
Itself reject the petitioner when the Lodge has acquiriid jurisdiction over the candl·
date. The only way to dispose of bis petition is by the ballot.
The Grand Master calls the attention of the Grand Lodge to the ract that its expenses far exceed its means, and suggests immediate measures to remedy this fault.

worded resolutions condemnatory of the Grand Orient of ~'ranee. We give two of
the most important:Res0lved, That all subordinate J,odgee nnder the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge
are strictly enjoined not to admit as visitors, or to treat in any manner as true And
lawful brethren. any professed Masons who mav come to us from such Lodges as
either deny or ignore the existence of God or the immortality of the soul. [The
types before us say," immorality of the son)," but we venture to make the correction .]
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge commends, as worthy of all honor, the aclion of
the seventy-six subordinate Lodges under the jurisdiction of the Grand Orient of
!<'ranee, who protes.ted against the unrighteous action of their Grand Body.

fact that "Elgin Lodge" had been officially ioformedThat in opening fraternal relations with the Grand Lodge of Quebec, they could

up, and will not repeo.t the same now. The reader may consider all that as done
already, and will excuse us if our review partakes somewhat of the hash of the
original.
The pamphlet before us is neatly printed and is ornamented by two fine engravings, one of Grand Master COTLER, and the other of the long time Grand Chaplain,
the Rev. Bro. HENRY W. Rooo. We like the looks of the latter, and, as he will be at
the head of the Correspondence Oominitree this year, shall look for a report that
will not belie that splendi4 eye and moustache, and massive forehead. We are only
sorry that our brother "parts his hair in the middle,'' but then absolute perfection
can hardly be expected in this imperfect and sinful world.
We have first an ebborate report of the proceedings of a Special Communication
held in Providence on the sixteenth day of October, 1877 , for the purpose of dedi·
eating the "Roger Williams Monument,'' recently erected in that city of his founding. Grand Master Cut'LER presided, and right well did he perform his allotted work.
We were somewhat surprised, however, at the statement that all this Grand Lodge
work was done in the Entered Apprentice degree. "We have no such custom " in
California, certainly. There was an immense turnout on this occasion:Among the Lodge furniture were two fragmentR of the famous slate rock on which
RooEB WILLIAMS landed, in the form of a rough and perfect ashlar. The former
bears the inscription, "What Cheer Rock, quarried May 2, A. L. 5860 ·" and the
latter, " This ashlar was taken from the rock on which RooER WILLIAMS, the founder
of Providence, first landed, A. D. 1636, when he was greeted by the Indian salutation, •What Cheer.'"
These ashlars belong to" What Cheer Lodge," chartered in 181i7, and are some 31!
inches high, 25 inches wide, 27! inches thick, We have a full page view of the Monu·
meat: "A figure of history In classic drapery, standing on the upper step, is writing
with a stylos upon the front tablet in plain script, the words, 'RooER WILLIAMS,
1636.'" And crowning the whole Is the statue of WILLIAMS himself. During the cere·
monies an eulogy on Masonry was delivered by Grand Chaplain Rooo. From the
address of the Chairman of the Committee on Parks, we gather this item of lnforma·
tion :._
We are now upon land once owned by RooE11 WILLIAMS, and bequeathed to the
city of Providence by Miss BETSY WrLLI!MS, his great, great, great grand-daughter.
The love she bore for the city her ancestor founded, and her reverence for bis mem·
ory, prompted this bequest, by which she prescribed that this tract of'land, which
containsl.about one hundred acres, might be fornver kept for public uses and be
known as "Roger Williams Park."
•
She died In 1871, the bequest was accepted by the city In 1872, and in 1874. the
design was adopted and the work on the monument commenced.
An elaborate historical oration was delivered by Professor J. LEwIB DIHAN, of
Brown Unive1·sity, from which we would be pleased to make liberal quotations. He
discusses at length the course and acts of WrLLIAll!B, and of the Plymouth Colony
saints who drove him into exile. WILLIAMS first commenced his settlement on the
wrong side of the Blackstone river, but on receiving another warning from those who
had made Boston too hot for him, he selected the present site of Providence, and
there commenced a city that has always delighted to do him honor. The Professor
evidently desires to say a good word on behalf of WILLIAMS' persecutors, and more
than hints that political reasons had as much to do as religious ones, on both sides. But
we will not follow him further in his argument. His oration will repay a perusal.
He defends WILLIAMS from the charge of COTTON MATBEll that he "had a windmill in
his head," i.e., was very vacillating. And yet he admits that though he became a
Baptist and started that denomination in Rhode Island, he subsequently withdrew
from their communion, and lived for the. rest of his dayij isolated f1 om all visible
church fellowship. Yet all must admit that he was a good, if not a great man, and
laid deep the foundations of civil and religio11s liberty, which his persecutor& talked
so mur.h about, and yet illustrated so little In their actual practice.

Pe.st Grand Master W1u1:0T G. DE SAUSSURE, having been requested so to do at
the last Annual Commonication, delivered an able, and we may well call it an
exhaustive address on the first establishment of Masonry in So uth Carolina and
other States. We have read this address with deep interest, and would like to make
copious extracts therefrom, that our readers might be equally pleased; but our
limited space will only permit the insertion of the closing paragraphs, which contain the ore.tor's summing up of all his facts and conclusions:After carefully examining the addressee of the M.'. W.'. Bro. PERCIVAL LOWELL
EvERETT and the R.-.
Bro. LEVI WOODBURY, and the early history of the Grand
Lodges of Pennsylvania and New York, I am obliged to believe thatthe senior continuous Grl\nd Lodge on the continent of North America, is that of Masse.chnsetts, whose
St. Joh n's Grand Lodge was organized in 1733, and on 5th March, 1791!, united with
the Massachusetts Grand Lodge, organized in 1769. The Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, organized in 1732, under a warrnnt from tbe Grand Lodge of England, ceased
to exist about 1793, and never united with the Grand Lodge which we.~ organized
under a warrant granted 20th June, 1764, by the Urand Lodge of England, according
to the Ancient Constitutions. The Grand Lodge of New York could not have been
organized earlier than the latter part of December, 1737, and appears to have become.
extinct about 1776, an'd a new Provincial Grand L Bdge warrant was granted 5th
September, 1781, and is that referred to in the report of the committee on 5th June,
1787. I have been unable to obtain access to the early history of Freemaaonr;r in
Virginia, but in MA.o~v's Encyclopedia it is stated that no Urand Lodge WllJI orgalllzed
before 1778. If my reasoning is correct in regard to the Grand Lodge of South
CMolina, it is tbe second senior continuous Grand Lodge on the continent of North
America. Wbile, then, in all probability, the first L<>Qge of Freemasons organized
in North America was that which met at the I;i:oop, .Water street, Philadelphia, in
1730, and the first c;rand Lodge organized, was that Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania,
which in 1732 elected WiLLIAM ALLEN as Its Grand Master, yet two, at least, of its
sister jurisdiction1, viz.: Massachusetts and Sooth Carolina, outr~uk Pennsylvania
in coutinoous Grand Lod¥es·
As a conclusion of this sketch of the early history of Ancient Freemasonry in
South Carolina, 1 desire to summarize It 11s follows: The first Lodge constituted jn
Sooth Carolina was Solomon's Lodge, No. 1, on 28th October, 1730. A Provincial
Grand Lodge was conatituted some time between that date and 20th Augnst, '1737.
Such Provincial Grand Lodge is traceable io the Gazettes until 1748, when, probably
for the reasons assigned by Bro. MACKEY, it disappears unt!l 1754. When it reappears
in tbat year, It does so with some of the same officers as were found in It in 1743.
It is then, with occasional hie.ti , traced untll 1774. Io 1776 it is fonnd, sum moned by
"order of the Grnnd Lodge," and desiring the attendance of all brethren throughout
this StaU!. In 1777 it installed BARNARD ELLIOTT as Grand Master of Masons in this
State. In Ootober, 1778, his funeral Is attended by the Society of Freemasons, of
which he was Grand Master. A silence then occurs until December, 1781, when It Is
again summoned a~ the Provincial Grand r,adge (South Caroliua then being overrun
by the British troops), and JoeN Dus is .elected as Provincial Grand Master. In
1783 the same body reappears as th·e Grand Lodge of the State, and JOHN DEAS is
elected the Grand Master. From 1783 to 1817 ft continues to be found, although
from 1787 to 1817 there is also a l'ival Grand Lodge. In 1817 there ls an union of
these rival Grand Lodges, on the same principles which governed io Massachmaette In
1792, and in England in 1818. From 18l7 to this date , it bas continued with its united
rival, as the Grand Lodge of Ancient Freemasons of South Carolina. This appears
to be such a connection and continuance with the Grand Lodge constituted in 1737,
as to entitle ii to oiaim 1737 as the date of the organization of the Urand Lodge of
South Carolina. It was tbe legitimate snccessor of the Provincial Grand Louge,
and became independent in December, 1776 .. aocording to the principles laid down
by eminent Masonic authorities, I therefore respect.fully claim that the Grand
Lodge of Allcient Freemasons of South Carolina, is, lo continuous sucoessioo, Chll
second in rank of the Grand Lodges of the United States, the Grand Lodge of ~lair

We have waited and wafted for this full fruition of our hopes; we have put our

throb quicker under its mystic influence. It holds out such inducements to be men

any evil deeds-but little lower than the angels-living and dying faithful to their
trust. Yea, my brethren, obey Implicitly the teaching of our Great Light, and abide
ever by the principles of our institution, and your lives will stand 11s a beacon of
light to the coming generations of craftsmen, and your paths will be the " paths of
peace."

WASHINGTON.
Our brethren of the North held their twenty-first Annual Communication in the
city of Olympia on the eighth day· of June, 1878,-the M.·. W.·. ROBERT CROSBY
HILL, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. THOMAS M. REED being Grand
Secretary. Twenty-two Lodges were represented.
The Address of Grand Master HILL fills sixtee~ pages of the proceedings; but
a great part is taken up with a discussion of some local differences of opinion as to
certain features of the Jaw of the jurisdiction. We find not many items calling for a
general notice. He gives some advice in the opening, which will do good if' followed
elsewhere. Speaking of the appropriate business of the Grand Lodge, he says:There should be no hobbies to ride, no axes to grind. The Grand Lodge is no
place for the gratification of selfi•h motives. When we cross its threshold to parti·
cipate in its labors, we should divest ourselves, as nearly as we can, of selfish and
mercenary promptings, strive to forget personal prejudices, bickeriags and animosi·
ties, and to repress personal ambitions and aspirations to accomplish ends and aims.
Yea, verily! worshipful Grand Master, but do they? Not always, we fear. Dispensations had been granted for two new Lodges. As a matter of rhetorical taste,
we wish the Grand :Master would not use the word "said '' quite so often ; we
counted it eleven times in one short paragraph, which is just eleven times too many.
A resolution adopted at the previous Communication required each Lodge to
furnish each candidate raised to the third degree of Masonry with a :Master Mason's
diploma, "the cost of which shall be included in the initiution fee." The practical
result seemed to bring this into confiict with a provision of the Grand Lodge Constitution, and the Grand Master discusses the matter at some length, and suggests
some modification of the resolution or a change of the Constitution.
A certain Lodge having initiated and passed o. candidate "who had lost the middle
finger of' his right hand," the subject matter of raising him was submitted to the
Grand Lodge at the last Communication, which referred it and the general subject of
maims and defects to the Grand Master; and he also submitted another question as to
w.hether a known gambler or the keeper of a dram shop could be said to come "under
the tongue of good report." 'l'he Grand Master discusses both questions at great
length, deciding the first against all maims or defects ; the second, he thinks, must
be thrown upon the responsibility of each Lodge to determine on the parties whose
case comes before it. He is not afraid, however, to give bis own opinion, which, as
to 11 gambler, is this:The Mason who knowingly recommends a gambler should b\) severely dbciplined.
The professed gambler should be excluded. The Mason who forgets his vows and
violates the law of the land by the habitual commission of the criminal offence
of' gambling, publicly or privately, should be expelled.
As Jong as keeping a dram shop is licensed by law, he could not say that in
and of itself it was a Masonic crime. But, if a Mason, by that occupation, "willfully
brings disgrace, injury, or min upon another," his license should not shield him, and
he should be held accountable to Masonic law for his acts and punished therefor.
The Grand Lodge endorsed the views thus advanced by the Grand Master.

The Grand Master publishes a num her of his decisions, of which we note only
one. While deciding that the loss of an eye disqualifies a candidate, be had decided
in another case that one who was near-sighted and compelled to wear glasses could
be made a Mason. Upon further rellectlon, he thought there was a manifest absurdity
in this distinction, and he suggested that a rule be-adopted similar to that in some
other jurisdictions, viz.: "that a candidate should he able to comply with all the
requirements of our ceremonies, and capable of giving the means of recognition."
This would, of course, let in the "one-eyed" man. But the Committee on Jurisprudence thought that would he going too far, and would violate some ancient" Landmark;" and so ." one-eyed" men will still be at a discount in the Badger State.

WYOMING.
The fourth .Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Wyoming was held
in Rawlins on the eighth day of October, 1878,-the M.·. W.·. ORLANDO NORTH:
Grand Master, presiding, and the R . '. W. '. WILLIAM G. TONN being Grand Secretary'.
Five Lodges were represented.
The Address of the Grand Master was brief. He congratulated the fraternity that
with them it had been a year happy and prosperous. He had laid the corner stone
of a new school house at La.ramie City. Business relations had prevented his official
visits to the subordinate Lodges, and he was afraid that generally Masons had
excused themselves from Masonic work, giving too ouch stress to the charge to the
E. A. "that our usn&! avocations must not be neglected." The following brief
advice to the officers and brethren will bo applicable and judicious in other jurisdictions:To the MBl}ters : Let m~ urge upon you the necessity of being proficient in the
work a;1d d,uties of your office. To the Wardens and subordiMte Of!!oers: Try to
be perlect JD your part. To the E. A. and F. C.: Learn well the several lectures
before you ask for advancement. .And, to Masons: Let each and every one resolve to·
do more and be better Masons in the future.

IRELAND,
We have given here some interesting items of history touching this Grand
Lodge. The earliest Masonic records of Freemasonry in Ireland are those of tho
Provincial Grand Lodge of Munster, commenced December twenty.seventh, 1726.
The Hon. JAME' O'BRIEN EYRE, was elected Grand Master. The present Grand
Lodge of Ireland wa< founded February third, 1729. During that year " the Parliament House in Dublin Wil.S about to, be built and Lord CARTERET, then Vice~oy, with
his suite, attended by the Corporation and garrison and a number of gentlemen
Freem~sons, marched in proces<lon and laid thefoolslone of the building with the
usual form~lities, 011 the third of February, 172J."
This Grand Lodge had several formal oppo•ers, viz.: " the Provincial Grand Lodge
of Muns1er;" in 1770, "the High Knight Templar Ireland K1lwir1ning Lodge" of
Dublin; and in 1B08, the "Grand Lodge of Ulster.'' How long these rival Grand
Lodge• continued is not stated. The:first "Freemasons' Hall" was erected in Dublin
in 1823.
Jn the year 1B07, the roll of Lodges .in Ireland numbered nine hundred and :fiftyone, subsequently increasing to one thousand and fourteen. Many of them were
militia and regimental Lodges, which long since ceased to exist.
" The IriHh ri tun! differs from any other, being, in fact, a compound of Irish,
York, and Scotch."

Like the previous messages of that officer, it is worthy of the close study and
careful consideration of the fraternity everywhere, and of the Ma<o11s of this jurisdiction in particular. In it, "that Htrict regard for the welfare of Masonry and devotion
to the true intent and meaning of its obligations, which have ever shone so brightly
in the official d oings of ourillustrio11s brother, ar e everywhere apparent, and should
incite in each of us an appreciative love for him and a resolve to imitate, as far as
lies in our power, his most worthy example. Masonry, with him, is eviden1ly not of
that theoretical, abstract kind which is great in professions but lnfiuitessimally small
in deeds, nor ii it of that holiday species, put on only for purposes of display
and as rendily thrown off again when duty calls for its recognition. It is rnther a
living r Pality-a practical exemplification in l ife's routine of its grand tencbings and
still grander objects - and thus he plainly discovers to us thnt the moks which we
are nil so prone~~ see in the m oral eyes of our fellows nre in most instnnces but the
magnified distortions occasioned by the b eams .in our own. Let us then carefully
treasure the truthful.and loving words of our Grand Mnster as contained in the i ntroductory part of his Address, nnd at once set about eradicating from onr own breasts
the evils there enumerated; all whicb, as stilted by him , lead effectually to " retard
the growth, interrupt the hnrmony, and paralJze the action of our Lodge organizations." Let contentious bickerings, jealousies, nnd ill-will, if any exiHt, from this
time forwnrd be forever banished from our midst, nnd be replaced with a charity so
oomprE:hensive that in all things we may do unto others that which under like circumstances we wou ld wish that others should do unto us; and to that extent, at leas\,
let us become living exemplars of that which we teach.
Your commitoee particularly commend for consideration thnt portion of the
message which has reference to the election of Masters of I,odges. The habit of
chnnging year after year, grading up step by step, is as unwise in policy as it is disastrous in consequences. No regard is thus had to the fitness of the b i"other for the
position to which he may succeed; and merit, which should be the chief and only
passport to s tation, is in no wise considered. That one1may fill a •ubo1 dinnte station
well nnd ably is no absolute evidence that he will make a successful presiding officer
of bis ).odge. The honor which attaches to nn office is in the quality of the work
that is done, and not in the nnme It bears. '. fhe humblest position may b~ filled with
a zeal nnd love so great as lo overshadow the highest if it be poorly filled. Rightly un<lerstoocl . th~re is no poor, no subordinate place in a Lodgeo·r Masons. Excellence in
work serves to exalt t he lowest in riink to a level with the highest. Hen! ability and
meri toriou~ labor should never bo overlooked j and the MaHter possessed of these
qualifications should, as suggested by the Grand Master, be retaiu(·d in office until
applicntion and study shall have provided one of equal merit to succeed him .
Another subject referred to by the Grand Master is deemed of too much importance to pas; by unnoticed. Your commiLtee allude 't o the late action of the Grand
Oric~t of France in suppressing the declaration that "Freemasonry holds as a first
principle the existence of God and the immortality of the soul," and in supplying in
its ste11d the atheistic doctrine that " its principles are nbsolute liberty o( conscience
and human solidarity ." This action cannot be too strongly condemn ea . It uunounces
to the Masonic world, in language too plain to be misunderstood, "that in France i\
Is no longer neces<ary that a Ma•on should believe that there is n God, or that man is
more thnn an animal." It is a cowardly, cnuseless yielding up of the fundamental principles of Freemasonry to the demands of atheism and unbelief,
and it gives into the hands of its enemies weapons more powerful for evil thnn envenomed ma.lice even could hope to i nvent. Most truly does our Grand Master say that

IT. The Grand Master calls t he attention ofll!asters to the provisions of Section 11,
.Article III, Part III, of the Constitution, and to the duty of a Master to require the
Secretary to read to the Lodge every six months the list of all who are delinquent
for dues; and he reports that "a diversity of opinion exists as to the right of a Master
to declare 11 member suspended for non-payment of dues, when the Lodge refuses to
take any action in the matter."
The language of the section mentioned is so plain that we are unable to see how t here
could be any diversity of opinion as to its meaning. The rule provided is simple. If a
member is more than Eix .m onths in arrears, he must be notified by the Secretary of
t hat fact, anc also that he will be suspended unless bis dues are paid be fore the next
atated meeting, or some reason for his neglect be shown, which shall be satisfactory
to the Lodge. When it appears that a member who is more than six months in
arrears has been notified, and has not paid, if the Lodge refuses to remit the dues or
extend the time for their payment, the Master's duty is plain. He mu1t declare the
delinquent member to be suspended. It is simply the judgment of the law which he is
called upon to pronounce. He has no discreti~n in th e matter and no authority to
delay the declaration. It is equally clear that, until the delinquent has been notified
and has had opportunity to show cause for his neglect, he cannot be suspended.

One of the first wante of man, after food and clothing, is shelter-some protection

In his primitive state Indifferent sbelter is found in rude booths and huts constr~ct.ed

About the same time, or more probably, as some maintain, at an earlier period,
Freemasonry was introduced into England, and a Lodge was established at York; it
being a dispnted point whether it was brought from Scotland, or, at an earlier date,
Introduced directly from the Continent. However this may be, many of the finest

Craft in England. To the introductio11 of Freemasonry into Scotla11d and .England
is, perhaps, d~e the perpetuation of the Order to the present time~ for ~t continued
to flourish, with some vicissitudes of fortune, in that more congP.mal s01l long after
it was utterly crushed out on the Continent by the unrelenting arbitrary power of its
. former patron, the Church of Rome.
When operative Masonry began to flourish in the earlier part of the middle ages,
the learning of the times was mostly monopolized by the priesthood. The architects
and superior builders and workmen of the higher degrees of Masonry, however,
must, necessarily, have been men of education and varied learning, well informed in
mathematics and in all other sciences then cultivated, or they could not have constructed edifices requiring a combination of so many qualities of mind and so wide a
range of varied !nformation. There were, doubtless, some others, outside the priesthood, well versed in the learning and sciences of the times. There would naturally
be similar tastes and strong bonds of sympathy between scientific and learned men
of all classes, which would bring them into association, whether within or without
the Order; and such was, in fact, the case. Accordingly, we find that, in process cf
time learned aud scientific men, not architects or practical masons, were, by courtesy' initiated into the Order, and "accepted" as Masons; and thus the term "ac'
cepted"
was introduced into the name of the Order-" Free and Accepte d"
.,asons. "
While the Order enjoyed the favor and patrona~e of the Church, learned ec~lesi­
astics were often admitted, and Cardinal Wor.sEY even became Grand Master. Highly
important consequences, naturally and logically, followed from this widening of the
field of eligibility. Intelligence begets inquiry; and inquiry induces examination,
and, in an a~soclation of Inquiring minds, discussion, which, perhaps, leads to doubts.
Dogmas, whether scientific or religious, are thus brought to the test of reason, and
a.re accepted or njected, as they stand, or fail to stand, the test applied .. In an
association of Jearn~d men of various professions and scientific pursuits, like the
Ma&onic fraternity, especially after the admission of learned men other than architects and operntlve ml\BODR, there ()OUl!I not fdl to be a spirit of free inquiry and
discussion• and such was, do11btlesA, the result In this case. New discoveries were
made in a~tronomy nod In other sciences, which were, apparently, in conflict with
many accepted dogml\I of the Church. These, as they became developed and
demonstra.ted, could net fail to be adopted by the Intelligent and scientific men found
in the Order even though rejected by the Church. Free inquiry was encouraged by
the Order ~nd the tendency of Its principles was to enlighten the mind; while, at
that dBy, both the tendency and policy of the Church w~s t? keep it in ignorance
and limit the sphere of Its operation and influence. ~he prmc1ples ?f the t":o organizations, therefore, came into silent, but though silent, no less 1rreconc1lable or
eft'ective antagonism;' l\Dd the jealousy of the Roman hierarchy be~ame grel\tly
cited against Its former protege. The O!'der was accused of promotmg the refor:ation, and otherwise Interfering with the interests of the Church. 'fhe .inven.tion. of
the art of printing, by aft'ording the means of multiplying books and d1ssemmat1~g
'deas rapidly extended and enlarged the circle of intelligence, the field of free d1s~ussi~n and Independent thought, and consequently of independent action. With
the rapid spread of knowledge, the number of competent builders, artificers, and
other skilled workmen multiplied outside the Masonic organization, so as to render
the Order Jess necessl\ry for the construction of religious edifices, and for the other

the Order continued to ~xist, though it sometimes languished. Even here it sometimes encountered the enmity and opposition of the Church. The Archbishop of
Winchester, during the minority of HENBY VJ, procured the passage of an act of
l'arllament forbidding the meetings of Lodges, but for some reason it does not appear
to have been rigidly enforced; and six years afterwards, a Lodge was actually held
under the auspices of the Archbishop himself. HENRY VI, after attaining his majority,
himself joined the Order; and HENRY VII became Grand Master. Queen ELIZABETH
appointed commissioners for the purpose of suppressing the Order, but upon examination some of them joined it. WILI.IAM III was also Grand Master. As the number of Masons received into the Order and accepted from among the learned men
outside the profession of architects and practical Masons increased, Masonry, by
degrees, lost its operative character and became in a corresponding degree speculative; until at length it wholly ceas~d to be operative and became purely speculative.
The change was gradual, and it is difficult at this day to determine the precise date
when it was finally effected. In 1607 the celebrated English architect, Ulwo Jo~EB,
became Grand Master, and undel' his auspices many men in England eminent for
their learning were received Into the Order as accepted Masons, and from that time
~he change was, doubtless, more rapid.
Among thos·e so received was ELIAS
ABHMOLE, the distinguished antiquary, who was initiated in 1646. He afterwards revised and recomposed the ritual, giving it the form, substantially, which it
has retained until the present time. He thus, doubtless, did much to give direction to
Masonic thought, and to stamp speculative Masonry with the characteristics which
now distinguish it. In 1666, or soon thereafter, Sir CHRIBTOPBEl\ WREN became
Grand Master. During the later years of his life Masonry declined, owing, it is snid,
to want of attention ou the part of the Grand Master on account of the infirmities incident to old age ; and it has also been said that, in the beginning of the eighteenth century, St. Paul's Lodge was the only one in England. It may have been the only one
In 8outhern England, but it is believed that the Order was in a more flourishing con·
dition in Northern England, as it certainly was in Scotland. However this may be,
the interest was revived in 1702, and in 1717 the four Lodges then In existence metat
the .Apple Tavern in Oovent Garden, and organized themselves into a Grand Lodge;
and in 1723 the Grand Lodge adopted new constitutions framed by ANDERSON, which
have since been known as the ANDERSON Constitutions, and which are, substantially,
the same as those under which the Order is now working.
Whatever the character of Masonry may have been during the seventy or more
years which may have been the transition period, from the time of the ndoption of
AsHMOLE'B ritual to the establishment of the ANDERSON Constitutions, there can be
no doubt that from the latter date Masonry ceased to be operative and became
purely speculative; and now, in the eloquent language of a former Grand Orator of
this Grand Lodge, now no more, "The implements of our craft are no longer for
1iperative toil. We do not now, as a part of our covenant, set fast the Doric pillar,
nor release from marble the ornament of the Corinthian Uapital. · We no longer
sketch the complications of Gothic piles, and cement buttresses of haughty towers
and carry up, course by course, the aspiring stones of pinnacles. The tools of our
craft are representatives now of speculative truth, and speak to the inward eye of
, laws and duties that make life noble and character symmet1ical and strong. Yet,
though we build no structures such as our ancient brethren reared ; though the
temples in which we meet are not the monuments of our own proficiency in the nrt,
whose instruments we cherish; we are builders and preservers in a richt•r sense: for
onr Order itself grows stronger and more precious with years, and its uses are more
varied and beautiful with the lapse of time ; and the Masonic organization, as now
constituted, is far more remarkable and wonderful than the noblest edifice it ever
added to the landscape of history."
