Masopry, thus reorganized upon the speculative basis, and thus rehabilitated in
a more liberal age, was soon transplanted from England into France, Ireland, Holland, Russia, Spain, Italy, Scotland, Germany, the United State~, and flnal.ly into
Africa, Asia and all the civilized parts of the world. In 1872 a Grand Lodge of the
Order was opened in -Rome itself, under the very shadow of St. Peter's and the Yati·
.can, and in the very presence of its implacable foe, the Head of the Church. In the
following year a Lodge was established by Americans in Jerusalem, almost within
the purlieus of King SoLOMON's Temple. During the last century Freemasonry has
.spread, and the membership of the Order increased with wonderful rapidity. There
are now in the world more than ten thousand Lodges, having a membership Qf probably more than one million Master Masons; and it is highly creditable, botb to the
principles of the Order and to the members of the fraternity for the very general
observance of those principles, that Masonry extends most rapidly and flourishes
most luxuriantly in those countries where knowledge is most generally disseminated
among the people, and where civil, political, and religious freedom most completely
prevail, as in England and her colonies, and in the United States of America. In the
latter country there is, doubtless, a mnch larger membership in proportion to the
population than in any other. In our own State of C•lifornia the date of the charter
of the oldest Lodge is .April 19, 1850. As I learn from the report of the proceedings
at tile last Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge or the State, there are now
more than two hundred Lodges within its jurisdiction, with a membership of more
than twelve thousand. Of the character of that membership nothing more need be
said than to call attention to the representatives of the various subordinate Lodges
who constitute the Grand Lodge of California, now assembled in this magnificent
temple, erected by and dedicated to the purposes of our Order. In all countries
where there exists civil and political liberty and complete freedom of conscience,
and where there Is a general dissemination of knowledge among the people, Masonry
has outlived Its persecutions, if not all opposition. It bas vindicated its character as
an institution In harmony with true religion; an institntion of patriotic impulses and ·
tendenclea; an ln1titutlon promotive of subordination to good government and
good order In the State, In the neighborhood, and in the family, and, by inculcating
the praotloe of all the virtues, conducive to tile best interests of man in all his relations,
social, religious, and polltloal.
Much use of the element or 1ecreoy, by means of which brothers of the fraternity
recognize each other among 1trangers and protect themselves from imposition, was
formerly made by the en~mle1 or the Order for the pnrpose of inflaming the prejudices of tho Ignorant and the jealoua, and, doubtless, with some effect. The publica·
tion of the pro0Hdlng1 of the Grand Lodges authorized during later years has, how·
ever, tended largely to allay these prejudices. In these published proceedings the
essential working• of the Ol'der are laid open to public examination and critici3m; and
no one can read them, as they appear from year to year, without being strongly impressed with the good tendencies of the principles of Masonry in all their practical,
as well as speculative, workings, as is there made known to all. We are no propagandists. We extend a special Invitation to no man to enter the precincts of Masonry. If one seeks admission to our society it is unsolicited and of his own free, unbi·
ased will, after a full Investigation of our principles and their practical operation; and
the fact that so many Intelligent men, among the most orderly and worthy classes of
society, seek a11oolatlon with us is ample evidence that our principles meet the approbation of good men, and that their tendencies are all to good order and to the
highest Interests of society at large. Speculative Masonry is not, and it does not
profess to be, a religion or a substitute for religion; but It inculcates a system of
the purest morals, which is an essential element and necessary ooncomitant of all
true religion. There are certain elements or principles which are universally accepted as essential to all systems of faith worthy the name of religion-such as a
belief in a Supreme Being; a recognition of the moral distinction between right and

\

Gr&-nd Lodge of California.

163

wrong; the obligation to recognize and cultivate the practice of all the virtues, such
as tempera.nee, sobriety, chastity, fortitude, prudence, justice, and, chief of all,
charity. On these principles all must and do agree. There are other points of faith
upon which the reason may and does pause, Inquire, doubt; and yet it is upon these
latter that zealoh and enthusiasts dogme.tize most confidently, dispute most furi·
ously, and hate mo~t Implacably. It is upon these very points, where we should be
most distrustful of the correctness of our judgment and most charitable towards the
views of others, that man is most confident, most obstinate, most uncompromising;
and it is upon these wl\ere he consigns his fellow-man to the dungeon, stretches him
upon the rack, and burns him atthe stake. Into that disputed territory Masonry' does
not enter. Its leading tenet, charity, forbids-all its principles prohibit it. It accepts
and plants itself upon those self-evident and universally accepted principles which
lie at the foundation of all true religion and all morality, and upon the recognition and
practice of which all human happiness must rest. It earnestly and constantly incul·
cates those principles in Its charges in the Lodge-room, its lectures, orations and
writings, and in all its proceedings, published and unpublished. It admonishes us
to seek after truth, and teaches that truth is an attribute of divinity and the foundation of every Yirtue. In the ' language of another,.already familiar to you, which
cannot be improved or too often repeated in your hearing-the Mason "is instructed
to put a due restraint npon his affections and passions; to preserve a noble and
steady purpose of mind, equally distant from cowardice and rashness; to regnlate
his life by the dictates of reason ; and to render to every man his just due, without
distinction. In Rhort, the three great duties of life are impressed upon his conscience-reverence to God, the chief good ; kindness to his neighbor, as prescribed
by the golden rule; and respect for himself by avo1dlng Irregularities and intemperance, which impair the faculties and debase the dignity of his profession.''
The Mason who cherishes these principles, and in all his daily walks conforms his
conduct to them, cannot fail ,to be an honest pure man, and in all respects a worthy
and highly useful member of society. And the tendency of the constant Inculcation
of these principles in the Lodge, In Its published proceedings, and In all the social
intercourse between Masons, 'cannot fail to have a beneficial Influence upon the members of the Order, and, through them, upon society at large, Masonry, therefore,
.though not a religion, or a substitut~ for it, is not antagonistic to true religion; but,
on the c.ontrary, by teaching Its essential and universally aocepted principles, it Is a
powerful auxiliary in its work or improving the oonditlon of man: and ho who would
reject its aid, as some are disposed to do because the Church covers the same ground
and more, would act upon the fanatical principle of the Caliph OMAR, when he
burned the great library of antiquity at Alexandria, giving as a reason for his barbarism that, " if the writings of the Greeks therein contained agree with the Koran
they are useless, and if not they are pernlolous and ought to be destroyed." The
fact that the teachings of the Church embrace the same fundamental doctrines does
not, therefore, render the Masonic Order useless, It may be true that if all men in
every particular, lived In strict accordance with the doctrines of the Church so
as
they are really essential to the well-being of man here and hereafter, there ~ight be
no occasion for Masonry a~ now organized. So also, if every human being was a
perfect Mason in theory and practice, there would be little need of the ~:Jhurch. But
human nature is not thns perfect.; and so long as it is constituted as it now is, there
is ample room for all organizations, founded upon the generally accepted principles
that lie at the foundation of all true religion and constitute the basis of all real happi·
ness, to exercise their proper influence without jostling each other. The Supreme
Architect of the Universe never made two objects exactly alike. Of the myriads or
leaves in the forest, of grains of sand upon the sea shore, or spires of grass in the
field, no two will be foun<i to precisely correspond in all their parts. So no two
minds are cast in the same intellectual or moral mould, Each views objects and principles from its own standpoint. Different circumstances 11.nd surrounllings often

produce dllferent lmpreeslons. One mind may be reached in one organization, and
another by another. The Lodge may take holu of some that the Church cannot, or
does not, reach. However this may be, if the inculcation of the .fundamental prin·
olplea or true religion is useful in one place, or organization, it must, also, be good in
another. The constant.contemplation of truth, of justice, of temperance, of charity,
whether In the Lodge or elsewhere, cannot fail to elevate the thoughts and ennoble
the character of the individual subjected to the influence ; and it cannot do otherwise
than lead, in a greater or less degree, to the practice of the virtues so contemplated.
Having thus briefly sketched the supposed origin, and the progress, vicissitudes, and
present condition of Freemasonry, and made some reference to its principles, to its
relation to other organizations, and to the interests of humanity, I shall conclude with
an ex hortation to the brethren to so conduct themselves as to afford to the world a
perpetual living illustration of the principles which we inculcate and the virtues which
we cherish. I find the precise idea which I desire to present, in conclusion, so aptly and
beautitifully expressed,by Grand Orator DOLPH, of the Grand Lodge of our neighboring State, Oregon, that I shall not hesitate to a.ppropriate his language : " Let the

be, if not only our foundation stands, but if the superstructure of individual character wblob we have reared proves acceptable to the Grand Architect and is found

Bro. WILLIAM C. BELCHER, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following reports relative to sundry matters presented in
the Address of the Grand Master :7o the M. •. W.-. Grand Lodge of California 1 I. In the matter of the proposed removal of Saint Mai·k's Lodge, N o. 85, from
Oleta, its present place of meetmg, to Plymouth, in the same county, the Grand
Master refused to a.pprove the resolution for removal because such removal would
largely diminish the territorial jurisdiction and practically destroy the usefulness
of Drytoum Lodge, No. 174.
The propriety of such removals is, by the Constitution, very wisely referred to
the Grand Master. He ha.a opportunity to inquire into the circumsta.nces, and very
rarely, if ever, ought the Grand Lodge to interfere with his judgment in the matter.
In this case it is believed that be exercised his a.uthority wisely, and it is therefore
recommended that bis action be approved.
II. In a case brQugbt to the attention of the Grand Master, a brother who was
elected Master of 11 Lodge, failed to que.lify, wa.s consequently not installed, and the
Master of the preceding year continued to act in that capacity. The Grand Master
recommends that the Constitution be so amended as to require the Master elect to

168

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 16,

qualify and be Installed within sixty days after the election, and, in case or failure,
that the office be declared vacant and a new election ordered.
The provision of Section I, Art. I, Part IV of the Constitution, is that the Master
and Wardens shall be installed as soon as practicable after their election, and that,
when Installed, they shall hold their offices until their successors shall have been duly
elected and in.~ialled.
It is certainly the duty or every Mason who a.ccepts an election to the office of
Master of a Lodge, to qualify himself promptly for the performance of its duties:
and if he neglects so to do, there appears to be no reason why the Master of the
preceding year may not, with propriety, continue to perform the duties of the e>ffice.
Under the law he is the Master until his successor is installed. If the Master elect
fails to qualify and be installed, and the former Master cannot or will not perform
the duties, the Grand Master may, upon the application of the Lodge, issue a dispensation under which the vacancy may be filled. Your committee see no necessity
for any amendment to the Constitution in tbis respect.
III. The Grand Master decided that when a man, not a Mason, removes from this
State and becomes a resident of another State, the Lodge within whose jurisdiction
he lived while here loses all anthority to consent that the degrees of Masonry be
conferred upon him elsewhere. Thie decision was plainly right, The occasion for it
arose upon an application from Union Lodge, No. 820, ·of New York, to Live Oak
Lodge, No. 61, of this jurisdiction, in the case of a man who had removed from tbie
State to the State of New York. and had there made application for the degrees before
he had resided there long enough to give the Lodge jurisdiction to receive and act
upon his petition, except with the consent of the Lod~ under whose jurisdiction be
had last resided.

IV. Section 2, Art. Ill, Part III, of the Constitution, forbids any Lodge in the
·u State" to reoelve an application for the degrees unless the applicant shall have been a

resident of the "~tate" for at least twelve months; but makes no such restriction
in regard to Lodl!'el out ot the Stftte, although in this jnri•diction.
A case aI'Oflo In Ariaonll Lodge, U. D., at Phamlx, in the Territory of Arizona, in
which a per1on who hail been 1everal years 11 resident of California, removed to
Arizona, and, aftor a retildence thero of seven or eight months, made application to
that Lodge for the degrees. Tho qae1tlon was asked of the Grand Master if, under
the oircumdaaoeti, the petition conld be received; an~ he held that as the applicant
had resided within the "jur!ld!ct!on" of tho Grand Lodge more than one year, and
within the jurl1d!ot!on ot the Lodge more than six months, the petition could
properly be received. Your oomm!ttee think the deci,ion right, and recommend that
it be approved.
V. In a CILIKI preaented, an applloant for the degrees was moving from place to
place, tarrying In each 111 the exigencies of his business might require. and the question aroRo 11.11 to where was his proper residence. The Grand Master decided that, if
he had solected a plaoe as his home, and had acquired the right to vote there, that
was hie place of realdenco. Your committee think the decision correct. Residence
very largely depend• upon the Intention of the party, and if a man selects some place
RB hie home, and aoqolres the right to vote there, it is his residence in law, and should
be so considered ln Maaonry.
VI. Under Seo. 6, Art. III, Part III, of the Constitution, the Grand Mnster
held that an objection to the initiation of a person who has been elected to receive
the degrees of Masonry In a. Lodge, may be made to the Master thereof at any time
before the initiation, either by simple oral statement or in writing, and either in or

1879.J

out of the Lodge. It is rnfficient if the Master i• advised by the brother objecting that
ho doe• object. This seems to your committee to be in strict conformity with the
lettor and spirit of the section, and the decision is therefore approved.

VII. The question was aqked of the Grand Master - "Is it the duty of the Secretary of a Lodge to take his financial books, and the semi-annual reports of the
Secretary a.nrl Treasurer, from the Lodge-room to the auditing committee for examination, or is it tbe duty of that committee to make such examination at the
Lodge-room?" We are at a. loss to conceive how any Secretary or auditing committee could be so unaccommodating and unreasonable as to give occasion for such
a question ; but it was asked, and the Grand Ma8ter was called upon for a reply.
Your committee do not quite agree with him that such a committee may summon
the Secretary to appear before them, at such place as they might name, with his
books and papers. It would be hie duty to deliver to them all books and papers requisite for their examination, and they could examine them in the Lodge-room, or take
them elsewhere at their pleasure; but they have no authority to summe>n him, or to
compel his attendance before them. Such an examination should be made where it
would be most convenient, and it would not matter whet.h er at tho Lodge-room or
elsewhere; and the Secretary should always be willing to attend at any convenient
place, and give such information or as>istancc as migb.t be desired.
Such proceedings should ever be attended with a reasonable degree of courtesy,
and if they were, such a question would not arise. If, however, such a committee
desired to conduct their examination at some place other than the Lodge·rooni, or
the place where the Secretary's books wera ordinarily kept, and the question of duty
as to moving them arose, your committee think that the charge of packing them
about would rest with the auditing cc•mmittee. Tha 8ecretary will have performed
the letter of his duty when he has shown himself to be reedy to deliver them at the
place of keeping.

Bro. JoNATHAN D. HINES, from the Committee on Finances, presented the following reports:To the M.-. W.•, Grand Lorlge of California:Your committee report that the claims for necessary expenses in attending the
Grand Lodge, presented by Bro. JoHN MtLLB DnoWNE, Grand Master, for $26-by
Bro. WtLLrAM HENRY CRANE, Senior Grand Warden , for $31-and by Bro. RonEnT
CnrnLEY BRODER, Junior Grand Warden, for $'9-amounting in all to $156, a.re
correct; and it is recommended that tbey be paid from the General Fund, as authorized by the Constitution.
Your committee have' given earnest consideration to that portion of the Address of
the Grand Master which relates to the proposed creation of a Grand l.odge charity
fund. Tbe kindly expression of a heart overflowing with generous impulses commands
the admiration and respect of every Mason. It is pleasant to bear te•timony to the
ability, goodness, and Masonic zeal of our honored Grand Master, and to join with
him in exhorting the fraternity to "actual and substantial charity." But the question is not whether charity shall be dispensed, but rather, how shall it be dispensed?
No Grand Lodge, so far as we are informed, has ever been successful in undertaking
to dispense direct charities. They have generally and, as we think, wisely, left that

170

Grand Lodge of California . .

to the 1everal subordinate Lodges and Boards of Relief, who, a.s a. rule, personally

according to law and properly approved and filed ; and they wish to bear testimony,

know the a.pplioa.nts and can judge of their necessities, and have thus far, be it said
to the credit of Masonry and humanity, ever shown themselves ready and willing to
1oothe the sorrows of the afllicted, and administer" actual and substantial charity"
to the poor and needy. A Grand Lodge i~ too remote and its officers too difficult to
reach, in a broad jurisdiction like ours, to dispense individual oharity. In times of
public calamity, when the fire-fiend devastates great oities or pestilence sweeps over
States, the Gr1md Master may safely act, as he did la.et year in the case of the yellow
fever sufferers-draw upon the treasury, and rely upon the generous emotions of the
grand Ma.sonic heart to sustain and applaud his a.ct.
'
The proposition to convert the Reserve Fund into a charity fund in no respect
alters the case so far as regards the practicability of e. Grand Lodge di•pensing
charities. Indeed, the Reserve Fund is now e. charity fund, held sacred for great
emergenciee. Whole States may be again effiicted with some destroying epidemic,
as was the case in Louisiana, Mississippi, and Tennessee la.et year, and this fund may
be needed to alleviate their sulferings.
The suggestion to abrogate the Reserve Fund altogether is quite another thing,
and might very well be considered-ip connection with a reduction of Grand Lodge
dues: but would the abrogation of that fund be wise or prudent? By reference to
page 141 of the Proceedings of the year 1871 it will be seen that while this Grand
Lodge was in session, the news of the terrible conflagration at Chicago, fl.ashed by
lightning across the continent, electrified its members, and in a mor::.ent $5,000 of
this ReserveFund was telegraphed to relieve that stricken people. What sorrow and
suft'ering it averted many know; and there, amid the smoking ruins of desolate
homes, gladdened hearts invoked Heaven to bless the ready donors.
In reviewing this whole matter your committee see no reason to change the views
e:i:pre1Rcd by this committee le.st year, which were to the effect that, in this jurisdiction, a Grand Lodge charity fund for general distribution is not feasible.
The judicious recommendation of the Grand l'llnster to abolish the Boe.rd of Trustees of the Bell6rve Fund is approved by your committeee, but, that having already
· been aocoropl!Mhed by an amendment to the third General Regulation , no action
on their part 11 required.

To t11e M.'. W. •. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee respectfully report that they have examined in detail the books,
vouoheT1, aooount., reporu, and oth'er papers of the Grand Secretary and Grand
Treasurer, &nd find them correct, and that all disbursements have b.een ma.de and
propor vouchcra taken, as therein stated and in accordance with our laws and regulations. They also find that tbe Grand Secretary has carried into effect the resolu·
tion recommended by himself last year, relative to tbe distribution of the surplus
yellow fever fund among the several donors, and that the same has been distributed
by him and proper vouchers taken therefor.
Your committee further report that they have examined the officii.l bonds of the
Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary, and Trustees of the Reserve Fund, and find them

Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer have kept the books and transacted the business of the Grand Lodge.
Yonr committee have had under consideration a petition from La Grange Lodge,
No. 99, wherein it is represented that Merced Lodge, No. 176, has surrendered its
charter; that La Grange Lodge has succeeded to some of the burdens tbat formerly
belonged to Merced Lodge, particularly to the support of a widow of a deceased
member who formerly received assistance from that Lodge; and that a few members
of the late M€rced Lodge, who were in arrears for dues at the time of the surrender
of its charter, have ~ince pa.id the same into the treasury of the Grand Lodge. The
petitioners urge that, inasmuch as suoh burdens have been transferred to La Grange
Lodge, No. 99, it should be entitled to the dues of the late Merced Lodge, to enable
them to meet this increased liability.
The request seems reasonable and just. It appears from the report of the Grand ·
Secretary that members of the late Merced Lodge, in arrears for dues at the date of
the surrender of its charter, have since paid to this Grand Lodge the sum of forty
dollars; and your committee therefore recommend the adoption of the following
resolution:Resolved, That all moneys received, or which may hereafter be received, by this
Grand Lodge from members of the late Merced Lodge, No. 176, for arrears of dues
to that Lodge, be paid over to La Grange Lodge, No. 99.
All which is respectfully submitted by

Bro. WILLIAM T. REYNOLDS, from the Committee on Grievances,
presented the following reports :To the M. •• W. '. (}rand Lodge of California :-

Your committee have had before them the appeal of Bro. ROBERT BAILEY from
the action of San btego Lodge, No. 85, in e.cq uitting Bro. WILLIAM W. STEW ABT of
certain charges of unma.eonic conduot, and, having carefully examined the record
and the testimony 'taken in the case, report that they find no error in the action of
the Lodge.
The accused is charged with having written an anonymous letter to one fl. H.
BIGELOW, the agent of the Home Mutual Insurance Company of San Francisco, suggesting that he investigate the circumstances of e. fire oc'curring in the saloon of Bro.
BAILEY, the accuser. Dro. l:lTEWABT denies writing the letter, or that he had anything to do with the matter. 'rhe testimony consists principally of the opinioifa
of experts as to whether the letter in question is in the he.ndwril ing of Bro. STEW ABT
or not. These opinions are very conflicting. The commissioners who tried the case
were certainly better judges of the weight which should be given to the testimony of
the several :witnesses than any of us; and, they having decided that the accused was
not guilty; your committee do not feel warranted in disturbing that verdict. They
therefore recommend the adoption of the following rP.solutioh :R esolved, That the action of San Diego Lodge, No. 35, in acquitting Bro. WILLIAM
W. STEW ABT of certain charges of unmasonic conduct, be and is hereby affirmed.

Th the JI,., W.•, Grand Lodge of C.allfornia: Your committee have carefully examined the report of the Grand Lecturer and
the reports of Inspectors accompanying it, and congratulate the Grand Lodge e.nd
the fraternity of this jurisdiction upon the uniformity and excellence Of the work,
as therein shown, and the generally cheerful conformity b;v the subordinate Lodges
to our Constitution and regulations. They commend the Grand Lecturer for the
interest and diligence which he bas manifested, and can only say thereof that the
fruits of bis labors are their sufficient reward.
Jn relation to that portion of the report respecting the matters to this committee
referred from the Address of the Grand Master, a separate report will be presented,
and it will only be said here that there seems to exist in some, perhaps in many, of the
Lodges, 11 feeling of opposition to the visits of the Inspectors. It would be uncharitable to suppose that this is to be attributed to any fear on the part of any Lodge a.a
to the results of an examination; and it is very possible that it is largely due to that
spirit of "emulation " existing among the brethren of the Lodges aforesaid toward
the Inspectors, as to who can best work and least agree.
The remedy lies in the recommendations heretofore submitted, and in the
awakening such brethren to a knowledge of the ability and labors of the Inspectors
and to a confidence therein . Your committee are sure that, if the Lodges which
have not deigned to reply to the communications of the Inspectors, and if the
Masters of the Lodges in the Twenty-second District who refased even to notice the
second persohal communication of the Inspector thereof, could have the pleasure
.of reviewing the reports of the Inspectors now before your committee, it would
induce in them a little emulation in courtesy, as well as convince them of the utility
of our system of inspection.
If your committee protest against such acts of the Lodges, in bow much greater
degree may they not censure the Inspectors who have been honored by such appoint·
ments and have negleoted to perform the duties incident thereto. No Inspector who
has failed in thiR reapeot should be re-appointed, unles$ some very satiofactory reason
be given for auob failure. lt le no excuse that they have not been invited to visit
their Lodges, and cannot aft'ord to do so without pay. They should, under such cir.
cumsta.nces, aaoertain the condition of their Lodges from other sources th1tn visitation, a.nd report \hereon with the explanations given by many who have thus
reported.
The Inspector of the Fifteenth n!1trlot, iu his report, requests that the attention
of the Grand Lodge be directed tow1ml the repeal of th11t regulation which requires
a Master to have the oortiftoat~ of an Inspector before ins1al111tio11. The Grand
Lodge, in dlreoting the prepRra1lon of nn lnMtallatiun service, of which the presentation of aueh oerililoate shall form a pa1 t, ha~ disposed of tba.t matter, and your
commit1ee have no di1p0Mition to recommend any change.
In the report of the In1peotor "or the Fifth District. handed in by the Grand
Lecturer almoat at the la..t momeut., as having just been rec. ived. (for which tlll'dinesM its excellence of preparation almost affords an excuse,) your committee are

.Anot.hcr matter, called to the attention of your committee by the same report, is
that of a failure to find in the reports of other Inspectors any information as to
whether the Constitution. in its provisions relative to the payment of dues by members of Lodges, is complied with. The absence of such information leads to the
supposition that there are no violations of duty by the Masters and Secretaries of
Lodges in this respect; and it Is thought that if the attention of Inspectors be
directed to the matter, a few such possible omissions may be corrected.
Your committee conclude by expressing the opinion that the Grand Lecturer is
entitled to and should receive the thauks of the Grand Lodge for his diligent attention to his du ties, and by recommending the adoption of the following resolutions :Resolved, That the ritual taught by the Grand Lecturer and the Inspectors is the
only work recognized by this Grand Lodge.
Resolved, That no Inspector, who hes failed to make the report required by law,
should be reappointed to such position unless satisfactory explanation be given for
such failure.
.Resolved, That the Inspectors of th" several Districts be directed to examine
whether the Lodges therein and the officers thereof fulfill the requirements of the
Constitution relative to the dues of members.
Your committee have carefully examinf!d all the proceedings of the Gre.nd Lodge
relative to the duties and compensation of InspectoNl, and find therefrom that, while
the Grand Lodge has uniformly and consistently imposed on such officers the duties
now demanded of them, it has, at times, evinced 11 disposition of indifference as to
the payment of the necesslll'y expenses incident. to the performance of such duties.
The aotion of the Grand Lodge at Its last Oommunioation, referred to in the
Address of the Grand Master, practically annuls General Regulation No.16,butyour
committee do not attribute such action entirely to undue consideration. They lll'e
inclined rather to the belief that many of the subordinate Lodges are unw!lling to
bear the expenses incident to an annual visitation by the District Inspectors, and
that they desire to regulate the frequency of such visitations by their own inclinations or by the condition of their finances; and, that suoh expenses are 11 burden
upon some of the Lodges, your committee do not deny. Unfortunately, in the opinion
of your committee, these are the Lodges that stand most in need of visitation by
Inspectors. To this indifference or possible Inability on the part of such Lodges is,
to a considerable degree, to be attributed the neglect of duty of some of the Inspectors. A few, it is true, are able to perforn1 their duty and be euftloiently rewarded by
the honor conferred, but many cannot afford to $pend their time and money for the
benefit of the Craft in general and the Lodges of their districts in particular, without
some compensation.
Your committee do not deem it pertinent to the present reference to odvert to
the system of inspection, nor to the powers or duties that lll'e or should be conferred
or imposed upon Inspectors. They believe that harmonious action may be secured
in the matter by the course proposed by the Grand Master and officially indorsed by
the Grand Lecturer; and they heartily concur in the recommendation "that the
necessity of inspecting a Lodge may be properly left to the discretion of the In spector," and think that such a course may remove, in a measure at least, any burden which a visit may cause, and at the same time provide for the inspection of
Lodges as heretofore contemplated. They therefore recommend the adoption of the
following resolutions:Resolved, That all resolutions of the Grand Lodge in conflict with General Regulation No. 15 be and are h6reby repealed.
Resolved, That General Regulation No. 15 be amended eo as to read e.s follows:15. The Grand Master shall . appoint for each district an oftlcer, to be called
Inspector, who shall be a resident of-the district for which lte is ap:polnted, and whose
duty it shall be to visit each Lodge in hid district whenever desired by any Lodge,

Your committee would have answered the question briefly that it is neither right •
n or legitimate for a Lodge to do work on the ·sa.bbath. When we speak of work, we
mean the ordinary work of the Lodge, and particularly of the conferring of degrees,
and n ever speak of tho performance of the burial service as work. The p roposer of
the question evidently so used the word. Our country is a Christian country and
our people are a Christian people, by whom the Sabbath is reoognjzed as a h oly day
set apt1rt for .rest and worship. Whether, as individuals, we are Christians or not,
or professedly religious or not, we do profess to be good citizens, obedient to th e laws
of the land, whether it be the land of our birth or of our adoption, and to be zealous
promoters of the good order and the best interests of society ; and it seems to your
committee that a decent r espect for the institutions of the country and the opinions
of the great body of the people requires of us, as men and as Masons, to abstain on
the Sabbath from our ordinary avocations or amusements.

Bro. WILLIAM
BELC~R, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following reports:2b the M.·. W.'. (}rand Lodge of Oalifornia:I. In the matter of the memorial of Bro. B. W. SHEPHERD, suspended by Sinoerity Lodge, No. 132, for non-payment of dues, the facts, as we gather them from
the memorial and from a letter written 9th November, 1878, by Bro. GEORGE w.
BOYDEN, then Master of the Lodge named, to the Masonic Board of Relief of San
Francisco, are that, in 1865, Sincerity Lodge, No. 132, removed from Rich Bar, in
Plu_mas county, to Taylorville, in the same county, and that one of the conditions upon
which the removal was agreed to was tbat all the members residing at Rich Bar were
to be made life members of the Lodge, and, from the date of removal , to be exempt
f~om dues; and that they were by the Lodge, subsequent to its removal, enrolled as
hfe members thereof, In accordance with the agreement. In l86G all wlio had been
so enrolled, except Bro. SHEPHERD and one other, requested, by a writing over their
signatures, that their name~ be placed upon the list of paying members; and in
December, 1866, the names of all who had been enrolled as life members, including
.Bro. SHEPHERD, were, by order of the Lodge, placed upon the list of paying members, and from that time dues were regularly charged against them. Up to 1873 the
Lodge, from time to time, remitted the dues charged against Bro. Sm~PHERD. In
November of that year be was declared suspended for non-payment of dues but no
notice of such suspension was given to the Grand Secretary. lu 1878, after d~e notification by the Secretary, he was again declared suspended, and notice was given to
and by the Grand Secretary of that fact.
Bro. SH&PHERD asks that the declaration of suspension be set aside by the Grand
Lodge, and your committee think that his petition should be granted. That he
should be me.de u life member of the Lodge and be thenceforth exempt from dnes
was a contraot executed between him and his Lodge when it plnced his name upon
the rofl of lta life members, and that Lodge bnd no power in 1873 or 1878, without his
consent, to re1cfnd that contra.ct; and its action in charging dues against him and in
seeking to enforce their payment was in violation of its contract and of the good
faith which we ought In all oe.sea to require our Lodges to observe.
Your committee 11re of tbe opinion that the declaration of suspension of Bro.
BHEI'llERD wnM without aathorlty of law and void, and that he is still a life member
of that Lodge In good 1tandln111 a.nd mUllt be so returned by the Lodge.
II. In 11n1wor to 111ndry queatlons proposed, the Grand Master gave the following
response•:Flnt. That the H111ter of a Lodge has no power to authorize a Past Master
to. open the Lod11e aud perform work during the absence of himself and Wardens that the Lodge cannot be opened except by or under the direction and with th~
presence of the Ha1ter or one of the Wardens.
Second. Thr.t, In the absence of the Master and Wardens, the Lodge cannot be
opened even for the burial of a brother, but that any Mason may on such an occasion
read the burial 1ervloe.
Third. That It la the province of the Master, in all coses when objection is me.de
to the admlllllfon of a vf1ltlng brother, to determine whether the objection is snfficicnt

Fourth. '!'bat when a Mason is charged with the commission of crime, the fact
that he has been aoqaltted by a civil court, or th11t a grand jury has refused to indict
him,, is no bar to his trial and conviction by a Masonic tribune.I for the same offense.
In all these cases your committee think that the decisions are clearly right and

Fifth. The Grand Master decided that t'be installation of a Master, who had not
received the certificate of qualification req?ired by General Regulation No. 16, was

void. In this we think his action should be approved, The prohibition of the regulation Is absolute.
Sixth. He also decided that charges should not be withdrawn after a meeting of
the Lodge bad been called for electing commissioners. We see no reason why, in a
proper case, the charges might not be witbdrawn as well after as before the election
of commissioners, inasmuch as the law says nothing in regard to a withdrawal. It is
true that the Master, under our regulations, may determine whether a charge pre1ented to him is frivolous and unnecessary to be entertained, and that he· ought to
determine that matter before be calls for an election of commissioners; bnt circum1te.nces may occur which might induce him li!'terward to conclude that the offenlle

Seventh. Construing the Seventeenth General Regnlatlon, the Grand Ma~ter decided that, ff either the accused or accuser desired to produce evidence before the

must cause It to be taken within sixty days after the announcement of the result of the

have carefully considered the regulation, and think his construction thereof to be

III. In Mariposa. Lodge, No. 24, charges were preferred against JOHN PERRY
DUNCAN, one of its members, for gross nnmasonic conduct. Commissioners were
elected, and be appeared before them, was tried and convicted ; judgment of e;z:pulsion was declared and entered, and no appeal was taken therefrom. The transcript of the record of the trial was referred to the Grand Master, and, upon ~.xamin
ation, it appeared defective in many particulars, and showed Irregularities in the
proceedings, such, as in his opinion, would lead to a reversal of the judgment; and
thereupon he made an order setting aside the judgment and ordering a new trial.
He informs ns that he is aware that be acted in the matter without authority, but
under a conviction that the best interestff of the Craft required prompt action. Your
committee are sati~fied that be acted from the purest motiveR and with the best
intent, but they think his action in the matter without warrant under the Coustltutlon,
and therefore void. The Constitution h88 made careful provision for appeals and
the revision of judgments in criminal oases, and under its provisions the Grand Lodge
alone bas power to vacate and set aside 11 judgment of tiuspens!on or expulsion. No
matter how defective the transcript, or how glaring the errors committed in the
progress of the trial, the judgment of the Lodge d'lust stand until reversed or modified by the Grand Lodge ; and, In the opinion of the committee, the said judgment,
expelling JOHN PERRY DUNCAN from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, is in
full force and effect to-day, as the final judgment of the Lodge in a matter over
which It bad jurisdiction under the Constitution; and that any subsequent action that
may have been had by the Lodge under the order is absolutely void.

Bro. W1LLIAM •r. REYNOLDS, from the Oommittee on Grievances1
presented the following reports :To the M. •, W. · . Grand Lodge of California :Your committee , to whom was referred the matter of the cr'oss appeals of the
accusers end the accused In the case or WEBLEY STEWART MCPHEETERS, who was
suspended by San Benito Lodge, No. 211, on the fifth day or April, 1879, submit the
following report:The first specification contained In the charge was "that the said Bro. W. S. Mo.
PHEETERS, at the time of seeking admisRion In this Lodge, held himself out to the
members thereof aud to the comm11uity at large, as a man of good character at that
time ~nd prior thereto, and upon whom at least no stigma or disgrace was resting ;
when lD fact be had before that time, to wit : on or about the ninth day of April,
1870, been convicted of grand larceny in the District Court for the County of Crawford, State of Kansas, and sentenced by said Conrt to two years' imprhonmen~ at
herd labor in the State Prison of said State-the disgrace of which be was resting
under at the time of seeking admission int<> this Lodge, but which he secretly kept
from the members thereof, thereby practicing a gross fraud upon this Lodge
and its member~ in procuring membership therein."
The accused moved to quash this specification. This motion was sustained by the
Master and the charge covered by this specification was set aside. From \hie ruling
the accusers appeal.
Your committee are of opinion that the ruling should be sustained. To bold other·
wise would be to refuse forgiveness to any man who had at any time made a mistake
during his previous life. It is the duty of the Lodge to satisfy itself, at the time of
application for admission, as to the moral character of tpe applicant; and this
having been determined, his status in the order must depend entirely upon hie

198

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 18,

conduct and oourse of life after his admission. Should be then prove himself
unworthy, the t'emedy against his misconduct is ample.
Tho 1eoond 1pecitlcation charges, in substance, that the accused, while acting ns
attorney for Bro. THOMAS M. REED, of Washington Territory, a brother Mason in
good 1tanding, and at the time the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of that
Territory, represented to that brother that a judgment which the accused had
obtained in his favor against one CARLETON had better be compromised, and
that he had done so, receiving therefor the sum of seventy dollars - remitting
to Bro. REED the sum of sixty dollars, and retl\ining to himself the sum of
ten dollars as fees ; while in fact the accused had received the fuli amount of such
judgment-being one hundred and four dollars - from CARLETON, and had appropriated the difference, amounting to thirty-four dollars. 1Jpon this specification
the accused was found guilty by a unanimous vote of the trial-commissioners,
and the finding appears to be amply sustained by the testimony. He was sensentenced to be suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry. Your
committee nre of the opinion that , for such nn offense, he deserved that, and
more , and they therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the action of San Benito Lodge, No. 211, in suspending
WESLEY STEW ART McPHBETERS, be and is hereby set aside, and that said MCPHEETERS
be and is hereby expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Your committee have had under cousideratlon the appeal of Bro. ELIAS L. z.ic0LURE from the action of Clay Lodge, No. 101, in sentencing Bro. ISAAC T. COFFIN
to be reprimanded ouly, aud report that, if the case stood aloue upon the record of the
trial, they would probably be of the opinion that the punishment was inadequate to

Bro. HENRY H. KNAPP, from a minority of the same committee,
presented the following report :7b the M.•• W. •. Grand Lodge of California :The undersigned, a member of your committee to whom was referred the petition
or OH~BLEB HOWARD GORDON, heretofore expelled by Woodbridge Lodge, No. 131,
for reatoration to all the rights and privileges of Masonry, submits the following :-

204

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 18,

He respectfully dissents from the opinion of the majority of yoar committee in the
above case. All the facts and circumstances connected with the trial ha1'e been
repeatedly presented to the Grand Lodge, and a recapitulation thereof is deemed
unnecessary at this time. It is sufficient to say that in 1873 Mr. CHARLES How ARD
GORDON was, after due trial, expelled by Woodbridge Lodge. On accouut of inform·
ality the Grand Lodge reversed the- judgmeut and remanded the case f'or a new trial
In 1874 a second trial resulted in a like judgment, and again, for informality, the case
was remanded. In 1875 the third and last trial resulted in a similar verdict. An
appeal was filed, but not within the time prescribed by our Constitution, and the
Grand Lodge dismissed the appeal, thus virtually affirming the action of the Eijlbordinate Lodge.
Our Constitution prescribes that when it is the intention of a person who has
been expelled from the rights and privileges of Masonry to petition the Grand
.Lodge for restoration, it shall be his duty to notify the Lodge which expelled him of
such intention, at least sixty days before the meeting of the Grand Lodge, etc. This
regulation has been complied with, and from the record it appears that said Lodge
not only denied a recommendation, but, by a unanimous vote, there being thirty-two
members present, earnestly implored this Grand Lodge not to grant said petition.
The nndetsigned, believing that the question of restoration, and none other, is
the one to be considered, and that the members of Woodbridge Lodge, who are per·
sonally acquainted with the petitioner and his character and conduct since said expul·
sion, are better qualified to judge as to whether he is worthy or unworthy than are
the members of your committee, and seeing that said Lodge has so emph11tically
expressed its sentiments, offers the following resolution and recommends its &~op·
tion:Besolved, That the petition of CHARLES How ARD GORDON, for restoration to the
rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby denied.
All which Is respectfully submitted by
HENRY H. KNAPP,
Of the Committee.

. sum or *26t.62 for the relief of the brother named, but it seems to have overlooked

In October, 1868, and which providesThat all moneys advanced by a Lodge or a Board of Relief to or for a member
of another Lodge, hla widow or orphans, within this jurisd~ction, s~all be refunded by
the Lodge of which the brother relieved le, or was at the time of Ins death , a member
In good eiandlng; pro1itde1I, tbat no more than twenty-live dollars shall be so advanced without the oonaent or the Master of the Lodge whose member shall be

Now Maripoaa Lodge la situated almost within hailing distance of La Grange
Lodge, and It dou not ap11oar that any elfort was made by said La Grange Lodge. to
communicate to her elater Lodge the fact that one of its members was in distress and

and for thl1 It deserves our sincerest commendation. Still it should have <tieen
remembered that It was proper to act In accordance with the reg11lation of the Grand
Lodge, and that, If It chose to pay OQt its fonds for a worthy purpose, it had no right to
call upon lt1 Nlater Lodge for reimbursement against the plain provisions of our law.
Marlpo1a Lodge does not wish to be considered as lacking in Masonic charity or
as de1lring to take advantage of any technicality to avoid the payment of a just
claim. It oontendR that La Grange Lodge paid the money without there having
been any necessity for its expenditure; that the deceased brother had ample fnnds
of his own at his disposal for the payment of all his debts; that La (}range Lodge
was too profuae In its expenditures; and that, even if the deceased brother was a
poor man, had It-Mariposa Lodge-received notification of his sickness and
probable de&th, it would have been so enabled to manage his personal ~state that
it would have been ample to meet all hie obligations.

that the other is conscientious in its opinions. One thing is certain-that La Grange

Which report was concurred in and the brethren therein named

The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grnnd
Lodge, as follows:BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOJINIA:The teak of the Grand Mester of Ma.sons appears to be ended with the lapse of a
certain time, the surrender of the gavel, and the mes•age in which he renders an
account of his stewardship. Not for the purpose of demonstrating that the talent
eutrusted to me was not buried in a napkin do I now render to you the accounting
of my labors. Far from underrating the vast importance of the trust and responsibility which you have delegate<! to mo, I fulfill this part of mY duty, requesting you
to con~ider that those things which I have done, I wal!'prompted to do by a sense of
Masonic duty, and that those things which were not done, were omitted, not through
neglect, but more through want of power tilan of will.
Well·might it be said of our institution that it is .~emper eadem, a boast of later and
less ancient institutions, but more properly attributable to ours, which demands
the preservation of the ancient landmark"; and therefore I deem that I followed my
duty in pursuing the course prescribed by previous Grand Masters and the laws and
decisions laid down by fo rmer Grand Lodges, holding in view this doctrine of preserving, as nearly as possible, the established lR w.
We can look with admiration and satisfaction upon the progress of our tenets.
While political convulsions sbake tbe earth, while rule or misrule calls forth the
approval or disapproval of nations, that one ineffaceable word and grand sentiment
emblazoned on our banner and device, lives and shines-" charity." Sweet word
and link which binds us to the Order, and makes ours the family, governed, not by
the autocratic will of the individual or the arrogated power of the few, but by that
consent of all , which, under the direction of the Grand Architect, is cemented
through a love, divine, in the absence of all selfishness, and in the presence of a
sa.orificing spirit binding man to man and brother to brother. It has always been a
matter of surprise that the bonds of fraternal love which should and which do exist
in Masonry' have withstood all the assaults caused by divergence in r eligious, economical, and political ideas, and why not? Is there, or bas there ever been, a grander
structure in ethics than that which inculcates the doctrine that where we are placed

The following questions. embodied in the correspondence during tho year, were
considered by me and d-eciderl :
To the question " .Does the constitution require, at a Masonic ~rial, the atte~d­
ance or presence of all the Commissioners elected, or can a me.jonty. proceed with
the trial?" I answered that a majority is sufficient, because the Judgment of a
majority of the entire Commission i~ considered as a decision of the whole; and t?is
be.a been thus answered so often before, that there hardly seemoo to be a neces5ity
for the question. I have also decided•
.
.
. •
That the laws regulating trials do not provide for filling vacancies which may
occur in a Commission, unless a majority thereof shall have been found to be
disqualified; and that a majority may act, (as above) but that, to convic~, ~he
concurrence of a majority of the entire Commission, and not alone the maJor1ty
of those present, is essential:
That for good reasons shown the Master of a Lodge may, in hi; di8cretion, adjourn
the trial for more than ten days :
That when funeral ceremonies are conduoted by organizations other than a
Lodge of Me.eons, the members of a Lodge cannof, as Me.eons, take part in the cere·
monies, but as private citizens only:
That where the Master elect has failed or refused to qua~ify, hie predecessor should
not continue in the functions of that office longer than until a special election to fill
the s•me can be held , under and by virtue of a dispensation issued to that effect by
the Grand Master, upon proper application:
That the installation of the officers of a Lodge in public is not permissible:
That the District Inspector is authorized to correct the work of a Lodge and
examine its records :
That an election for officers of a Lodge, held at any other meeting than the stated
one prescribed in the Constitution for that purpose, is illeg~ and _void; a~d that a
Lodge, failing to elect its officers at such meeting, mnst obtain a dispensation from
the Grand Master to hold a special meeting for that purpose:
That a Masonic Lodge cannot hold its meetings in a he.II situate in a town or vii·
lage other than that in which it is sought by dispensation to establish the Lodge. In
.'.bi~ case the di-p~neation wl\8 denied, for the reason that the .petitioners aeke.d lea~e
t<1 meet at the hall of a Lodge in a neighboring town. I did not feel justified m
grwting a dispensation to Masons to form a new .r,o~ge, w~o ~ad. not provide~ a safe
and suitable hall for their meetings and work w1thm the Jttrisdiction of their proposed Lodge.

4th. A communication dated on tl1e twenty-fifth <Uy of June, 1880, from sundry
persons at Constantinople, in Turkey, who represent ·themselves to be Masons and
to be~" Oomiw Ma,onnique de Secoui·s au:i: ajfaml,s d'AnatO!ie" (Masonic Committee for the relief of the famished people of Armenia), enclosing some two hundred printed circulars, with the request that they be sent to the Lodges of our
jurisdiction. Having no knowledge in regard to the signers of that communication,
or· of the Lodge or Grand Lodge· to which they might or might not belong, the undersigned did not deem it prudent to send out the circulars, as desired; but. supposing
that, if the subject were a proper one for action, the great Grand Lodge of New York
would have information thereupon, after consultation with our Grand Master, a
telegram of enquiry was sent on the seventeenth and a letter on the twenty-first day
ol August last to the · Grand Secretary of that State. In due season replies to both
were reoeived, the letter saying that they of New York were " as much in the dark"
as were we of the Pacific upon the subject, although circulars like those addressed
to us had been received. At a later date, on the twenty-first day of September last,
the Grand. Secretary of New York writes, that "no new light upon the Turkish
question 'has been received;" but he adds that" our Grand Master hos written to the
cha.irman _of the Anatolia Famine Relief Committee," a.nd transmits a copy of bis
letter, in which, for apparently very good reasons therein set forth , he declines to
permit the circulars before mentioned to be distributed among the Lodges of the.t
jurisdiction. Under these oircumstan~es our Grand Master has not thought it expedient to have them distributed in California, but has directed that the matter be laid
before the Grand Lodge, as it now ls, with all the papers and correspondence therewith connected.
At an earlier portion of this report it was promised that some notice should be
taken of those Lodges which appeared to he.ve been unnecessarily dilatory .in trans·
mitting the certificates of the election and installation of their officers; and io accordance therewith, the following is set forth for tile information of those whom it may
concern, and of the Committee on Returns, to which it should be referred.
In the sixth clause of Section 1, Article V, Part IV, of the Constitution, it is written that it-shall be the duty of the Secretary of a Lodge to "transmit to the Grand
Secretary, immediately after each election e.nd Installation i~ the Lodge, a certificate
thereof, in the form prescribed in Article III, Pe.rt VII;" a.nd in Section 12, Article
II, Part III, of the Constitution, 1t is prescribed that " for the neglect or violatio~ of
any duty herein imposed upon a Secretary, his Lodge shall be heM responsible."
During several years past_ there has been much carelessn.ess on the part of Secretaries· in this respect, some sending their certi.flcates many weeks-even mouthsafter the time when they should have been forthcoming; and it is thought that the
presentation of the names of the Lodges thus d~linquent during the present year,
may have a good effect hereafter, not only npon them, but upon those who perchance might follow so pernicious an example. To that end the following Lodges
are reported, with the date of the installation of their officers and the date when
the certificate thereof was received at this ofHce:-·

By reference to pe.ges 148 and. l7&, of the Proceedings of the last year, it will be
seen that, on the twenty-sixth day of September, 1879, Violet Lodge, No. 138, resolved
to surrender its charter; and that, on the sixteenth day of October of that year, said
surrender was accepted by the Grand Lodge and the >Grand Secretary was directed
to take the usual measures for closing up its affairs. In accordance with that d1rection, on'the eighteenth day of December last the undersigned requested Bto. JAMES
MooN, late, and durlni;t many years past, Master of that Lodge, to act as his agent
in the settlement of it~ affairs ; and it will suprise no one, who has been fortunate
enough to be aoqnainted with that brother, to learn that all the business connected
therewith has been translicted in a manner most praiseworthy and satisfactory. The
final settlement shows a balance due to the Grand .Lodge, after payment of all the
liabilities of the Lodge, of $137.20, which amount has been reoeived and will he
found accounted for in the financial portion of this report which follows. The
correspondence and accounts relative to this settlement are herewith submitted;
It will also be seen at pages 30 and 179, of the Proceedings of the last year, that
on the twenty-seventh day of September, 1879, Dibble Lodge, No. 109, resolved to
surrender its charter; and that, on the sixteenth day of October of that year, said
surrender was acoepted by the Grand Lodge, the Grand Secretary, as usual, being
charged with the closing up of its affllirs. Knowing no one to depute for that purpose more reliable than Bro. JOSIAH SANDERS, who, for many years past, has been
the efficient Secretary of that Lodge, he was authorized to perform that duty and
bas done it in a manner eminently satisfactory. The correspondence and accounts
in this case are also herewith presented. It will be seen that the members of that
Lodge desired t.o retain, out of the moneys resulting from the sale of its'·ellects, the
sum of $35, being the balance of an amount due for the erection of tombstones to
the memory of their deceased brethren; and it is unnecessary to say that a request
for a purpose so praiseworthy was at once assented to. The balance of the }'ro·
ceeds of sales of the effects of tile Lodge, $52.80, has been received, but at too late
a period to appear in the financial report for the year ending on the thirty-first day of
July last.

The Grand Lecturer presented hie Annual Report to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :To thq M.·. W .·. Grand. Lodge of Oalifornia :In present ing my annual r eport I regret to state that, owing to an extraordinary
pressure of business engagem ents, I have been u nable to follow, to any con siderable
extent, that syst em of personal visit&tion and insp ection of the Lodgee which, in

[Oct. 12,

past yea.re, has been so sucoeesfully· inaug.urated and practiced. But the ritual
adopted by the Grand Lodge has been so thoroughly di..eminated, and the efforts
of competent and zealous Inspectors in the various distticts have proved so enceeesful,
that no harm has resulted from my inability to discharge this portion of my' duty.
I would not, however, recommend that the system of visitation, as h eretofore practiced. be abandoned, for to this, in my opinion, may be attrib11ted in a great measure
the uniformity of work in this jurisdiction. Frequent visi ts of Grand Officers to
the subordinate Lodges stimulate zeal, inspire confidence, promote harmony, and
create &healthy spirit of emulation.
I have visited officially but one of the districts during the past year, that being
the twenty-fifth, under the inspectorship of Bro. SA»UEL W. BORING. and comprising
eight Lodges. This visit was made in company with the (Grand Master and Grand
Tre&~urer. The attendance of the brethren was very ~&tiefactory, representatives
from most of the Lodges being present, and the work was exemplified in the first
and third degrees.
During the year I have issued certificates of qualification to the Masters of the
following Lodges, viz: Nos. 1, 8, 127, 186, 151, 177, 191, 219, and 251. Certificates
of qualification of all the Masters in the jurisdiction have been received, except from
Oon.fidenoe Lodge, No. 203, and Ai-izona Lodge, No. 257.
I have, during the year, given instruction to all Inspectors who have applied to
me for that purpose, and I have reason to believe that the time thus employed has
been well bestowed; ·and, from conversation and correspondence with Inspectors of
the various districts and with Musters of Lodges, I am enabled to report that, so far
as the ritual is concerned, the officers &re generally proficient and zealous in maintaining the uniformity enjoined by the regulations of the Grand Lodge.
The financial depression, which for some years has operated to retard the prosperity of many of the Lodges in this jurisdiction, has had the effect to lessen the
degree of proficiency to which the officers, under more propitious circumstance~
would have attained; for mind, as well as matter, suffers from long disus.,, and in
• many instances the lack of work has somewhat impaired the skill of the workmen :
yet, with recurring prosperity, this defect will soon disappear, &nd the intellectual
me.chine, polished by friction, will work smoothly and harmoniously as before.

as follows:I find, what probably other Inspectors of larger jurisdictions have often found,

come over them, and, like Bos AcRJ'!s' courage, their zeal had oozed out at their
fingers' ends. It is and has been a difficult matter to keep the officers to the strict
phraseology of the ritoal of the Grand Lodge. In fact I have been told that ii was
a farce. But I would not condemn all, as Jam pleased to report that many of them
are anxious and witling to make themselves proficient; and, could an entbosiasm be
awakened in the minds of oar younger members, that one day or another they, too,
would occupy the Master's chair, it would render the duties of an Inspector much
more easy and pleasant, instead of, as one might Ray, his hand being against the
whole Lodge, and the whole Lodge, or at least its officer8, against him.

During the past year Death has depri\led us one of our most zealous and efficient
Inspectors. On the eleventh day of June, last, Bro. ·FRANCIS E. WARREN, In•pector
of the fourteenth district, departed this life at his home in Mendocino. He was
born in Cooperstown, Otsego county, New York, on the thirtieth day of June , 1828,
being at the time of his death nearly fifty-two years of age. He came to Ca!ifornla
In 1850, since which time he has been actively engaged in business in this State and
in Arizona. He received t.he degrees of Masonry in ·Abell Lodge, No. 146, and after
the organization of Mendocino Lodge, No. 179, he affiliated with that Lodge and
served three years as its Master, and at his death was one of itR trustees. In 1877,
he received the degrees of Royal Arch Masonry in SW1ta R osa Chapter, No. 45, an~
was a member or thatChRpter at the time of his death. He 'i'as an active and zealous
Mason a.nd had, for several years, faithrully discharged the du tie• of Inspector of his
district; and it is greatly to be regretted that the discharge of these duties, 8hortly
before bis death, aggravated the disease which at last proved fatal. In his death this
Grand Lodge has Inst a faithrul officer, society a useful member, and his afflicted
widow a devoted and affectionate husband.

ALABAMA.
The Grand Lodge of this Jurisdiction held its fifty-ninth Annual Communication
in the city of Montgomery, on the first day of December,1879,-the M.·. W.'. HENRY
CLAY ARMSTRONG, Grand Master, presiding, and the R .-.
DANil!L SAYRE being
Grand Secretary. One hundred and eighty-nine Lodges were represented.
The Grand Mas~er's Address Is well written, but very brief, and deals entirely
with local matters. He olfers his congratulations to the Fraternity for the auspicious
circumstances under which they had assembled. Throughout the jurisdiction there
was an enthusiasm In favor of the Institution that awakened the most pleasurable
emotions and Inspired the strongest hopes for the future. " Words of comfort and
cheer come from every quarter of the State, assuring us that the principles we
.are endeavoring to represent are practised and observed generally by the
Fraternity.''

Mason.'' He gave this decision in obedience to an express provision of the Constition, (similar in this, we believe, to most of the Grand Lodge Constitutions,) but in

brother appeals from the action of his Lodge suspending or expelling him, and the

brother suffer the loss of membership in his Lodge? In other words, be punished for
a crime he had not committed? "Why not," asks the Grand Master, "wake the

The Grand Master's Address is somewhat ambitiously written, but still interesting. He congratulates the Fraternity that their Lodges were out of debt, and that
peace and harmony prevailed in all .t heir borders. He bad issued dispensations for
five new Lodges, which is doing vecy well for so young a jurisdiction. Two of his
decisions related to the question of physical disabilities. One was that a person
with only one eye could not receive the degrees; the other was in favor of a candidate
who had "both eyes healthy, but a cataract covered one and he was unable to see
with it; but his physician thought the cataract might be removed by an operation,
and the sight restored."
" 'Tie strange such difference there should be,
Twixt tweedledum and tweedledee."

The Grand Master presented for consideration a somewhat anomalous case. The
· by-laws of a certain Lodge required a personal application for a dimit. A brother
requested another to apply for hie dimlt. The Secretary was directed to inform him
of the requirement of the by-laws, and no further action was had thereon. Subsequently it became necessary to summon all the members for some particular busmess.
The brother did not obey, and when called to account therefor, said be waR not a
member, as, having applied for a dimit, the Lodge had no choice but must grant tne
same. Charges were then brought against him !Or not obeying the summons, but
the brother refused to attend, alleging ns his reason that he had joined the Roman
Catholic Church, and was,'" tberefore, positively prohibited from visiting the Lodge."
It appeared upon inquiry that the brother bting. as was supposed, upon his death·
bed, was persuaded by bis family to call in a priest of tha.t Church, who refused to
administer its rite.s unless he would renounce Masonry. Hence his request for 11
dimit. The case being finally referred to the Grand Master, he decided that "Free·
masonry being a voluntary association, a brother cannot be oompelled to continne
his membership contrary to bis own inclination, and if he is in good standing and
clear of the bonks, u dimit, if asked for, either in person or by written application,
known to be his own act, must be granted." Hence the brother should not be tried
for bis neglect to obey the summons.
,
The matter was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, who reported

The Address of Grand Master ABBOTT is an elaborate and appropriate docnment,

spar8ity of population in and about the localities from which the requests emanated.

of time," most of.which he h11.d denied, and very properly.
In stating the fact that a Colorauo Lodge had made a request on an Iowa Lodge
to reimburse it for expenses incurred on account of the sickness and burial of a
member of the latter, the Grand Master says:It hardly seems necess.ary to reiterate that which has heretofore been so plainly
expressed by this Grand Lodge upon this ·subject. It seems to me strange that
Craters can be found who, losing sight of the vital principle of our Order in its
universality, cannot divest themselves of that mutual stock benlifit idea which has no
affinity in the domain of Masonry. II\ the cose referred to, I have followed the posi·
tion heretofore taken by this Grand Lodge, that there .is no Masonic law, either local
or general, giving either a Lodge or individual brother, a claim per se upon another
for such services or expenses.
Such being the established policy of so many Eastern Lodges, it" seems strange"
to us that our brethren will continue the not very brotherly practice of sending
their consumptive members to Colorado and California, with just enough funds to
land them at their destination, and then coolly leave them to the care and expense
of the brethren who find the destitute brothers in want, sickness, and distre•s, and
who, of course, relieve them to the utmost extent of their ability. Then, when a
modest and reasonable reqnest is made !'or a partinl reimbursement for these heavy
expenses foisted upon them by these parsimonious "Craters," we are met with
almost a howl of indignation, because (as is said) we of the Pacific Coast violate the
law of .Masonic universality! Is it not possible, we ask these indignant Grand Mas·
ters and Grand Lodges, that the boot is sometimes on the ot)ler leg?

who knew him not), because unaffiliated . He loved the Institution dearly, but left
his curse to rest upon a damnable la10 which degrades the poor mnn and makes af!ili&tion the sole test of worth and merit. A soldier of the war of 1812, rendering honorable service and honorably discharged; a native of New Jersey, born January 15,
1793; a pioneer of Iowa, where he sought a home in the summer of 1837; moving
finally to St. Louis in 18n0, he toiled on until 1875, when he buried the wife of his
earlier years (having in 1866 celebrated their golden wedding); then, with eyesight
diminished and slackened pace, he sought the home of his first born, in Iowa City,
Iowa. Here, in a few short years , in the calm twilight of au August morning, 1879,
he died at a ripe old age . This to the memory of the father and brother is rendered
by the brother and son, THEODORE SUTTON PARVIN."

KANSAS.
The Grand Lodge of Kansas held its twenty-fourth Annual Communication in the
city of Leavenworth on the fifteenth day of October, 1879,-the M.·. W.·. EDWIN D.
HILLYEB, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. w... JOHN H. BROWN being Grand
Secretary. One hundred and eleven Lodges were .represented.
The Grand Master, in his Address, congratulated the Fraternity on the fact that
" Providence had kindly spared the members of the Grand Body, and that during
the past year nothing had occurred to disturb the general peace and tranquillity of
the craft in the jurisdiction." He had granted dispensations for nine new Lodges,
and eight special dispensations "to confer degrees out of time.'' He thought, however, that these requests were becoming altogether too frequent. We should think
80 , too, and so it will continue, until Grand Masters set their faces like a flint against
the granting of such questionable privileges. Two Lodges had surrendered their
charter•, and several others intended to do so soon.
One Lodge asked for a dispensation to lay the corner-stone of a new Masonic
Temple on Sunday. The Grand Master refused, "believing that such a proceeding
would be calculated to do violence to the feelings of a large clas~ of our fellow
citizens unacquainted with the solemn and sublime symbolism of Masonic Rites and
Ceremonies, if not in actual violation of the spirit of our Order." All honor to the
Grand Master for his noble stand.
He has a word or condemnation for the mass of non-affiliates who aftlict
Masonry in Kansas, as well as elsewhere. He calls them "Masonic drones," and
rightly too. He recommends ·a change in the time of the Annual Communication

KENTUCKY.

The eightieth Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge was held in Louisville

MasteT, preeidi.ug, and the R.· .. W.·. HIRAM BASSETT being Grand Secretary.
Seventeen Past Grand Masters were in attendance, and representatives from four
hundred and nineteen Lodges.
The Address of Grand Master PETTIT is quite long, but an able: well written
document. He first refers, and at some length, to a conflict of jurisdiction between
Kentucky and Tennessee, growing out of the action of two Lodges situated ou the
borders of the State. A member of the Kentucky Lodge had resided some two years
within the jurisdiction of the Tennessee Lodge, and was by this last tried and condemned for a gross Masonic crime. While admitting that justice had been done to
the 1•ffender, ~till the Kentucky Lodge claimed that it was it~ right and prerogative
to discipline its members. The Grand Master takes strong ground in favor of the
Kentucky Lodge. He says: "I feel that there is a connection existing between the
Lodge and Its members which no other Lodge has power to sever 9r annul, and •
should not have. Grant It, and you give a. Lodge power to suspend or expel the
membership of a. rival Lodge, a.nd blot It from exietenC'e." We ha.ve only to say that
the law of California permits the trial of a. Mason either by the Lodge of which he is
a member or that under the jurisdiction of which he resides.
The Grand Master thinks some guards should be thrown around the suspension
of brethren for the no11·payment of dues, and suggests a law which he thinks would
protect the Indigent Mason a:nd yet reach the wilfully delinquent.
He refers to the case of "Rio Verde Lodge, No. 588," whose charter had been
arrested because It had wilfully refused to contribute to the " Masonic Widows' and
Orphans' Home," as required by an edict of the Grand Lodge. He thought that pnnlehmeat too harsh, and, now that the success of the Home had been assured, he
thonght the act of this Lodge, that had done so well in all otlier things, should be
condoned or forgiven arid the chart.er restored. The Grand Lodge restored the
oharter, and cited the Lodge to appear fol' trial at the next Annual Communication.
The Grand Master had officially visited this Home, and speaks eloquently of its
efficiency In the good work committed to It. He appeals to all th~ brethren to forget
all unpleasant feelings in the past, and rally to the support of an institution which
retlects so much credit upon Kentucky Masone in the eyes of the Masonic world.
A bout one hundred and forty of the loved <111es of deceased brethren were now ehel·
tered there.

I am about to leave Kentucky, and I hereby constitute the great Masonic Fraternity the custodians of myhard.·earned reputatwn. Mark ye! l do not say character.
Character is what a man is; reputation is what others think 1im to be. I will take

should be cowardly assailed, when I'm no longer be~ to defend it, as hitherto I've
never failed with uncowering spirit to do.
Left a fatherless boy at five years of age, without a brother, and with no strong
and wealthy living family connections, I've had single-bandetl to fight my own battles,
aided only by those valiant friends whose partiality and prowess I have won by
energy, determination, and devotion to the cause of patriotism and pbilailtbropy,
reason and religion, God and the good. Always frail of body, mine has been a bold
swim up stream, with the drift-wood bearing down upon my feeble breast,•and pushing back, with the current, the steady strokes of my feeble arms. But, when almost
ready to sink, friends have shouted cheer-words from the shore, and thrown me a
buoy, so that I have always been able, after some sort, to hold upon my upward
way. Sensitive at the start as the mimosa, I !Jave so toughened that I almost feel I
belong to the Jlachydel'mata.
Bat oh! I do rejoice in the abounding friendship and fraternity' which is ~iving

as when in life's dewy morning I tried my 'prentice band and wooed and won my
maiden honors.
I go from you to work and watch and wait for the final triumph of the trne, the
beautUul and the good. I go, loving my friends, and carrying grateful memories of
them in my heart. I go, with a quiet pity and a prayer for pardon upon my enemieR.

Here's a smile to those that bate,

Whatever be the cause-like those cunning Indian arrows which, hurled from the

The Grand Lodge of Maine held its sixtieth Annual Communication in the city of
Portland, on the sixth day of May, 1879,-the M.·. W. •. EDw ARD P. BURNHAM, Grand
Master, presiding, and the R.·. w.·. IRA BERRY being Grand Secretary. One bun·

The Address of Grand Master BURNHAM is a !borough business paper, mainly con· .
fined to the affairs of the jurisdiction. Dispensations had been issued for three new
Lodges. One Lodge had complained of 1ru.ckte Lodge, No. 200, of California, for
an alleged violation of ite rights, in making a Mason of CHARLES H. BARTON, who
hbd been rejected by the Maine Lodge in 1867. Grand Master BROWNE investigated
the matter and found that BARTON had lived in California for a year p1for to his appli·
cation to Truckee Lodge, and six months within the jurisdiction of that Lodge, and
had not been rejected by any Lodge within twelve months of his initiation. He had
therefore been received in accordance with the law of California, and the rights of
the Maine Lodge had not been violated.
In reference to the proposed observiluce of St. John the Baptist's day, on the
forthcoming anniversary in Portland, the Grand Master has these words, some of
which appear to be what ARTEMUS WARD would call" sal'kastical," but the hint is a
good one for all managers of processions to profit by :In showing respect to the memory of St. John the Baptist we need no costly
array or sumptuous feast, for we read of him: " And the same John bad his raiment
of camel's hair, ann a leii.thern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and
wild hooey." Here let me speak in behalf of the ancient brethren of our day.
Though it is true that" a line is a point continued and a figure of one capacity, namely
length," yet I trust that the Marshal will bear in mind that to march from Munjoy to
Bramhall and elsewhere .about Portland, as he may .direct, may weary the most
devoted follower of St. John.
