The Grand Master had received petitions for the formation of four new Lodges,
and referred the same to the Grand Lodge, with a concise but telling argument
against any increase of Lodges In that jurisdiction. He believed that most of the
troubles of the Craft can be traced to the needless multiplication of Lodges. He
says very p~intedly : " A certain expense attends starting a Lodge. In many cases
it is underBtood that this expense, or a portion of It, is to be p.a id from the proceeds
of the work. We daily meet members of the Order who are totally unfit, morally;
Intellectually, or socially, to be Masons. We wonder how they came to be made.
Investigation will show that in a majority of cases they were made In Lodges which
•must work.'" And he goes on to hint very strongly t hat many Masons join and
give attention to other secret societies because they pay better. All this may be
sound doctrine in the abstract, but there are except ions to all rules, aud sometimes
there are so many as virtually to abrogate the rule itself. About this whole matter
we fully endorse a remark made by Bro. DRUMMOND in his v ery able Report on
Correspondence, that " Masonry will arrogate a good deal to itself when it under·
takes to determine and prescribe what other associations one of its members may or
may not connect himself with." But then some Grand Masters would be as exclusive
as t.he Hard·shell Baptist preacher mentioned by one of our fellow Reporters. He
said that 110 one ought to belong to any other AOclety than his Baptist Ohurch I

After quoting in full the majority and minority reports of the Committee on
Grievances, on the CHARLES HOWARD GoRDON case, Bro. D. has this comment, which
we copy in full, as containing some very thoughtful suggestions:-.
When a Mason has been deprived of his, Masonic rights for a length of time,
that shall be adequate punishment for his offense, and he petitions for restoration,
the following questions arise :'
1. Shall his conduct, while under discipline, be considered?
2. If his conduct, since his conviction, has been such that there is no objection
to his restoration on that ground, is it proper to take cognizance of another offense
committed before his expulsion or suspension, and for which he has never been tried,
and deny restoration on that account!
3. What weight shall be given to the objection of the Lodge? Shall that suffice,
without reason given, or should the Grand Lodge require the reasons and judge of
their sufficiency?
As restoration is pardon, it may be said that the Grand Lodge will act upon each
case according to its pleasme. Of course it has the power to do so, but still it would
be wise to act upon well-defined principles, instead of upon the impulse of the
moment. It is pretty well settled, in practice, that an applicant for restoration must
show a good record as to character, far enough back to make it reasonably ce~tain
that his character is permanently good.
Upon the second question, we have never met any express adjudication. One
instance has occurred in our own Grand Lodge, in which this conHideration was
urged by the opponents of restoration, which was refused, undoubtedly, in con·
sequence'of that consideration. The question is not without difficulty. On the one
hand, we are punishing a man for an offense of which he has never been found guHty;
and on the other, he may have committed an offense which it was not necessary to

1880.J

Grand Lodge of Oalifornm.

479

Include in the charge, and his trial for which would be utterly prevented by his
restoration.
The third question is a new one with us, but it seems that the Grand Lodge of
Oalifornia gave weight to the protest of the Lodge, but whether the reasons were
given does not appear.
We can inform Bro. D. that reasons were given in detail, as "plenty as black·
berries," but whether a correct decision was reached, ·upon the record, we have many
doubts. But we will not reopen the discussion of this very disagreeable case.

The Address of the Grand Master has the merit of brevity, which somebody hes
said " is the soul of wit." While the numbers of the Craft had not materially increased,
as appeared from the reports of the Inspector~, yet he did not think any ground
had been lost. The proceeds of the Grand Masonic Fair had enabled the Board of
Managers to pay off' one mortgage of $26,000, for $15,000, which was accepted by
the holder~. This left about $9,000 to apply to another mortgage of $40,000, and .
having raised enough from other sources to reach $30,000, that amount was accepted
in full, and the mortgage was released. So the handsome total of $68,000 of the
debt of the Grand Lodge had been extinguished, making an annual saving of $4,347
in interest.
One of the Grand Master 's decisions grew out of some singular action on t he part
of a certain Lodge, 1>nd is thus reported :A Lodge donated to a dropped or suspended member the amount r.f dues owing
by him, and then proceeded to credft him with the amount as though paid , ~re­
liminary to reinst~tement, the brother's object being to dimit at once and jom a
Lodge in another State, where be is now residing, for the purpose of seeking assist·
ance. Held, that the proceedings were irregular and void, that the dues must be
actually paid before the brother was in position to make application ; a nd that In
this instance the applicant's avowed object rendered the whole prooeedings improper
and void, even if he had paid up his dues.
We thank the Grand Master for this, Had .all others done the same It would
have saved the brethren · on this ooast from much of the depletion of their Lodge
fund s, for the support of Masonic tramps, sent out here for the express purpose of
preying upon us. And then if we ever ask those who sent the traveler to reimburse
a small amount expended in " cha1ity " to such, Bro. Roee11<s, of Illinois, raises the

cry of" Shylock " and the" pound of ftesh. "

the sum of $23,000, and prevailed upon Mr. JORN W. GARRETT to advance a like sum,
with which to save the Temple and honor of the Grand Lodge. Subsequently Bro.
BURNS assumed the entire obliga.tion, and the debt is now due and owing to his
estate."

In commenting upon the acts of a certain Lodge in borrowing money and issuing
bonds to build a ball, and the consequences that often follow such improvident actions,
the Grand Master has these very judicious and common sense observations:The individual who incurs obligations to his fellows without resources to meet them,
dishonors himself in the e:ct. May not our subordinate Lodges bec~me obnoxious to
the charge of like gravity, an~ it" so, who m~re to blame th~n this Grand L?dge,
which, baving plenary restrai111ng powers, fails to exercise 1t for the protect10n of
its subordinates, its own credit, and the best Interest• of the Craft.
The Grand Master brings before the Craft the question of the serious differences
between the Grand Lodges of Minnesota and Dakota. As we have heretofore given,
at some length, the views entertained by Dakota, we, in simple justice to Minnes.ota,
now give the other version of the story, that our readers may form an enlightened
opinion as to the true merits of the case.
As preliminary to the statements which follow, it will only be ·necessary to say
that, after the formation of the Grand Lodge W" Dakota, two Lodges in that territory,
chartered by Minnesota, refused allegiance, and were upheld therein, as was alleged,
by the Grand Lodge of Minnesota. It was also further charged bv the Grand Master
of Dakota that he and his Grand Lodge had been treated discourteomly by Minnesota, and even contemptuously, hy silence, as to the complaints made. For this
alleged discourt.esy some of our brethren of the reportorial corps have said some
sharp and severe things against Minnesota. But it is time to hear the other side,
The Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence, to which this matter was referred,
reported that they had at length been able to obtain the correspondence of the late
lamented Grand Master, JAMES C. BRADEN, and they feel confident that" a careful
perusal of the same will jastify and vindicate his action and that of the Grand Lodge
in relation to the matter." 'fhis corre•pondence is published in full, as a part of
their report, and we give the gist and substance thereof.
Past Grand Master BRADEN asserted that no official notice had been given him, or
the Grand Lodge of Minnes51ta, of the organization of the Grand Lodge of Dakota,
until a letter was received from Grand Master BROWN in February, 1876, nearly a
year after such organization; that the Grand Lodge was constituted solely hy the
Lodges which had been chartered by Iowa, and that the two Lodges at Bismarck
and Fargo, in northern Dakota, chartered by Minnesota, were not even notified of
such intention, nor invited to attend and participate. On the other hand it is alleged
that notices were sent by mail, but that they never reached their destination. We
give the letters of the two Grand Masters, as they will give our readers full insight
into the original cause of the misunderstanding :.i...

MISSISSIPPI.
The sixty-second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of l\Iissi•sippi was
held in Jackson on the fourth dav of Februarv, 1880,- the M.-. W.·. FRANK BURKI'l'l",
Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. J. L. POWER being Grand Secretary.
Two hundred and forty -five Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master's Address covers fifteen pages of fine print, is well written, and
attests that its writer had been and is a weJI •killed and faithful workman. The
year just closed had not been an exceedingly prosperous one, but still a kind Providence had blessed them with an average harvest, and had shielded them from the
ravages of the terrible pestilence. Though no mat••rial progress in the Oraf't could
be repotted, yet he could assure them Masonry had not retrograded. Harmony and
brotherly Jove appeared to prevail. The pale Reaper had taken away some of the
brethren, and a just tribute is paid to the memory of their worth and npright Jives. ,
The condition of the finances was not so good as it was two years ago. The chief

492

Proceedings of ihe

[Oct. 12,

cause of this, in his opinion, was that the Grand Lodge Htill persisted. in keeping
itself "on wheels."
The Grand Master publishes a large number of his decisions, and in o,iany cases
gives his reasons therefor. One related to "post burial services," or performing the
Masonic burial service long after the interment, a practice quite common, it appears,
in some of the Southwestern States. The Graud Master justly characterizes such a
practice as "meaningless," and suggests that, in case the services cannot be held at
the time of burial, it would be better to hold a'' Lodge of Sorrow."
Here is another curious question submitted to him, and his answer: "A candidate for the Fellow Craft degree is seventy years old, but is very stout, vigorous,
and healthy, and retains all his faculties perfe ctly. Would he be considered in his
dotage? Answer-I know of no rule fixing an age at which a man may be considered
in his dotage; and if the brother is stout, healthy, and vigorous, and retains all bis
fe.cnlties, I would not call him a dotard . Besides this, the Lodge had already decided
the question by conferring the .Entered Apprentice degree upon the candidate."
When we read of such questions being gravely submitted to a Grand Master, we
cannot but think that the brethren in such a jurisdiction must deem that worthy to be
only a target to "speer" foolish questions at. We once heard a Grand Master say
tliat he " conveniently forgot to answer such questions," and we do not know but he
was more than half right.
It may also be matter of interesting information to candidates for the degrees in
Mississippi to know that if by "a gun-shot wound" the " metacarpal bone of the
index finger" has been fractured and destroyed, he cannot be made a Mason.
For good and sufficient reasons the Grand Master had arrested the charters of ·
thirteen Lodges. Most of them had neither paid dues nor been represented in Grand
Lodge for two years.
When Past Grand Master WHEKLEB, of Tennessee, was stricken down by yellow
fever, he was the editor and proprietor of the Masonic Jewel. The publishers of
the Masonf.c .Review at Cincinnati now ma.de this offer, "that for every subscriber
of the Masonic Jewel who will subscribe to and pay for the Masonic Reoiew at the
rate of two dollars per annum, one-half of such subscription shall be paid to Bro.
WHEELTiR'S widow so long as said subscription shall continue." As the Masonic
Jewel was the recognized organ of the Craft in Mississippi, the Grand Master urges
a general compliance with this most liberal offer, and pays a glowing tribute to the
departed Bro. WHllilliLBR, to which all who knew him personally or by reputation
will say Amen.
Bro. POWER, the Grand Secretary, submitted an elaborate report of the work of
his office during the year, and particul!lrly of his action as disbursing officer of the
moneys forwarded for the relief of the yellow fever sufferers. He had received a
total of $7i ,269 34, viz.: From Masonic sources, $48,357 44; Odd Feilows,
$16,160 60, and miscelianeons, $12,751 24. He had expended $77,398 18. A committee of the Grand Lodge found his accounts to be minutely correct, and the Grand
·Lodge reimbursed him for the amount expended over the receipts. This is a record
of which Bro. PowER may well be proud. Ail his brethren will say, "Well done,
good and faithful aervant."

We shall regret both the cause and necessity fo1· breakin~ off our .Grand Lodge

dictation. We endorse the resolutions of Connecticut, and say, in conclusion, that
Missouri will be beard from in good time, if Scotland does not abandon the European

NEVADA.
We have before us the proceedings of tbe sixteenth Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge of Nevada, and of a Special Communication held at Reno on the fourth
day of October, 1879, for the purpose of 111ying the corner-stone of the Reno 8chool
House. The Annual Communication was held in Virginia City on the eighth day of
Jnne, 1880,--the M.·. W.-. DEWITT C. McKENllEY, Grand Master, presiding, and the
R.·. W.-. JOHN D. HAMMOND being Grand Secretary. Nineteen Lodges were represented.
The Adllress of the Grand Master was brief, well written, and mainly confined io
tbe affairs of the jurisdiction. He utters some very plain spoken words about the
vices of intemperance, gambling, and profanity, to which he feared some of the Fra·
ternity were addicted. He appeals to them, for their love of Masonry as well as
their own welfare, to abstain therefrom. He remarks:Masonic banquets, where Intoxicating drinks are offered, are, in my jndgment, a
fruitful source of evil and against .the spirit of Masonry. As Masons, we are bound
to protect eaoh other from hatm, and therefore whatever is likely to injure our
brother we should studiously avoid. At our social entertainments we have brethren
with us who have, by the sheer force of will power, broken the chains that bound
them to this debasing habit, (drinking), and yet, when they see a large number of
the l''raternity freely indulging in the use of intoxicating beverages, they are very
likely to argue that a little upon this occasion will do no harm, and quite frequently,
when that conclusion is reached, they partake, and, as a consequence, fall, never
more to rise to the dignity of men or Masons. I had the pleasure of attending a
Masonic banquet, shortly after the adjournment of the Grand Lodge last year, where
no beverage of an intoxicating character was offered to the gne'!,ts, and I commend
the brethren that had the management for their good sense and firmness in the
right.
We feel like reaching across the Sierras and giving the Grand Master a cordial
hand-shake on that paragraph. Well might the committee to whom this Address
was referred commend these sentiments to the earnest ·attention of tbe Fraternity.
One drunken Mason does more ,harm to tbe institution than all the anti-masonic
fanatics could in a tw~lve month.

The Grand Master'• Address is well written, outspoken, and of reasonable length.
He was glad to report that peace and harmony prevailed within the jurisdiction. At
no time during the existence of the ~rand Lodge bad there been so much real quiet
in the fraternity. There was the comparative absence of all" hum" in Masonry,
bnt in his view, that was not to be regretted, for Masonic work is of such a character,
aud is so deeply grounded, that its intents are best advanced by steady, unobtru·
sive, persistent effort.
He had received a circular announcing the formation of "the Grand Orient of
Louisiana," but having recognized the Grand Lodge of that State as the supreme
and only Masonic authority, no notice could be bken of this new rival. 'l'welve
Lodges of the Soottisb Rite in France had also formed a Grand Lodge and asked
for a recognition. But although not now ou terms of amity with the Grand Orient of
France, yet it bad been recognized as the legal head of 1''rench Freemasonry, and
not knowing what rehttiou the new Lodge had to that power, he would not advise
any action at this time.
The Grand Master devotes much of his Address to a glowing account of the very
successful fair held by the ladies of St. John, in aid of Freemasons' Hall in that city.
It was quite the event of the year, and the very handsome sum of $5,908 was real·
ized.

appropriate tribute to the memory of Past Grand Master ROBERT RuBLING, who had

fill. "Truthfully, zealou~ly, and heartily," says the Grand Master, "he performed

deceased Masons who had made their mark, are also remembered.
The Grand Master takes strong ground against Scotland, io her encroachments upon the rights of Quebec. This Grand Lodge can hardly be sneered down on account
of its youth, as was attempted in the case of Illinois.
He also "sits down heavily" on the Masonic tramps who are forever wandering
about seeking whom they may devour, as did their old patron, who was the first
tramp in tho garden of Eden, and the name of whose followers is legion. He suggests a good remedy against imposition, by always communicating with the Lodge
from which the tramp purports to hail, before granting the asked for aid. Another
effec~ive remedy would be for eac)l Lodge to keep oa hand a pile of sand, or a few
cords of unsawed wood, and set the fellows at work. It would thin out the applicants wonderfully.

openi~g:.-

Meeting all, whether the aged veterans on whose brows the snows of many winters have left their traces, or the young who now for the first time enter the councils

While congratulating the Craft on tlie harmony that had prevailed, be utters a

saved in the mlleage, etc., of about a dozen Past Grand Mastera, would be dearly

While we regret th is unfortunate result of this untoward affair, we can but reiterate our remarks of last year, that we cannot see how there can be two opinions on
this question. Masonic law, equity, and common sense are too clearly all on the side
of New York. A familiar illustration will show this to our readers. ·Suppose some
members of the Lodge at Truckee, in Oalifornia, without dimiting from their Lodge,
or asking or receiving any permission from any quarter, and even without changing
their State residence, should join in a petition from certain brethren in Nevada for a
Lodge at Reno. The Lodge is established and these California brethren are named
as a mong the charter members. When subsequently called upon to pay their dues
to the Truckee Lodge, they plead that they are no longer member• thereof, but of
the Lodge at Reno. The Grand Lodge of Nevad11. being appealed to, sustains t hese
brethren and claims that. by their own unauthorized act they severed their connection with California., and became Masons of the jurisdiction of Nevada. T hat is the
whole guestwn in a nutshell. Would California quie tly submit to such an outrageous
doctrine? .we apprehend that she ·would not for one instant. So we fully justify New
York, and express the hope that wise counsels may prevail in Connecticut, and that
fraternal Intercourse be speedily resumed.
.A certain brother BEOKNER, publisher of the "Corner Stone," which he claims to
be the "only live paper " in Masonic quarters, was expelled by bis Lodge, a year or
more ago, for an atrocious libel that appeared in bis paper upon a Past Grand Master and other Masons. The Grand Lodge, a year ago, confirmed the expulsion. This
year, the committee say, " he invokes the clemency of the Grand Lodge and comes
before yonr committoe in a penitent manner, expressing sincere regret for the causes
which led to bis expuliion, and, if his prayer is granted, he promises that his future
Masonic conduct will never cause the Grand Lodge to regret its kind exercise of
clemency and charity." Bio Lodge also asked for the restoration, and on the recommendation of the committee, the prayer was granted.
As chairman of the Committee on Co1Tespondence, we are weekly honored with
a copy of this live paper, and while we will not say \Vith Bro. VINCIL, of Missouri
that this infliction is 0 11 account of some previous sin we have committed, we ca~
but remark that our brethren in New York must have a queer taste if they bestow
upon this "live "paper a living support. Prior to the late election in that Grand
Lodge, we often thought we were reading one of the hot-house partlzan papers of
the day. If that be Mas~nry in the Empire State, we are happy to say that we want
none of it in California.

NORTH CAROLINA.
The ninety-third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of North Carolina
was held in the city of Raleigh on the second day of December, 1879,-the M.-. W.·.
WILLIAM R. Cox, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.-. W,,, DONALD w. BAIN beiug
Grand Secreta1·y. One hundred and eleven Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master commences his very l\hle Address with some well chosen
words of advice and counsel to his brethren to govern their lives by the precepts of
the Holy Bible-, the "moral and spiritual trestle-board" of our faith. He pays a just
tribute to the good influences of Masonry, whose "holy mission, e\·en amid the
angry dash of arms and the fierce conflicts of civil war, was to relieve suffering and
misery, to pour oil into the gaping wounds, and to provide for the dead suitable
burial. Hence it has witnessed the rise and fall of dynasties, and has survived to
command the co.nfldence and respect of all, and to receive within its fold the good
and great of every age and nation."
One of bis decisions was on this case : " A profane applies for admission into a
Lodge in this State and is rejected. He goes on a visit to his native country, Sootland, and while there receives the degrees. Upon bis return to his home he presents
his credentials and applies to enier the Lodge. Decision-The Lodge should not
receive him. He was a sojourner while abroad, and could only have been admitted
into the J,odge in Scotland by withholding Important information, to wit: the fact of
his application and rejection in North Carolina."
The Grand Master utters some well-aimed words at the non-affiliates, and yet
suggests to Lodges that they should go slow in turning out members for the mere
non-payment of dues.
The Oxford Orphan Asylum, a deserved pet of our North Carolina brethren,
receives a warm and hearty commendation from the Grand Master. "It is a touch·
ing and interesting spectacle," he remarks, "to see gathered into one houR~hold so
many desolate ones, homeless, motherless, fathel'!ees; rescued in many instances
from virtual slavery, taken from want-stricken homes, from beside newly-made
graves, and brought together members of a happy family. Their wants are relieved,
their physical energies strengthened, their mental and moral nature cultivated, until
suitable provision is made for them to go forth into the busy conflict~ of life." St.
John's Day was celebrated at the Asylum with appropriate exercises and an oration
by ex-United States Senator Bro. MERRIMON. · The North Carolina Baptist State Con·

NOVA SCOTIA.
The fourteenth Annnal Communication of the Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia was
held in the city of Halifax on the fourth day of June, 1879,--the M.-. W.-. JOHN
';IMBURN LAURIE, Grand Master, presiding, &IJd the R.-. W-. BENJAMIN CURREN being
Grand Secretary. Forty-six Lodges were represented.
An Emergent Communication had been held In the city of Halifax, on the seventeenth day of July, 1878, at which the same Grand Officers were present. It was
called for the purpose of laying the corner-stone of the High School building. Ad·
dresses were made by the Grand Master and the Mayor of the city. They had a
grand time of it on the occasion, nearly all the high dignitaries of the Province being
preEent.
The Address of the Grand Master at the Annual Communication was of very res·
sonable length, and is almost wholly confined to a record of his official acts. Peac
if not prosperity, had marked the year, for which they were duly thankful. Hee=~
pre_sse~ himself . as opposed to t~e . incorporation of Lodges, believing that such
action 1s subversive of the true prmc1ples of Masonic government. He condemned
the aggressive acts of the Grand Lodge of Scotland upon that of Quebec, and hoped
that all the Grand Lodges on this continent would unite in maintaining what all con·
sidered as a recognized right. He had declined to issue a dispensation to authorize
the degrees to be conferred upon "a young gentleman, son of a worthy brother
Mason, but under twenty-one years of age ."
The Grand Secretary submitted an able and well arranged report. From it we
learn that the number of Masons in the jurisdiction had increased from 2,150 in 1870
to 3,400 in 1879. During the same years they had suspended or dimitted 2,510. H~
submitted some very judicious suggestions, tending to stop this increase of the large
number of non-affiliates.
The Grand Lodges of Cuba and New Mexico were fraternally recognized.
The salary of the Grand Secretary was reduced from $600 to $500 per annum.
Elaborate reports were submitted by the District Deputy Gran~ Maeters, but they
contain items of local interest only.

PENNSYLVANIA.
We have received the " abstrar.t of the proceedings'' of the Grand Lodge of
Pennsylvania, during the year 1879, being for several Quarterly 'communications and
the Annual one. At all of these the M.-. W.-. MICHAEJ. NrsBl!T, Grand Master, pre·

The first Quarterly was held on the fifth day of March, 1879, at which a petition
was received for a new Lodge, and an amendment to the By-Laws relative to the
Stewards of the Stephen Girard Charity Fund was adopted.
The second Quarterly was held on the fourth day of June, ninety-four Lodges being
represented. The following proposed By-Law was offered and refened to a committee to report at a future Oommuoication : " Whenever thereuuto requested in
writing by ten or more Master Masons, members of the Lodge, it shall be the duty
ef the Worshipfuf Master to convene a special meeting."
The Grand Master called attention to the violation by a certain Lodge (no names
are ever published in these proceedings, and the blanks therefor look as if somebody
was swearing fearfully, judginlt by the number of dashe•,) of an agreement made
with the officers of the Grand Lodge and the applicants for the warrant of that
Lodge. It appears that it was stipulated that no charter member should become a
life member of the Lodge for a less sum than fifty dollars. A number of the brethren
paid that amount, ostensibly, but it appeared that they only paid twenty-five dollars
in cash, and gave a due-bill for the balance, and then the Lodge voted to return them
the due-bills, thus making the expenditure to be only twenty-five instead of fifty dol·
lars each. The subject was referred to a special committee for future report.
The third Quarterly was held on the third day of September, sevent.y·Bix Lodges
lleing represented.
.
The Committee on Landmarks submitted an elaborate report on the proposed
By-Law, oflered at the previous Communication, which was unanhnously adopted by
the Grand Lodge. The committee refer to and quote from the Landmarks and old
Constitutions, and come to the conclusion that no member or number of members
can dictate to the Master as to his ·action as presiding officer of the Lodge. They
say "among the prerogatives most frequently mentioned and recognized Is, at his
will and pleasure, without let or hindrance, or dictation from or by those he governs,
to assemble his Lodge fa emergency, to preside therein, and at his like will and
pleasure to open and close his Lodge. When coovene.d, no major!ty o.f his members,
however great, can require him to adjourn. He, In his lofty stat10n, is presnmed to
know what work is needful to be done, when it shall be done, and see it is well done,
in accordance with the landmarks, customs, and usages to which he must r~nder strict
obedience," They also quote this sentence from a recognized work on Mason1'c Ju·
risprudence :The Master has the right to convene his Lodge at any time, and is the judge of
any emergency that may require a special meeting.
Of course, the proposed By-Law was negatived.
The special committee on the acts of a certain Lodge relative to payments for lifememberships, also reported in full, finding the facts to be as alleged, and that the acts
ef the Lodge were an evident evasion of the conditions of its charter; that the charter
members who participated in this evasion were " guilty of conduct derogatory to
their high position in the Fraternity, and that they deserve , and hereby receive, the
censure of this Grand Lodge.'' Each delinquent was ordered to pay the additional

TEXAS,
The proceedings of the forty.fourth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Texas come to us in a bulky volume of over five hundred pages, an evidence of
the growth and magnitude of the Masonic body in this empire State of the Southwest. The Communication was held in the city of Houston on the eleventh day of
December, 1879,-the M.'. w,., JOHN B. JONES, Grand Master, presiding, and the
R.'. W.'. GEORGE H. BRINGHURST being Grand Secretary. One hundred and seventyseven Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master's Addre~s is a well written, business-like document. Of the
growth during the year he says :As a general thing the membership has not increased as rapidly as heretofore,
and there have been fewer applications for new Lodges than for a number of years
past. While this may to some extent be attributable to the scarcity of moner and
general J;ard times, I am inclined to accept it as an evidence of a healthy reaction in
the views of our brethren in regard to the necessity for so many L odges, and in
regard to the moral fitness of those who are received as members among them. I
know of some Lodges which have worked harmoniously the whole year witho~t
having conferred a single degree, and yet they are prosperous and happy. This
indicates a healthy and sound organization, and I take pleasure in alluding to it.
The Grand Master feelingly and appropriately alluded to the loss sustained by the
brethren in the death of Bro. E. H. CUSHING, who for many years had been the very
ac.ceptable Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence. We missed him much,
when death compelled him to lay down his pen. Of him the Grand Master says:Within my own knowledge he has been an active participant in all our labors for
the past twenty years. He was emphatically a working m.em.ber•.z ealous and ~e­
voted in his attachment to the Order and the noble prmc1ples mculcated by its
teaching•, he never flagged in the discharge of his duties as a Mason. He never was
a ca.ndidate for any posit!Dn, but worked faithfully and eft'ectively in .whatever pl~ce
he was assigned. He served several times as Chairman of the Committee on Foreign
Correspondence, and was distinguished as one of our soundest and ablest writers.
We feel well assured that he bas received bis reward as a Mason and a Christian.
There had been five applications for new Lodges, but he had granted only one,
the rest being deficient in form or substance. As more than an oft'det to this light
increase, five mITT"ibund Lodges had given np the ghost during the year.
We freely admit the foll sovereignty of each Grand Jurisdiction, and that it is no
outsider's business what local provisions each may incorporate into its Constitution
or By-Lawe; but we cannot but think that one of the edicts of this Grand Lodge
works hardship in some cases, if its iron rule admits of no relaxation. Occupancy
of a Lodge room in common with another society is positively prohibited. A country
Lodge was thus situated, occupying in common with the Odd Fellows. The officers,
in explanation, stated that their " paraphernalia" was always safely kept in a trunk,
and the room was safer than any other that could be obtained in the town. But the
ax fell, and the charter was arrested for that unpardonable sin in Texas. We die·
courage such joint occupancy in this jurisdiction, but have no such edict; and as a
matter of fact, in several places, small in population and very limited in resources,
pecuniary and otherwise, Masons and Odd Fellows do occupy the same Lodge room,

One of the questions submitted to the Grand Master, and his decision, were as
follows:Question.-Should a candidate who has conscientious scruples about swearing,
but will affirm, be estopped therefor from taking the degrees?
Answer.-Yes. There is '!0 place in the Ritual where th~ w~rd affirm can be
substituted for any word that 1s used. One who cannot conscientiously conform to
all the requirements of our Order has no place among us.
Tbe Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence, while affirming this decision, as being
in perfect accordance with the Ritual, thought a change might be made therein, and
so referred the question to the Committee on Work.

thought.
Another Lodge expelled a member when "the only witness offered to sustain
the charge was a profane, of bad character for truth." The Biblical rule about" two
or three witnesses" was evidently ignored, and the Grand Lodge rectified tbe matter
without sending the brother back to the Lodge .
In another Lodge, which had a membership of over one hnndred, only ten voted,
and expelled the brother by a vote of six to four. The Grand Lodge tl.tought that
that Lodge had better try it over again.

UTAH.

The eighth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Utah was held in Salt
Lake City on the twelfth day of November, 1879,-the R.'. W.'. FRANK TILFORD,
Depnty Grand Master, presiding, Jn the absence of the Grand Master, and the R.·.
W. ·.CHRISTOPHER DIEHL being Grand Secretary. Six Lodges were represented.
Grand Master CLOHECY transmitted bis Address, which was read by Past Grand
Master Sco'l"l'. He exhorts all the brethren to exemplify the moral tenets of Free·
masonry in their lives. By the contrary course too many of the Fraternity "daily
afford tlie enemies and detract9rs of our beloved institution with weapons and arguments with whic.b to cast reproach upon it. Vice .in every shape," he continues,
"should be visited with condemnation. If hy mild and lenient measures a weak
brother cannot be brought to realize the error of bis ways j if in violation of the
duties be owes to his God, his family, and himself, he persists in his evil course, then
visit upon him the severest punishment. Masonry in Utah bas suffered sufficiently
from su.ih causes, and the time has arrived when we must proceed to cut off these
worse than dead branches."
He pays a feeling and deserved tribute to the memory of Past Grand Master R.
H. RosERTSON, who had been called away during the year. He was one of the pio·
neers of Masonry in Utah, and says the Grand Master: " Masonry, generally, owes
mnch to our departed brother, and his memory will ever remain green in the hearts
of the Fraternity of this jurisdiction." A Lodge of Sorrow, in his commemoration,
was held oo the eveniog of the ninth of February.
The Grand Master had visited, officially, all the Lodges in the jurisdiction, a.ad,
with the exception of Weber No. 6, had found them in a satisfactory condition. To.
the last named he administers a firm rebuke for their want of harmony and lack of
zeal. The brethren took the same in good part, and promised better things for the
future.
He publishes three of his decisions, one of which was that "a soldier or seafaring
man gains Masonic residence wherever temporarily located ; otherwise that large
body of useful men might be forever debarred from the privileges of the institution.''
The Committee on Jurisprudence approved of the spirit of this decision, but, as the
course recommended would involve· an amendment of the Constitution, they recom·
mended the same, by waiving the requirement of a twelve months residence when
the e.pplicant was "employed in actual service In the army of the United States.''
This will let in the good and true men of Camp Douglas, to whom the Masons and
other Gentiles of Salt Lake City owe much of their freedom from the tender mercies
of the "Danitos."
The Gre.nd Master ls strongly opposed to the project, submitted at the last Communication, to place the Grand Lodge upon wheels. He advises its" permanent
anchorage in the city of Salt Lake."
The Deputy Grand Master also submitted a brief Address relating to his own official work as the acting Grand Master for a portion of the year. He earnestly recom~ended the Grand Lodge library to the attention and support of the Fraternity.
Grand Secretary DIEHL made report of his action as such, and as Grand Librarian,
in two well written papers. He had compiled and had printed a codification of the

workman in its compilation. The history of Masonry in Utah, which accompanied
the digest, Is of itself n full remuneration for whatever cost may have been incurred.
He truthfully remarks, in relation to this history, that he "was not only a witness of,
but also e. participant in the early struggles of Masonry in Utah, and most of the
events detailed in the sketch were fresh in his memory." He thinks there is a bright
future for Masonry in Utah. In conclusion he announced his intention to retire from
the posilion. We give here what our brother says on this point:-

WEST VIRGINIA.
The Grand Lodge of this jurisdiction held its fifteenth Annual Communication in
the city of Wheeling on the eleventh day of November, 1879,-the M .., W.'. GEORGE
BAIRD, Grand Master, presiding, and the B .'. W.-. ODELL S. LONG being Grand Secretary. - Seventy-six Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master's Address opens with some excellent advice to the Fraternity
to Illustrate the more.I principle&of Masonry in their daily lives as well as in the mere
compliance with the letter of the Ritual. No new Lodge had been constituted during
the year. He had granted a number of special dispensations, but had refused them
in the case of two Lodges that he.d asked permission to re-ballot on the application of
a profane, a brother having stated that he had cast a black-ball by mistake. The
Grand Master refused these requests, because they " had been made through a violation of a landmark of Masonry, viz.: the secrecy of the ballot." He holds a.a the unchanging law of Masonry, that no Mason has a right to disclose how he had voted,
either favorably or unfavorably. This may be strictly true, and yet be a he.rd le.w,
which may unbend a little nnder peculiar circumstances. A committee on an application, in one sense, discloses its ballot when an unfavorable report is made. This
is so clearly the fact when a ballot is required after an unfavorable report, that in our
jurisdiction the report, or even that of a minority, rejects, and no ballot is had.
Some of the best Me.sons hold that it is not only the right, bnt ~be duty, of a brother
to take steps to rectify a ballot cast under a mistake. It Is at least an open question,
and we cannot see that the serious results predicted· by Grand Master BAIRD would
follow, even if a brother should se.y in open Lodge, "I cast a black ball under a
misapprehension, and desire to correct the mistake."
The Grand Master publishes fourteen of bis decisions. One was that a "Lodge
cannot confer the degrees in Masonry on ministers of the gospel free of charge." All
right, undoubtedly, and yet the Lodge in which the writer was made a Me.son did so,
of its own free will and accord, aud we never heard of any moral or Masonic earthquake resulting in consequence. Why not permit a Lodge to do a.a It pleases on such
an immaterial point?

WYOMING.
The fifth Annual Communication of this young Grand Lodge of the Rocky Mountains was held in Laramie City on the fourteenth day of October, 1879,-the M.·. W.·.
JAMES H. HAYFORD, Grand Master, presiding, and the Jl.·. w.·. WILLIA.I.I G. TONN
being Grand Secretary. Foor Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master, in his AddreBB, congratulated the brethren upon the favorable
auspices under which they had assembled. Peace and harmony had prevailed. "All
the subordinate Lodges report a healthy growth, a sound financial condition, and
brotherly love prevailing." Fraternal relations with sister Grand Lodges throughout
the world were of the most amicable character.
Gross unmasonic charges having been made against the Master of Cheyenne
Lodge, he bad snspended him, and notified him to appear before the Grand Lodge
for trial. The Grand Lodge found the charges fully sustained, and expelled the unworthy brother from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
To make the Lodge meetings attractive, he recommended that the Master
" should assign to some member of the Lodge, at each communication, on!' of the
emblems upon the chart to think, study, and write about, and at the next meeting
to devote half an hour or more to hearing how much light, bow mnch moral and
Masonic instruction, he and others could derive from it." An excellent suggestion.
this, and we could wish that it might be adopted by some of our own Lodges.
We fear, from a remark of the Grand Master, that in that small jurisdiction, as
well as in the larger ones, brethren forget that the eyes of the world are upon them
a8 ;Masons, and 80 act and live as to bring reproach upon the In~titution itself. He
s11.ys: "So long as irreligious libertines-so long as men who are in the constant·
habit of disregarding their obligations to God, their neighbors and themselves-so
long as men who are seen staggering about our streets in a state of beastly intoxica.tion and engaging in di•graceful broils-are permitted to come into our sacred circle,
or to remain in good standing in the Lodge, good men will n~t seek to ally themselves
with us in close fraieroal relations." He adds, and we concur in his snggestions :- ·
. The black·ball is not used enough, or at least not with enough discrimination. Jt
has been well said that Masonry was never designed to make bad men good, but only
to make good men better. It is not a source of regret or anxiety to me that our
jurisdiction is so small In Lodges and membership, If it could come to be knowh
that none hut the very best of men could gain· admission to our sacred circle, and
·t hat to be a Wyoming Mason was a passport to the respect and confidence of good
men everywhere, we should occupy a position which many older and larger jurisdictions might well envy us.
In the balloting for Grand Officers some little feeling was manifested because the
Officers of the Grand Lodge cast a vote as such, also as representing a subordinate
Lodge, and again in their own right as Past Masters. Tlie Grand Master overruled
the objection to such voting, but would have been clearly wrong under our Constitution . With us Officers of the Grand Lodge may take their choice to vote ·as such or
as Past Masters, but not in both capacities. Should one, however, be a Master,
Warden, or Representative of a Lodge, he could cast the vote ·of the Lodge, as such,
In addition to bis personal vote ; but not twice in his own right. The G~and Lodge
Constitution of W,yomlng may be different, and support the ruling of the Gl'and Master; but if so, the brethren wonld do well to amend it, or serious trouble ma.y arise
in the future, when the jurisdiction bas largely increased.
The Report of the Qommittee on Correspondence· was submitted by the Grand
Secretary, and Is almost entirely devoted to questions of difficulty that have arisen
between other Grand Lodges, and the comments of the writer thereon. There is no
formal review of die proceedings of other jurisdictions, the reason being, we appreh~nd, the scarcity of Grand Lodge funds, and inability, therefore, to meet the printing
expense.
There are five Lodges in this jurisdiction, with a membership of three hundred
and thlrty·nine. The Grand Master and Grand Secretary were re-elected.

FOREIGN BODIES.
We fear that our epitome of the work of Foreign Masonic Bodies this year will
be what old DAVIE DEANS called" short commons." We have usually, and we may
say, uniformly, depended upon the New York report-the translations in which
have always been full and interesting. But on opening the Proceedings for 1880,
we were disappointed in finding a skeleton sketch only. Bro. Sil!i!ONS says, and we
must be content with his explanation:.·
For m ore than twenty years the Grand Lodge of New York, in behalf of Masons
in the United States, has, to use the expressive phrase of tho Virginia Committee,
•·tiled the door for the rest." We have labored in every possible way to obtain
recognition of a principle we cannot, and will not abandon-the right of exclusive
jurisdiction in our own territory over all matters of Ancient Craft Masonry. T.he
result obtained is an offer to allow us to establish Lo(lges in our obedience in German territory.
If our friends over there were reall:y serious in making this proposition, and we
were inclined to accept it, two difficul.ties would stand in the way. First. we should
be violating the verv principle for which we are contending, by creating Lodges beyond the lines of our territory; and second, as stated last year, the German law
distinctly sets forth the fact that such Lodges would not be allowed to exist.
It seems idle, therefore, for us to be printing arguments to which those to whom
they are addressed are detHmined not to listen, CJr to persist in the attempt to conciliate those who, if not openly hostile, are clearly not friendly-except in fine
phrases-to the Masonic powers of the United Stat.es.
Our proposition is that we quietly cease relations with the German Grand Lodges,
and cease advertising them until it shall appear that they have at least some color of
interest in our welfare, and a desire, however faint, to recognize our right to attend
to our own business in our own Masonic household, without the interference of parties three thousand miles away.
The u1timate inten tion of our brethren in Germany may be right, but it must
be admitted that they have a dreadfully poor way of showing It, and we now take the
liberty , in behalf of the Grand Lodges of the United States, of saying that, until such
acknowledgment as we have asked for is made, our roads will diverge; and if at
length we get so far apart that we can no longer hail each other, it will be the fault
of those who, after long years of persuasion, have refused to recognize what is clearly our right.
With this explanation, we proceed with our summary .
ENGLAND.
At the last Quarterly Communication, the first business was to rescind the action
of the Grand Lodge in December last, in appointing a committee to inquire into the
lack of uniformity of the Ritual. The Prince of Wales was again and unanimously
elected Grand Master. The sum of $15 ,000 was appropriated for the purpose of
cleaning and decorating Freemasons' Hall.
For the following information relative to the right of visitation in English Lodges,
by Masons of foreign jurisdictions, we are not indebt.ed to our New York brethren,
as will appear from the reading:A few years ago, in our own Grand Lodge, the R . ·• W.·. Bro. RICBABD DALE, of
Sacramento, Past Junior Grand Warden, stated on the fioor of the Grand Lodge, as a
fact within his own knowledge and personal experience, that no Mason from America
could visit a Lodge in England unless he first presen ted a diploma or certificate emanating from his Grand Lodge. Not even an examining committee would be appointed without snch presentation in the first place. This statement was questioned,
and was denied by some brothers, and alleged facts to the contrary were cited. Bro.
DALE having spoken, as we have said, from personal experience, he having visited
London without such certificate, and having been refused admission to a Lodge,
wrote to a friend in England, and in reply reoeived the following from a Mas·
ter, and from the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of England. It will be
seen that his statement is fully verified, and it is well therefore for brethren
hero and elsewhere to know that, if they wish to visit Lodges in England, they
must take with them a Grand Lodge certificate. No other "avouchment" will
answer:-

In the South African Colonies of Great Britain there are three English District

CEYLON.
The Provincial Grand Lodge of Oeylon was duly formed on the ninth of October,
1878, under the Irish Constitution, a majority of the Lodges holding warrants from
the Grand Lodge of Ireland. A new building, erected by the government for a
Sailors' Home, was turned over to the Oraft and dedicated as a Masonic Temple.
Bro. Capt. W. J. OORMAN is the Provincial Grand Master.
CHINA.
Freemasonry is quite prosperous in Ohina. A.t Shanghai there are three Lodges
working under English Constitutions, two under Scotch, and one under German, besides two Chapters, one Mark Lodge, and several bodies of the Scottish Rite.

DENMARK,
Denmark numbers 2460 Masons, viz: Grand Master; three Grand omcers; 31i0
inembers of the Chapter of five degrees; 200 members of the Lodge of Bl. AnaretO
with three degrees, at Copenhagen and Odensee; 1900 members of the Lodge of St.
John; three at Copenhagen, one at Odensee, one at Heisinger, one at Aarhus, and one
at Aulberg. The Grand Lodge of Denmark follows the Swedish system, which com·
prehendil eleven degrees. A society, formed in 1824, with twelve members, and
which now numbers over five hundred, has for object, the aiding of Masons' wid·
ows and orphans. It distributes yearly, two thousand francs to the poor. The past
year it aided sixty-five widows and supported fifty children.
GREECE.
At the meeting of the Grand Lodge of Greece, held on the 22d of July, 1878, Prince
RHODOCANAKIB was unanimously re-elected Grand Master. In his address to the
Gra.nd Lodge he expre88ed regret at the action of the Grand Orient of France in
striking. from its Constitution the belief in God and the immortality of the soul.
No candidate can be admitted into the Order in Greece, if he does not acknowledge
that he believes and trusts in God.
TUNIS.
Mark Masonry is quite prosperous in North Africa. Kingston Lodge, No. 322,
Tunis . at a special meeting held May 1, 1879, conferred the Mark Degree on four
candidates. The ceremony was repeated in the English, French, Italian, and
Arabic languages, as it happened that the four candidates were of different nationalities and understood no common language. Application bas been made for the
Constitution of a Provincia.I Gra.nd Mark Lodge for Tunis and Malta.

CONCLUSION,
Although we have given under each review the number of Lodges and members,
we have compi)ed therefrom no table of statistics; but, 118 we find a very elaborate
one in the report of Bro. DRUlllHOND, of Maine, which brings all down to June of
this year, we give a summary therefrom as a substitute. He gives 118 follows:
Number of Grand Lodges, 54; of memberR, 573,817; of those· raised, 19,685; of
admissions and restorations, 17,528; of dimissions, 17,102; of expulsions, 929; of
suspensions, 461; of suspensions for non-payment of dues, 28,210; of deaths, 7,113;
of rejections, 3,615. Oompared with our own table, a.a compiled in 1879, there
appears to be a decrease in membership of about 7,000; the mass of these, we apprehend, are included in the item of suspension for the non-payment of dues.
And now, having completed another walk through the green fields of other jurisdictions, and jotted down the many pleasant things found therein, with many thanks
to our brethren of the Reportorial Oorps for their kind and even flatter ing noticed
of our humble efforts, we again make our Mutual Admiration Society bow.
All which is respectfully submitted for the committee by
WILLIAM H. HILL, Chairman.

Bro. THOMAS H. CASWELL,. from the special committee to whom
had been referred tbe Address of the Grand Master and the Report of
the Grand Secretary, presented the following : To the M. ·• W. ·• Grand Lodg~ of Oalifomia :Y~ur committee, to whom was referred the message of the Grand Master, having
carefully examined that paper, are pleased to note from the record therein presented
that the interests of the Grand Lodge have not been in trusted to careless or incom. patent hands-that Its welfare, and the harmony of the Fraternity at large, have been
the sole incentive to action when Mtion was needed, and have guided in counsel
when advice was given. This is evinced by the gratifying ass'urance that ''the Craft
within the jurisdiction" is generally prosperous, and that " our relations with other
Grand Lodges are of the most amicable character." Most truly does our Grand Master picture the charitable tenets of our Order, " which give undying existence and
adorn with grandeur our institution," and teach us "to aid, encourage, lift up, and
help" the weak and unfortunate, by counsel, advice, and means, if the need is discoverable.
•
It is no small gratification to this Grand Lodge that, through the guidance and
care of our chief.executive, our institution still occupies that higher plane so graphically described, and from which we, RS its votaries, can look down upon worldly strifes
and pursuits with the proud assurance that we are secure from, and can overcome, all
the aggressions of its adversaries; whether instigated by ignorance, envy, or bigotry.
Thus may it ever be; and so will it be, if we are but true to ourselves and to the
obligations we have taken.
Your committee desire to call particular attention to tb:it portion of the message
which refers to the remissness of Inspectors in reporting upon the condition of the
Lodges in their respective districts. 'fhis, in the language of the Grand Master,
"should not be passed by.without notice." The rule of the Grand Lodge is imperative in this regard. What shall be said, then, of the fifteen Inspectors who have so
greatly neglected the duties of the office a~sumed by them? No brother should
accept a trust so important without a firm i·esolve to discharge Us duties, and. in
whatever manner discllarged, he should report to the Graqd Master, that that officer
may be informed as to tho condition and.wants of the Craft throughout the jurisdiction. Your committee therefore recommend that so much of the message as relates
to this subject, M also all other matters referred to as gathered from the reports
submitted by tho Inspectors, be referred to a special committee, of which the Grand
Lecturer shall be chairman, with instructions to report a plan by wbioh the fn!ler
discharge.of the duties of Inspectors may in the future be secured.
Your committee further recommend that .so much of the message as relates to
the decisions of the Grand Master-ta the appointment of Bro. LEWIS 0. WITTENMYER
to preside at a trial in Alamo Lodge, No. 122-to the charges against the Master of
Buckeye Lodge, No. 195, and the ruling thereupon, together with the appointment
of Bro. FRANCIS.E. BAKER to preside at a trial therein-and to the decision" that t.h e
Grand Master cannot stay or interfere with the judgment and sentence of a Lodge,"
and the further ruling in connection therewith-be referred to the Committee on
Jurisprudence.
That so much thereof as relates to the appeal for aid from the Grand Master of
Masons in the District of Columbia. and to the bonds of the Grand Treasurer and
Grand Secre~ary, be referred to the Committee on Finances.
That eo much thereof as relates to the claim of the San Francisco Board of Relief
for money advanced to the widow of a deceased.member of Washington Lodge, No.
20-to the refmal of that Lodge to refund to Baker".field Lodge, No. 224, the money
expended by it in the removal of the remains of a deceased member of said Washington Lodge from Bakersfield to Sacramento-and to the memorial of Bakei·sfield
Lodge relative thereto-be referred to the Committee on Grievances.

Yonr committee unite with the Grand Master jJ\ tho well-merited euloizy paid to
Dro. JOHN BANKSON HEWSON, Past Junior Grana Warden, and to Bro. SAMUEL
Ga>.VES, Grand Bible Bearer of this Grand Lodge, Especially do they concur in the
expressions of affectionate esteem in which the decease of our venerable Grand Bible
Bearer is announced, and commend the characteristics so prominent in the life of
that honored brother and officer, as worthy of imitation by us all. His was a lifelong devotion to the principles and interests of Masonry ; and, that this Grand Lodge
ma.y give fuller expression to its sorrow, and tender its sympathy to the families of
onr deceased brethren, it is recommended that so much of the message as relates to
our honored dead, be referred to a epecial committee.
In conclusion, your committee would recommend tbe excellent message of our
Grand Ma~ter to the careful perusal or every Mason. Great good will result therefrom .. It will giv~ greater knowledge of the laws and customs of the jnrisdiction,
11nd serve materially to lighten the very onerous duties which of necessity devolve
upon your chief officer.
Your committee, to whom was referred the twenty-fifth Annual Report of the
Grand Secretary, respectfully submit the following :"Paint me as I am. If you leave 'o ut a wrinkle or a scar, I will not pay you a
ehilling,"-was the language of the renowned CROMWELL to the arti>t when sitting
for his portrait. " The great Protector did not wish all that was characteristic in bis
countenance to be lost.'' "He was content that his face should go forth marked with
all the blemishes which had been put on it by time, by war, by sleepless nights, by
anxiety; but with valor, policy, authority, and public"care written in all its princely
lines." It is thus that your committee propose• to paint the official portrait of your
Grand Secretary during the quarter of a century in which he has served this Grand
Body. Rut instead of " scars and wrinkles," they will present a partial review of his
labors for the Grand Lodge, wherein have been expended "sleepless nights, anxiety,
public care, policy, and valor" so great that, if not written in "princely lines" upon
his face, have nevertheless impaired a vigorous manhood and produced a record of
lo.hors seldom equaled and perhaps never excelled - a lifotime, as it were, iu the
service of the Grand Lodge - a brief resume of which is here presented:In May, 1855,when our Grand Secretary first entered upon the discharge of the duties
of that office, there were upon the roll of the Grand Lodge seventy-eight subordinate
Lodges, with an aggregate membership of two thousand six bundr!Jd and sixty-one.
To-day, there are borne upon ouv roll two hund1·ed and thirteen existing Lodges,
with an estimated membership of twelve thousand four hundred. During the period,
one hundred and eighty-three Lodges have been instituted-the last chartered one
being. numbered two hundred and ,fifty-seven, with four under dispensation. The
Constitution of our Grand Lodge-the most perfect in all its provisions that it has ever
been the privilege of your committee to examine-is the result solely of his labor and
research, arid was prepared and submitted in 18.57 and adopted in 1859. The Funeral
Service of our jurisdiction, which, for its elegance of diction and for the affecting and

The hour for the special order having arrived, the Grand Orator,
Bro. EDGA.it F. P~ESTON, delivered the Annual Oration to the Grand
Lodge, as follows:MOST WORSHIPl'UL GRAND MASTER AND
.

BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE : -

It bas fallen to my good fortune to address you, as Orator of this Grand Lodge,
at this our Annual Communication, and certainly no theme was ever given upon
which learning and eloquence could be more worthily bestowed, nor which appeals
more forcibly to all that is noble, that is good, and that is pure in our natures.
Comiog to us f,rom the dark ages of antiquity, wrapped in tbe mantle of Faith, Hope,
and Charity, Masonry bas so instilled ij.s life.giving principles into the hearts of its
followers that Time, which is said to conquer all things, has lelt no traces upon her
fa.ir brow. Founded upon principles and truths as enduring as the rock·ribbed hills,
fed and nourished .by the nature of mankind, she is as fresh, as enchanting; and as
vigorous to-day as in the olden time when the cedars we1'6 hewn on Lebanon and the
stones quarried in the bills of Jerusalem, and she united into one band of brothers
the craftsmen who wrought with such cunnjng at the building of King SoLollloN's
Temple.
Dynasties have risen and fallen. The great, the good, the illustrious of earth
have lived and died. :E'rom the few sparsely populated countries of Europe, man
has extended his domain over the entire world, annihilating space with iron and
electric bands, and yet, throughout the universe, the all·bebolding sun is witness of
the life, the strength, the power, aye, the immortality of Freemasonry. It stands
forth to-day as bright and glorious.as though it carried not .the age of centuries upon
it; and it is well for ns, my brethren, to pause awhile in the struggle of life and to
reflect upon these truths; to ponder and ask ourselves the reason; to fathom our
minds and find why it is that Masonry bas existed so long as one of the principal
institutions of the human family; and if, in answering ourselves, we discover that it
is because she carries within herself the germs of immo.rto!ity, that her maxims and
truisms are but the repetition of the utterances of divinity itself, and that to the
weakness and frailty, as well as to the perfection, of man is to be attributed that
which sustains and supports her; if, in fact, we find our beloved institution resting
upon human nature itself, rendered necessary to us for the reason that we are only
weak, struggling men, we not only are better fitted to understand why it is that
Masonry has Andured so long, but we will again turn to her and, with our enlarged
understanding, love her the more dearly and follow her the more devotedly.
It bas been ea.id, and well said, in words far more eloquent than I can hope to
utter, that "Freemasonry is an inexhaustible mine of wealth to the mind and to tbe
heart. No single vision niay scan the whole of its glories. No one cunning craftsman has explored the extent of i1s quarries, for they are as unbounded as the universe. No single mind may grasp its mysteries in their entire.ty. One sees a prismatic fragment of its beauty; another appreciates a separate portion of its strengtb;
another fatboms , here and there, little by little, detached parts of its ini:ffable
wiodom; but not until this mortal shall have put on immortality, not until he shall
have entered that Celestial Lpdge where the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe
forever presides, shall one soul measure all its wisdom, strength, and beauty."
It is not until we study the foundation upon which the superstructure of Freerllasonry is erected that we can appreciate the truth and force of these words, and it
is my purpose to present to you, briefly, as the occasion demands, a few remarks
upon the application of the Order to the most ordinary promptings of our nature.
With the history of Freemasonry you are all more or less familiar. The connection of the ·Craft with architecture has often been expatic.ted upon be.fore you, but
if you will go with me into the human heart, observe its throbbings , its pulsa~ons,

1880.]

(}rand Lodge of OaUfornia.

553

its hopes and fears, its virtues and its vices, its strengtl_>. and its weakness, we may
glean much that will enlighten us upon the true vital principles of Freemasonry.
Above the little village of Bethlehem arose that bright star which has .ever since
continued to reflect its effulgent beams over the entire ciYi!ized world. The wise
men who with anxious gaze, were scanning the heavens, followed its beckoning
finger , uniil in the lowly manger waa revealed to their worshiping sight the Divinity
who, for love of man, sacrificed himself upon the cross. The Son of God was brought
before the world and the religion of Christ, with all its infinite wisdom and mercy,
was given to us. The dying sinner, upon the bed of death, turns his rapturous gaze
towards the portals of the heaven which he h&.s thus been permitted to enter, and,
with exultant thoughts of the world to come, cheerfully resigns himself to pass the
black river. Eternity robbed of its terrors, the sunlight of God glanoing across the
tomb, and the soul of man, immortal as the God who gave it, permitted to return to
its Maker, are but some of the results of faith. Strip us of that immortal boon, rob
us of the power to believe, and our intellect becomes but the miee~e.ble r~mnant of
what might have been a glorious mind. With it, we are men; without 1t, we ~re
nothing. With it, as one of our attributes, we may kneel as devotees at the ~hrme
of Freemasonry ; without it, the mysteries of our Order must forever remam as a
sealed book.
FAITH then, as one of the cardinal tenets of our Order, simply expresses one
i.ttribute 'of the mind which we, as Freemasons, but share in common with the entire
human family, and to which the world owes nearly all that is sacre~ and divine.
Unto nearly all lives there comes a day of darkneas, when the hght seems to fade
from the face of the earth, and the voice of gladness makes unto us strange discord.
Misfortune in its thousand forms never ceases to pursue, and with unwearied pinion
hovers over us from the cradle to the grave. When reverses come and their shadow
falls upon the soul, chilling with its gloom the flow of joy and mirth and happiness,
HOPE , one of God's best gifts to man, extends her shining wings, files to his aid, and
from the vortex of desp&ir will place the wearied and de•pondent mortal where he
may bask in her bright rays, and fill his soul with grateful praise and love.
It did not need the divine command, "Hope to the end," to cause us to love the
gentle goddess, for, like the mother's love for her offspring, it permeates every
fibre of our being, and every thonght and aspiration, •every gift ot' noble origin, ls
breathed upon by Hope." It is not strange, then, that Masonry, whose cardinal
tenet; are interwoven with every one of our heartstrings, should have ohoseu this as
one of the foundation stones upon which to rest its superstructure, and that during
the lapse of ages it still stands fl.rm and unyielding. Faith may be lost in sight, but
Hope, to every mortal dear, remains with us to the end.
' Each individual, whatever be his rank, his talents, or his wealth, comidered as an
isolated being, is weak and helpless. To the good offices of his fellow-man he is more
or less oblige.ted at all times for the helping hand, the sympathetic voice, the friendly
counsel, and that kind and considerate judgment of his motives and aotions which
we all so much desire. To err is human; to be perfect is only an attribute of
divinity. The passions, the prejudices, the weaknesses of the heart we all know, and
Truly, then, do we ssy80 do we 11.ll know our dependence upon our fellow-man.
" But the greatest of these is charity." Nothing is nearer God, for it is divinity
itself. It extends to all countries and to all climes. The bronzed Arab upon the
burning desert, the wild Tartar upon bis ne.tive steppes, the cultured child of civilization, all recognize its existence and its worth, and render unto it the same homage.
"In faith nnd hope the world will disagree,

l:lut all mankind's concern is charity."
At the very portal of our institution we meet with" Faith, Hope and Charity, best
boons to mortals given "-not exclusive to us as Masons, but shared by us in common
with all our fellow-men as the best, dearest and brightest virtues we can eJ''<ciee or

BROTHERLY LOVE, RELIEF AND TBUTII. Another world of truisms, another field
which we but share as tenants in common. Nothing peculiar to Masons, but a broad

brotherly love we are taught, not simply to cherish a kindly feeling, but, in its more

RELIEF. Buffering, destitution, want, helpless widows, and fatherless orphans ca.n

would prize. The reward of having done so would be that his soul would be filled

As we look upon this shining silver and observe the forms of usefulness and
beauty into which it has been wrought by the skilled hand of a cunning craftsman,
and consider its durability, we behold an emblem of the purity of character and of
the good deeds with which the past life of our brother has been illustrated, and we
wish, from the depths of our hearts, that length of days e.s bright may be his, without
any shallow of misfortune to impair his usefulness or mar his happiness.
· Take, then, to our distinguished, honored, and beloved brother this tribut\i of our
admiration and affection.

are so subtle and so concealed, the secret keys which may touch its tender chords
and unloose its treasured melodies are so varied, so delicate, and so intangible, that

let the Imprisoned glories forth. It was at the touch of the !nYpired prophet only

explore Its mysterious labyrinths and unfold its secret thought and impulse ? Who
can tell which delicate chord wlil be rudely broken and which will not be reachedwhich will respond in storms and which in heavenly harmony ?
D id I spaak for myself it would be an easy task indeed. I should simply cast all
shackles off, and, giving free flight to every thought and impulse, march straight on
to the simple declaration of whatever I might chance to think or feel. But, in this
representative capacity, I must hold myself within the limits which another would
not transcend if he were here. I must not compromise his dignity or his pride. I
must display no tenderness which he might deem nnworthy of his own well-balanced
manhood. I must give utterance to no feeling or emotion which would be pronounced a weakness when tried before the tribunal Of his just but independent spirit.

an intellectual error. And thus, although the natural field 'for this response is broad

Your committee have carefully examined the transcript of the trial-record in the
case of CHARLES PHILLIPS, who was expelled by Ourtis Lodge, No. 140, on the
twenty-first day of February, 1880, and report that, while they feel great regret in so
doing, tbey a.re forced to remand the case to the Lodge for a new trial, for the reason
that the whole preliminary proceedings are irregular and in complete violation of our
constitutionsl provisions.
'
The record shows that the Oommissioners were not elected until the twenly-fourth
day of January, 1880, while the Master had , on 1he twenty.seventh day of December,
1879, appointed the second day of February, 1880, as the day for trial, and bad
ordered the Secretary to issue e. notice to the Uommlssioners to appear on that date,
although they had not then been elected and were not named until nearly a month
thereafter had elapsed.
The Constitution allows the accused thirty days' notice of the day on which his
trial is to be had, and that time runs from the date on which the Commissioners are
elected. Other irregularities appear, but the foregoing is sufficient and your committee offer the following resolution:Resolved, That the action of Ourtis Lodge, No. 140, in expelling CHARLES
PHILLIPS from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be reversed and set aside,
and that the case be remanded to that Lodge for further proceedings.

Your committee have carefully considered the needlessly voluminous testimony
in the case of WILLIAM FINDLEY SMITH, who was expelled by J!J.r.celsior Lodge, No.
166, oo the third day of De cember, 1879, and report 11s follows:While they give due credit to the Master of the Lodge for his evident desire to
ensure the accused a fair trial, they cannot but blome him for allowing a large
amount of unnecessary and Irrelevant testimony to go upon tbe record; and they
feel compelled to censure him, In that be allowed the insolent remarks and insulting
questioDB to the witnesses by,, the accused to" go unpnnished or without rebuke. A
Commission, in a trial; represents the Lodge !tile!', and aoy viofation of propriety In
conduct or language before it should be as promptly aod severely reprehended as if
the act occurred in open Lodge.
Your committee also condemn in the strongest manner the employment of a short·
hand reporter to take down the testimony. Onr laws prescribe the manner in which
t~e testimony at Masonic trials shall be perpetnated. It is the duty of the Secretary
to write it out in full. F'or that reason only is he required to be present at the trial,
and for such service he Is supposed to be adequately remunerated by his Lodge. In
this case the Secretary seems to have been a mere cypher, all bis duties having been
performed by a stenograpbe~, who subsequently appears to have translated his notes
to the Secretary, who then put them in shape to be transmitted to the Grand Lodge.
Whether the original recorcis of the trial appear in the archives of the Lodge, written
out In good English that all can read and understa~d , as our law requires, or whether
they appear in the shape of sundry hieroglyphics which only an expert can decipher,
your committee know not, but they fear that the latter Is the case.
Your committee are informed that, for the services of this st.enographer, the Lodge
expended nearly three hundred dollars. This Grand Lodge has repeatedly ruled that
Lodge funds should only be used for charitable purposes or for the payment of
necessary expenses; and this expenditure by 1!.'.uelsior Lodge of so large an amount
for an absolutely useless purpose was manifestly Improper and unjust to those of its
members who might be forced to call upon it for assistance in time of need.
The accused has appealed from the decision of. the Lodge expelling him from
• all the rights and privileges of Masonry. Why he does so, or oo what grounds, your
committee are unable to understand. He was charged with repeated acts·of adultery,
and with having, while io the possession l)f a very large income,(as he himself testifies,)
refused to contribute ooe cent towards the support of his owo child or of his wife,
unless &he would consent to his obtaining a divorce from her so that he might be able
to marry the woman with wbum he was infatnated. Other gross charges were
brought against him, but the above are clearly substantiated by the evidence; and
your committee are unanimously of the opinion that tbe verdict of the Commissioners
should be sustained. They therefore offer the following resolutions and recomioend
their adoption : -

In reply to the inquiry of Bro. CHARLES G. EWING as to what would be the statua
of a Milster Mason who had been sentenced to reprimand by a Lodge, and was, on
· appeal, suspended by the Grand Lodge, should he afterwards be restored by the last
named body, yonr committee report that, in their opinion, he would occupy the
position, which is commonly expressed by the phrase In frequent use, of "a Mason
at large." In other words, we do not think that his restoration by the Grand Lodge
would operate, in and of itself, to restore him to membership in the Lodge. That
membership ceased upon his suspension, whether that suspension was by the subordinate Lodge, affirmed by the Grand Lodge, or by the last named body directly;
and that connection, having been thus completely extinguished, could only be
revived In the manner prescribed by Sec. 1, Art. J, Part V, of our Constitution. We
do not think that it would be in the power of the Grand Lodge to restore him to
membership. He would be entitled to all the rights and privileges of Masonry ezoept
those which are incident to membership in a particular Lodge ,' These latter peculiar
rights and privileges he could only acquire by affiliation, upon petition and election
·
in the regular mode.
At our last Annual Communication Bro. GEORGE B. MACKRETT introduced a resolution prohibiting the use of any "Masonic sign or emblem" for certain purposes
enumerated. In 1854 this Grand Lodge adopted a standing resolution to the effect
that the use of "Masonic emblems on signboards" was nnmasonic.
Whether there is now, or ever has been, any ocoaaion or necessity for any legislation upon this subject, the other members of this Grand Body are as well informed
as your committee. Bnt If there is such necessity or occasion, neither the resolution
of 1854, nor that of Bro. MAOKllETT, now before us, is sufficient to meet the requirement. The resolution of 1854, as will be seen, is limited to the use of "Masonic
emblems on signboards." That of Bro. MACKRETT is limited to" signs or emblems"
for the purposes which he enumerates in the resolution. Your committee think that
the use of the name "Masonry." or of the word " Masonic," for advertising or bnsi·
ness purposes, would, in many cases which can be readily Imagined, be quite as
reprehensible and quite as much a violation of the spirit of Freemasonry as the use
of its signs, symbols, and emblems. Yet neither of the resolutions would inhibit the
use of 11ny words, but only the use of signs and emblems.
Bot there are many, or at least some, purely private business enterprises where
the use of the names, signs, and symbols would be perfectly proper and legitimate,
though need for the exclusive purpose of promoting such enterprises. The "Masonic

11

564

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 14,

Hall A11oclatlon !' of this city, and the "Masonic Cemetery Association" thereof,
are, In the strictest sense of the term, private bnsineBB corporations. The "Masonic
Mirror" was, and the "Masonic Monthly" is, a purely private business enterprise.
They are all conducted for the sole purpose of gain, yet no one doubts the perfect
propriety or the use of the name of Masonry, or of its signs, symbols, and emblems,
in connection with these enterprises. Many other cases will suggest themselves of
similar character. It follows that whether thA use of the name and emblems ot
Freemasonry In business matters is censurable or not depends largely upon the
natu·re sod character of the business io which they are used; and from this it also
follows that any resolution which is to accomplish the desired object, without at the
same time doirig an absolute wrong in some cases, must be comprehensive in its
character and very carefully guarded in its details and exceptions. The resolution
before us does not meet these requirements and we therefore recommend that it be
.not adopted.
