Bro. LEONIDAS E. PRATT, from the same committee, presented the
following report :To the M. ·. W. ·• Grand Lodge of Oalifomia :Your committee have considered the amendment to the Constitution proposed by
Bro. FRANOIB E. BAKER at the last Annual Commnnicatlon.
This amendment, If adopted, wo~ld reduce the minimum fee, for which the three
degrees may be conferred lo this jurisdiction, from fifty dollars to thirty dollars.
We are opposed to any legislation for the purpose of making Masonry any cheaper
to profanes than It already Is. We would rather, If possible, reduce the burdens of
those who are already Masons. Our theory runs counter to the spirit of the proposed
amendment. We would prefer, if It were practicable, to place the fees for the degrees
at such a figure that the Lodges would need no other source of revenue; and thereby
rid themselves of the ceaseless and expensive annoyance of collecting does, suspensions for non-payment, notices thereof, extensions of time, restorations, and the
whole unhappy series of vexations, wrangllngs, and heart-burnings which result
from the present system.
We do not suppose that this theory can be carried Into present etl'ect, and we do
not now urge 'it, but. simply suggest it. We are very confident, however, from what
we know of the financial condition and the necessary expenditures of many of our
Lodges, tbat any reduction in the fees for the degrees would soon involve .the neces·
sity of an increase of the dnes; and that thus those who are already Masons would be
made to contribute Indirectly towards 1011king Masons of others. In our judgment
Masonry Is already popular enough and cheap enough, and we therefore recommend
that the amendment be not adopted.
AU which is respectfully submitted by
LEONIDAS E. PRATT, )
LEWIS F. JONES,
THOMAS H. CASWKLL,
Committee.
FliANKLIN H. DAY,

Bro. LEONIDAS E. PRATT, from the same committee, also presented
the following report :To the M. •• W. •• Grand Lodge of California :Your committee have had under consideration the amendments to the Constitution
proposed by Bro. AMASA W. BISHOP at our last Annual Communication. The effect
of these amendments, if they should be adopted, would beFirst, to reduce the expenses of organizing a new Lodge-that Is, of its fees for a
dispensation and charter-from one hnodred and twenty.five dollars to seven ty·five
dollars:
Second, to reduce the fee for a dispensation to hold a special election of officers
from ten dollars to five dollars.
Ir the object of the first clause Is to encourage and facilitate the formation of new
Lodges by reducing the expense thereof, we have no relish for it. We think that, if
a body of b~~thren were. truly zealons for the formation of a new Lodge, and if they
had the ability to establish such a Lodge on a sound financial basis, the additional
expenditure of fifty dollarp would not deter them ; and. if such conditions did not
exist, such Lodge ought not, in our judgment, to be formed. This jurisdiction has
suffered enough already from the unnecessary and injudicious Increase of Lodges.
Many have dragged tlirongh years of useless existence, have at last become utterly
inoperative, and have been literally compelled to surrender their charters. New
Lodges should be created only when tliere ls a decided and preBBing necessity or
preprlety therefor, and then only upon good assurance that such financial atatui1 can
be maintained as is essential for good M11sonic work. We do not tbink It advisable
to pull down any of the obstacles which the Constitution has Interposed to the
formation of new Lodges.
As to the second propositl.on. If a Lodge, with the plain provisions ot the law
before It, should neglect to hold Its election at the proper time, It would be fortunate
If it were permitted to atone for this willful neglect by paying a much larger sum
than Is now required. The cases In which these dispene11tioos are required through
calamity or from unavoidable causes are very few, and the burden now Imposed Is,
we are sure, not very onerous.
If the object of the brother is retrenchment, we suggest that he commence his
operations in some otber quarter. The relief which his amendment would bring
would not reach the great body of Masons. It would only reach n few remote and
Isolated cases, and those of a class which do not commend themselves at all to our
favor. We recommend that the proposed amendments be rejected.
All which is respectfully submitted by

Bro. WILLIAM H. HILL, from the Committee on Correspondence,
presented the following additional report:To the M. •. W.·. G1·and Lodge of California:Your committee have had referred to them four communications, named in the
Report o! the Grand Secretary. Upon examining them we tlnd but little requiring
further notice than has already been given them by that officer. The first two, being
respectively in the Spanish and Italian languages, we cannot translate, but we take
it for granted that the purport thereof is as stated by the Grand Secretary, who is
supposed to know pretty muoh all the languages.
The first, from Spain, appearing to be only the announcement of certain facts,
requires no comment; and the second, from Italy, giving information of the decease
of the late illustrious and venerated Grand Master of Masons in that Kingdom, impels us to express, on behalf of our Grand Lodge, the sorrow which we feel for the
great misfortune which has thus befallen our Italian brethren.
The third is from the Grand Master of Connecticut, and simply announces to the
fraternity of his jurisdiction the edict of the Grand Ma.star of New York, forbidding
Masonic intercourse with the Masons of the jurisdiction of Connecticut, on account
of the action taken in the so-called "Webotack" matter. We have already alluded
at length to this unhappy affair, in our general report for this year, and can only
repeat the expression of our regret at the result now rea.ohed, a~ between these two
jurisdictions, and of our hope that wiser counsels may prevail and that good ieeling,
brotherly love, and fraternal intercourse may soon again exist between those neighboring Grand Lodges.
The fourth communication, referring to the petition for aid to sufferers from
famine in Asia Minor, is so fully and minutely described in the report of the Grand
Secretary that further comment is unnecessary. The papers sent have a euspicioua
look and yet all may be correct. The Grand Master of New York ha.a addressed a letter ·
of inquiry to the iw:tiee who have sent these circulars to the Masonic jurisdictions

Your committee have examined the special report of the Grand Treasurer, show.mg the condition of the Reserve Fund, and find that he has collected all the interest
as it accrued upon said fund and has converted the same into Uaited States bonds,

Yonr committee, to whom was referred the petitions of Aztlan Lodge, No. 177,
and Arizona Lodge, No. 257, both which are located in the Territory of Ari zon
praying for a remission of their Grand Lodge dues. upon the grounds of ~overt.y and

such remission. They are not now and never have been charged with representative
dues, and the same reason offered by them would be equally good with many of the
Lodges in California which regularly pay their dues. It is therefore recommended
that the prayer of the petitioners be denied.

Your committee, to whom was referred the Reports of the several Boards of Relief
of San Francisco, Sacramento, and Los Angeles, have carefully examined those
documents and find as follows:·
The Report of the San Francisco Board, as for many years past, presents e. complete and intelligent exhibit of its receipts and disbursements for the last year,
showing in detail the amount of money received-when and from what sourcese.11 payments and disbursements-to whom paid-the jurisdiction from which the recipient hailed-and that each payment was accompanied by its proper voucher. It
&\so shows in detail the sums paid into the Board by the several Lodges of San
Francisco, which sums are derived from a tax upon each member of ten cents per
month, and of two dollars and fifty cent3 for each degree conferred. The sum thus
raised for the past year was $3,836 00, and from all sources the Board has r eceived

1880.J

Grand Lodge of California.

569

$10,124 64, which, added to a bale.nee on hand at the date of its last report, made
the total sum applicable to its work of charity during the past year, $12,800 11.

Of this large. sum it has disbursed to MIU!ons in distress, to their widows and
orphans, and for funeral and other exi>enses, the sum of $11,SOO 87, leaving a present
be.lance of $1,499 24. Of this, $947 55 was paid for the relief of MW!ons of this jurisdiction; $3,997 05 for MBBOns of other jurisdictions; $2,520 07 for wives, widows,
and orphe.ns of Masons of California; $2,85.5 50 for wives, widows, e.nd orphans of
Masons of other jurisdictions ; and $980 70 for necessary expenaes. The report also
gives the operations of the Board since 1856, showing a total expenditure for the
whole period of its existence of $169,337 27. A due regard for the proper limits
of our report forbids a more extended synopsis of this interesting paper; but your
committee must not neglect to note that not a cent of this great fund goes to any
member of the San Francisco Lodges, or their widowR or orphans. They are provided for by the Lodges to which they belong. The charities thus extended by thi.8
· Board to Masons and their families have often gladdened the hearts · and homes
of sorrow and want in every part of the world; e.nd, inasmuch as the chief burdens
of Masonic charity for the Pacific Coast fall on this Board, it seems only just and
right that this Grand Lodge should donate to it with its accustomed liberality.
The Report of tile Sacramento Board of Relief shows in proper form its operations for the past year, and is quite satisfactory In its details, exhibiting to whom and
on what account its funds were disbursed. It shows receipts, from all sources,
amounting to $2,078 52, and disbur;iements of $1,246 05 ; leaving a balance of $827 47,
of which $660 12 is not available to that Board for all purposes, having been donated
by individuals in trust for particular uses, and which ought properly to have been
left out of the report. Sacramento being a railroad centre, the burdens of its Board
are necessarily considerable.
The Report from the Board of Relief for Los Angeles would have been more satisfactory had it given Its operations more in detail. It shows, however, the receipts
and disbursements, the first having been $205 04, and the last the same, leavi,ng
nothing on hand. Since the opening of communication with Arizona and the East,
the burdens of the Los Angeles Lodges are, without doubt, increasing, and th~y will
probably be called upon in the future for much greater sacrifices in the name of
MBBOoic charity.
In consideration of the foregoing, your committee o~er the following resolution
and recommend its adoption :Resolved, That the sum of twenty-nine hundred dollars be appropriated from the
General Fund, to be distributed as follows :-To the Masonic Board of Relief of San
Francisco, twenty-five hundred dollars ; to the Masonic Board of Relief of Sacramento, three hundred dollars; and to the Masonic Board of Relief of Los .Angeles,
one hundred dollars.

Bro. ADOLPHUS HEWEL, from the special committee to whom had
been referred that portion of the Address of the Grand Master relative
to Inspectors, presented the following report :To the M. •. W. ·. (}rand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the Address wliich refers
to the remissness of Inspectors in reporting upon the condition of the Lodges in their
respective districts, with instructions to report a plan by which the fuller discharge
of the duties of Inspector niay in the fatare be secured, report as follows:They have carefully considered that portion of the Address referred to, as well
as tl1e action of this Grand Lodge he.d upon the subject, especially at its last Annual
Commankation, at which time a special committee, appointed to consider the same
snbject, In an elaborate re,Por~, (found upon pages 180-182, Proceedings of 1879, and
in which report your present committee in the main concur,) presented a resolution
amending General Regulation No. 15, so that it would read as follows:15. The Grand Master shall appoint for each di8trict an officer to be called
Inspector, who shall be a resident of the district for which he Is appointed Rod
whose duty it shall be to visit each Lodge in his district whenever desired by any
Lodge , or wheneuer he may deem it necessary for the faitliful performance of hill
duties· to inspect the work, and, if necessary, correct the same in accordance with
the w~rk as adopted by this Grand Lodge ; and to report the working condition
of each Lodge in his district to the (:}rand Lecturer on or before the first day of
September In eacb 'year; and farther, to examine the records and all the books of
each Lodge, and the manner of transacting its business , with reference to its con·
formity to our Constitution and Regulations, and report thereon to the GranrJ, Master
at the same time. Each Lodge shall pay such necessary expenses of the Inspector
as may be"incnrred In performing the duties of the visitation berein required:
Which amended resolution was adopted by the Grand Lodge and is now its law upon
the subject, and which, in the opinion of your committee, is amply sufficient to nieet
all requirements. The duties of the Inspectors are clearly defined ; the time when , to
whom, and upon what subjects to report, is plainly prescribed; sufficient power to
enable the Inspector to discharge the dntles enjoined upon him is given by conferring
the power of visitation at bis discretion ; and compensation is provided by compelling
the Lodges to pay the expenses incurred by the Inspector In making his official visits.
Yet we are confronted with the fact that, notwithstanding that the law upon the

1880.J

Grand Lodge of Oalifornfu.

571

subject is thnA explicit end plain, fifteen oat of the thirty.three Inspectors have
neglected to make a report t.o the Grand Master; and, having thus failed to discharge a duty so plainly enjoined upon them, your committee are asked to present
a plan by which the .d ischarge of such duty may in futnre be secured!
In the opinion of your committee, the brother who, being appointed to an
lnspectorsbip and accepting the trust, fails to discharge the duties thereof, and more
especially who fails to make the reports required of' him in the absence of an excuse
considered as sufficient by the officer to whom such report should have been made,
deaerves and should receive the censure of this Grand Lodge, hie appointment should
be revoked, and thereafter be should not be re-appointed; and, holding these views,
they think that the remedy for the existing evil is not to be found In a change of the
law, but in the enforcement of It as it already exists. TheAe officers are to be
appointed by the Grand Master, under and In pursuance of General Regulation No.
15. No term of office being prescribed, their tenure ls nece11arlly subject to the wiil
and pleasure of the appointing power; and hence, for any dereliction of duty on the
part of the Inspector, bis certificate may at any time be revoked and somebody
appointed In his place who will discharge the duties of the office.
Adverting again to the report of the committee of last year, a resolution thereby
reported (see page 181, Proceedings of 1879,) and adopted by this Grand Lodge,
was as follows:-

Resol'Ved, That no Inspector, who bas failed to make the report required by law,
should be re-appointed to such position unless &atisfactory explanation be given for
such failure:
Which resolution, in the opinion of your committee, coverA the entire ground and
renders any additional action in the premises by the Grand Lodge unnecessary.
All which is respectfully submitted by

Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the Grand S~cretary's
Report relative to the dilatory transmission of certificates of election and installe.tion of officers from sundry Lodges, have h11d the same under considere.tion and
report as follows:The Grand Secretary reports that these Lodges appear to have been unnecessarily dilatory. lu the opinion of your committee they have been inexcusably
negligent of a duty simple to perform and made pie.in by the Constitution, which
says (see the sixth clause of Sec. 1, Art. V, Part IV,) that the Secretary of a Lodge
shall transmit to the Gre.nd Secretary, immediately e.fter en.ch election and installe.:
tion Jn the Lodge, a certificate thereof in the form prescribed Jn Article III, Part
VII; which certificate is always furnished to the Secretaries In a ble.nk form so perfect
that five minutes Is ample time to complete the work. The Constitution further
• says (see Sec. 12, Art. II, Part III.) that, for the neglect or violation of any duty
herein Imposed upon a Secretary, his Lodge shall he held responsible. Your committee find it a little difficult to say in what manner a Lodge should be held responsible for the -neglect of importe.nt duties · by its Secretary, but, as something in that
direction, they recommend the adoption of the following resolutions:R esolved, That, whenever the Secrete.ry of a Lodge fails to report to the Grand
Secretary the election and installation of its officers for a period of ten days after
such election and installation, the amount which would otherwise be allowed to the
represente.tive of such Lodge shall be withheld.

Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of SAMUEL STILLWELL JOHNSON from the action of Excelsior Lodge, No. 166, in expelling him from all the rights
and privileges of Masonry on the second day of June, 1880, have examined the testimony as it appears in the transcript of the trial-record and report that, while the
evidence does not appear to be entirely conclusive as to the guilt of the accused, they
are of the opinion that the action of the Commissioners, who were fully conversant
with all the merits of the case, should not be disturbed; and they therefore offer the
following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the expulsion of 8.AMUEL STILLWELL JOHNSON from all the rights
and privileges of Masonry by Excelsior Lodge, No.166, be and is hereby affirmed.
Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. TILMAN H. BnocK
from the action of Buckeye Lodge, No.195, in acquitting Bro. WILLIAM TROOP BELL

Your committee, to whom was referred the case of THoi1us BOBIBNER, who was
expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry by Valley Lodge, No. 135, on
the twenty-eighth day of October, 1879, have examined the transcript sent up and
report as follows :They are satisfied, from the statements of various brethren, including the Master
of the Lodge, that the transcript of the trial-record does not contain 11 full statement
of all the proceedings had at the trial, as required by onr laws, and that all parties
will be fully satisfied ii' the case be sent back to the Lodge for 11 new trial. They
therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the action of Valley Lodge, No. 195, in expelling THOMAS Son1BNER from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be reversed and set aside, and
that the case be remandecl to said Lodge for further action.

In regard to the removal of Saint J.ouis Lodge, No. 86, from Saint Lonie, in Sierra
eonnt.v, to Howland Flat, in the same county, your committee recommend that the
Grand Master's approval thereof be affirmed, inasmuch as the reasons for suoh
removal appear to be sufficient, and the law concerning snch cases appears to have
heen fully complied with,
In the matter of Bro. BENJAMIN W BHBPBERD, of Sincerity Lodge, No. 132, who
was suspended in 1878 for non-payment of dues, the Grand Lodge, at its Annual
Communication last year, set aside the order of suspension and declared Bro.
8HEPHBBn to be still a Ute-member of that Lodge In good standing. In this action
the Grand Lodge proceeded entirely upon the statement of facts contained in the
memorial of Bro. SHllPHERD, and In a letter from Bro. GsORGE W. BOYDRN, the Master
of the Lodge, addressed to the Masonic Board of Relief of San Francisco, fully corroborating the memorial. These statements were uncontradioted, and, being taken
as true, ah owed that Bro. SHEPHERD was, at the time of bis suspension, a life-member
of that Lodge, owed no dues, and was illegally suspended.
Now, however, Bro. BOYDEN, wbois stillM11.ster of that Lodge, flies with the Gr81ld
Secret~ry a statement, which he repeats and amplifleB before your committee, to the
effect that all the material statements of Bro. SHEPHERD'S memorial and of bis own
letter are entirely erroneous; that he was misled by what he had beard and supposed
to be true ; and that, having since examined the records of the Lodge and obtained
other and further information, he discovers that Bro. SasPHEBD never became or was
a life-member of that Lodge. He therefore desires that action be taken looking to
the rescinding of the order of t.he Grand Lodge in this matter.
It does not appear that Sincerity Lodge formally asks any action of the Grand
Lodge, but only that Bro. BOYDEN applies as In behalf of that Lodge. It does not
appear that Bro. SHEPHERD has had notice of any application to, or of any action
desired of, the Grand Lodge in tbie matter. Under these circumstances, your committee cannot recommend that any action upon the merits of the case be taken at this
Communication. If any error has occurred, It has resulted solely from the presentation to the Grand Lodge, as reliable evidence, of that which was in fact only hearsay
and untrustworthy. In order to avoid further trouble from such cause, and in view
of the importance of the matter to Bro. SHEPHERD aud his Lodge, your committee
recommend that Sincerity Lodge, No.182, be advised to present a formal application
to the Grand Lodge for such action as it may desire in this matter; and that it also

In Penta/pha Lodge, No. 202, one LYHA.l! 0ATHAN HUDSON was elected to become
a member by affiliation. Some time thereafter he failed to prove himself, in the
customary manner, to be a Mason. The Grand Master very justly censured this
action of the Lodge in no very gentle phrase. He might have been stiHmore severe,
If that were possible, without exposing himself to censure.
But an examination of the papers has disclosed the fact that the fault was mainly
attributable to the committee to whom the application was referred. They reported
favorably, and the petitioner was naturally enough elected. By what right did they
make suoh report without inQfiring whether the applicant was a Mason or not ? They
should have commenced their Investigation at that point; and it is most unfortunate
that the members of that committee have not, In some manner, beeu punished for
their shameful neglect of duty.
Your committee think that no application for affiliation should be received until
the applicant has, In some of the methods known to Masonic usage, proved himself'
to be a Master Mason; and to preclude the recurrence of such awkward accidents,
they recommend the adop\ion of the following resolution :Resolved, That no Lodge in this jurisdiction shall hereafter receive an application
for affiliation until the applicant shall have proved, to the satisfaction of the Master
of such Lodge, that he is a Master Mason.

Bro. LEONIDAS E PRATT, from the same committee, also presented
the following report :To the M.'. W.', Grana Lodge of California :Yonr committee have carefully examined those portions of the Address of the
Grand Master which have been referred to them, .and all the various papers, documents and correepondenoe pertinent thereto ; and they are happy to report that, of
all the numerous decisions rendered by him, some of them upon delicate aud complioated questions, there is one only which does not receive their hearty concurrence.
Before proceeding to the consideration of that one, your committee deem It proper
at least, and they think it to be their duty, to comment briefly upon the conduct of
the 111.aeter of Buckeye Lodge, No. 196, as disclosed by the charge and specifications
made against him by six members of his Lodge. The Grand Master declined to 11.p·
point Commissioners to try this charge, and in this he was probably right. Bat if
th~ matters charged are true, then the conduct of this Master, while presiding at the
trial of Bro. TJJO.MAS KEKPE, wae in such execrable taete, so ill·&<lvlsed, so unbecoming
to the judicial position, BO partial, prejudicial, and unfair, that a fraction more of like
conduct would certainly have subjected him very properly to the proposed disolpllne.
Masters cannot be too careful and guarded in their deportment on each occasions.

582

Proceedings of the •

(Oct. 15,

Their province is simply to decide such questions or law as may arise during the trial,
with perfect indifference as to the effect or result of ench decision. To attempt to
suppress evidence; to badger, confuse, or. annoy a witness; to endeavor to pot
words into his mouth; to express his own opinion. as to the knowledge of the
accused in regard to certain facts, or as to his purpose or motive in doing certain
.t hings; or to declare his opinion as to the valne, weight, or effect of certain evidence;
is entirely beyond bis proper province and cannot be too severely reprehended. He
is there simply to declare the law. The Commissioners are to settle all questions of
ract, without reference to the opinions, surmises, or suspicions of tbe Master ; and it
is not proper for him to indicate bis opinions, suspicions, or sarmises.
From OoluBa Lodge, No. 142, a charge was preferred against the Master by some
of his bretht·en, but the Grand Master refused to appoint a Trial·Commieeion on the
ground that it. was a simple matter of business which should be adjudged in a civil
conrt, and not before a :Masonic tribunal.
Your committee find themselves compelled reluctantly to differ with the Gra.nd
Master. They are aware that our Grand Lodge has set its face firmly against taking
cognizance of mere business controversies, in which there is no fraud, breach of trust,
misrepresentation, or bad faith ; and in this position your committee most cordially
and heartily concur. Masonry deals with violations of the moral law alone; but
when there is an obvious violation of that law, the Mason should not be permitted to
shield himself behind the fact that it occurred in the course of a business transaction.
In the case under consideration it appears from the charges, which for present
purposes are to be taken as true, that the Master of said Lodge became indebted to
one of the members thereof in a considerable sum of money; that after repeated
promises to pay, through a period of three years, the creditor, becoming impatient,
commenced a suit at law ,caused an attachment to be issued against the property of the
debtor, and placed the same in the hands of the sheriff for service; and that, while
the sheriff was .holding said attachment and threatening to levy the same, the debtor
begged the creditor not to make any further costs, but to hold back th" attachment
and he would pay the money in a few hours. Relying upon this assurance, the creditor instructed the sheriff not to levy the attachment. Thereupon the debtor, instead
of making any effort to pay the money, proceeded with all expedition to file his petition in lnsolvenoy, obtained an order staying all proceedings at law against himself,
and procured a decree of the proper court discharging him from all his debts and
liabilities.
To say that upon this state of fade there was nothing upon which a Masonic tribunal should act, is pushing the doctrine of non-interference a little too far. Your
committee do not base their opinion upon the mere fact thnt the creditor lost his
money. Indeed, that, in their view, would be a false factor in the case. They think
that such premeditated falsehood, treachery, and deceit on the part of one Mason
towards another, if true as charged, ought to be .Maeonlcally punished, regardless of
its pecuniary consequences to either party. If they are correct in this view, the Grand
:MaRter should have appointed Trial-Commissioners as requested.
Your committee readily comprehend the reasons upon which be was acting when
be refused to do so. He was simply pursuing a general principle to which this Grand
Lodge has fully committed itself, and to that general principle your committee fully
subscribe. But they do not think it advisable to carry the doctrine any further than
it has already been carried. In other words, tliey think that the facts of this particular case are such as to place it outside of the established doctrine, and they do not
propose io extend that doctrine so as to include it. They therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the Grand Master be.requested io appoint Commiesioners as soon
as may be practicable, as provided by the Constitution, to bear and determine the

Bro. THOMAS H. 0ASWELL, from a majority of the Committee on
Jurisprudence, presented the following report:'.lb the M. •• W. •• Grand Lodg-, of Oal·ifoi-nia :-

At the last Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge the following question wa.s
proposed:"Does a Master Ma.son, who is a member of a subordinate Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Ca.lifornia, violate any of the laws, regulations, or
edicts of said Grand Lodge by participating in the funeral ceremonies of a Masonic
Body of a higher degree, no subordinate Lodge, as such, performing any ceremonies
at such funeral?"
It is a recognized rule in this jurisdiction that no Lodge shall participate in any
funeral ceremonies, nor individual members in the clothing of Master Masone, unless
such Lodge shall have entire control of the ceremonies. Thi• Grand Lodge knows
nothing of " funeral ceremonies of a Masonic Body of a higher degree." It recognize• but one Masonic funeral service-that prescribed for a Lodge of Master Masons.
If there is any other funeral service which is styled by those who perform it as
Masonic, and if the parties conducting it are willing that individuals who are
Masons should take part therein, we know of no reason, should such individuals
desire so to p1i.rticipate, why they should not do so. Nor do we think this Grand
Lodge would trouble itself about the matter so long as the rule above stated waR
observed.
All which is respectfully submitted by
L11:w1s F, JONES,

THOMAS H. CASWELL,

The foregoing statement shows that during the~present Communication one hundred and ninety.five chartered Lodges, being all except fourteen, were represented, to·
gether with the four Lodges acting under dispensation. It also shows that to thirtynine Lodges no a.llowance baa been made. Of these, twenty-one-being Nos. l, li, 22,
30, 44, 61, 120, 127, 136, 139, 144, 166, 169, 188, 212, 215, 216, 219, 225, 244, and King
Solomon's, U. D.-althoagh represented and their dues fully paid, are located in the
City of San Francisco, or its immediate vicinity; fourteen-being Nos. 32, 41, 88,
96, 145, 147, 150, 182, 184, 206, 227, 281, 288, and 249-have paid their dues, but have
not been represented at all ; three-being Nos. 21, 177, and 257-are located without the
State and are not chargeable with dues to this fund or entitled to receive anything
therefrom; and one-No. 28-the dues of whioh were paid, was represented by a
Past Master residing in this city. It will also be seen that allowances have been ma.de
to six Lodges which were not represented on the first day of the Communication, viz.:
Nos. 5, 14, 20, 110, 156, and 181, the representatives thereof having been excused by
the Grand Lodge for the lateness of their attendance.

Bro. GEORGE HINDS, from the special committee to whoJil was
referred the Report of the'Grancl Lecturer, presented the following
report:To the M. ·. W. •. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was r eferred the Report of the Grand Lecturer, have
considered the same, and, like all previous reports from that officer, find it replete
with information valuable to the Grand Lodge, inasmuch as it shows the general
condition of the Craft throughout the jurisdiction, and, with but few exceptions, the
condition of the individual Lodges thereof.
Notwithstanding the inability of the Grand Lecturer to make as many personal
visits of inspection as heretofore- regretfully expresi!ed by himself-the report shows
that his. interest and zeal in his work have in no wise relaxed; and, were it not for
what seems to your committee the inexcusable neglect of the Inspectors of the sixth,
fifteenth, and twenty·first districts to report to the Grand Lecturer the working condition of each Lodge in bis district, a• required by the fifteenth Regulation of the
Grand Lodge, he would have had the proud satisfaction of presenting information
concerning every I.odge within its juri>dlction. It is to be hoped that in the future
no Inspector will neglect the important duty of reporting to the Grand Lecturer as
required.
The report is fall of interest, and your committee commend it to every member
of the Grand Lodge for careful perusal. They refer with pain to that portion of it
embodying the report of Inspector PoCKMAN, of the eighteenth district, relative to
the Master Of Tehama Lodge, No. 3. The Inspector recites in effect as fol!o~s: that
the brother has been elected Master for five successive yea.re-that, on hie first election, although but indifferently que.lified, he gave him a certificate on a promise of
steady application-that he has twice renewed this certificate upon the same promie0<1
-that in the meantime the Master promised that whenever he had work in his Lodge
he would notifY him, that he might be present and inspect it, but that he had failed
to fulfill such promise-that on his re-election the present year he, the Inspector,
twice r equested him to convene bis Lodge for inspection, but that he did not comply
with these requests, notwithstanding that for a period of nearly three months he
was in. close proximity and in readiness to suit his time to the convenience of the
Master-and that instead of applying to him for inspection in private, or in presence
of hie Lodge, he obtained his certificate from the Grand Lecturer on the strength of
what he bolds himself in readiness to show were mierepresentationd to that officer.
Bro. PocKMAN, the Inspector, was not before your committee, owing to important
duties as Warden of the State Prison which rendered his presence impossible. The
Master of Tehama Lodge, No. 3, was, and stated in his own behalf, in substance-that
he was examined by Bro. PooKMAN, the Inspector, in 1874 and 1875, and believed
himself entitlod to a certificate of qualification under a resolution of the Grand Lodge
adopted in 1877-tbat he had notified the Inspector of t he time of meeting of his Lodge
-that he had said to the Inspector, when requested to call a meeting of his Lodge,
that during the holidays he was very busy and could not do it-that the Inspector
said to him that if he got a certificate from the Grand Lecturer i t would be a.II right

Grand Lodge of California.

and be would make no complaint-that the Inspector did not ask for an examination
but only that hie Lodge should be called together-and that he had intended no dis:
respect to that officer.

Bro. GEORGE J. HoBE, from the special committee to whom had

•

1b the M. ·. W." Grand Lodge of California :Your committee,appointed to consider that portion o! the Grand Master's Address
referring to the death of Past Junior Grand Warden JoHN .BANKSON HEWSON, submit
the following : Again the summons of the Great Destroyer has been heard, and another of our
brethren has passed into the spirit life. When a brother dies, whom we have loved
and honored, and whom we shall miss at our meetings, our labors, and our periods
of rest, it is fit that we should make for the living a record of his works, his excel·
lencies, anu his good deeds.
Bro. JOHN BANKSON HEWSON was b~rn in Newark, New Jersey, on the twentvseventh day of August, 1823, but, his parents soon after removing to Augusta,
Georgia, his early life was spent there and in Louisiana and Texas. In 1847, after
the taking of Vera Cruz by General ScoTT, he was appointed chief clerk of the
Subsistence Department, which position he held until the affairs of that department
were all settled. In August, 1849, he arriv!ld in San Francisco, whence he proceeded
to the mines; and in January, 1851, he returned and settled in the city of San Jose,
Santa Clara County, where he resided until bis appointment as Chief Deputy of the
Secretary of State of California in the beginning of the year 1876. He then removed
to Sacramento, the seat of Government, where he died on the first day of January,
1880.
Of hiA early Masonic life we have little information, but we find that during
eleven years he served San Jose Lodge, No. 10, as its Master; Howard Royal Arch
Chapter, No. 14, five years as High Priest; and San Joae Commandery, No. 10, two
years as Commander. In the Grand Lodge he was elected Junior Grand Warden in
1862, and in all the various positions to which he had been called by hia brethren, he
ever proved himself most competent and worthy.
In his relations with the world our brother was faithful to every trust reposed in
him, and always performed his duties with unswerving fidelity. A good and enterprising citizen, of unobtrusive charity to all men, a kind and affectionate husband
and indulgent father, he has left a void that time can never fill ; and your commit·
tee offer the following resolution for adoption:Reso~IJBd, That, as an evidence of our affectionate remembrance, a mourning page
be devoted to the memory of Bro. JOHN BANKSON HEWSON in our proceedings.

Bro. WILLIAM T. REYNOLDS, from the Committee on Grievances,
presented the following reports :To the M. ·. W. ·• Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :Your committee, to whom was referred the record of the trial of FRED. CBUNE'l'l',
an Entered Apprentice, who was expelled by South San F,.ancisco Lodge, No. 212,
on the seventh day of October, 1880, after carefully conside·r ing the same, have come
to the conclusion that the evidence elicited at the trial fails to substantiate either
of the specifications set forth in the charge. They therefore offer the following
resolution and recommend Its adoption:-,
Resolved, That the action of South Sar; Francisco Lodge, No. 212, in expelling
Bro. FRBD. CBUNETT from all the ·rights and privileges of Masonry, be reve'rsed and
set aside, and that said charge be dismissed.
'Yonr committee have carefully examined the case of THOMAS KEEFE, who was
sentenced to be reprimanded by Buckeye Lodge, No. 195, on the twenty.fourth day
· of January, 1880 ; who was again tried and sentenced to be reprimanded on the
twenty·aecond day of May, 1880; and who was for the third time tried and sentenced
to be expelled on the nineteenth day of June, 18RO; and report that in no one of these
three cases do the transcripts of the trial·records show that any Masonic crime has ·
been proved against the accused. The trouble originated in certain bnsiness trans·
actions In which the alleged violation of a certain contract or agreement between
the accused and another brother bore a promine'llt part. All these matters should
have been settled In a civil court, and should never have been brought before the
Lodge; and yonr committee feel confident that the action of Bucke11e Lodge can
safely be reversed without Injury to the Interests of Masonry. They therefore offer
·the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the action of Buckeye Lodge, No.195, in all the above named cases,
be reversed and set aside, and that the several charges be dismissed.

PROPOSED AMENDMENTS

TO THE

CONSTITUTION OF THE GRAND LODGE.

17 00

Total amounts received to 31st October, 1880,. ........ $14,266 40 $3,030 25
.' '
Making an aggregate sum of receipts of......... $17,291 65

At the Annual Communication in October, 1879, the following amendments to
the Constitution were proposed, viz.: to
Amend Sec. 8, Art. Ill, Part Ill, by striking out the word "State," in the first
line thereof. and inserting instead the word "Jurisdiction;" by striking out the
word "fifty." in the second line thereof, and inserting instead the weird "thirty;"
and by striking out, in the second and third lines thereof, the words "nor shall any
Lodge without the State, and under this jurisdiction, confer them for a less fee than
thirty dollars."
So that, in case those amendments should ,be adopted, that section would read as
follows:SEo. 8. No Lodge wit.bin this Jurisdiction shall confer the three degrees for a
less fee than thirty dollars; and in every case the entire fee for the degrees shall
accompany the application, else such application shall not be received. Provided,
however. that, if the applicant has already received the first degree, or the first and
second degrees, in another Lodge, the fee to accompany his application for the
remaining degrees or degree shall be such proportion of the fee for all the degrees
as the by-laws of the Lodge may provide.
No report upon these proposed amendments was made at that Communication
by the Oommittee on Jurisprudence; but, at the last Annual Communication, in
October, 1880, an adverse report was made by that committee, notwithstanding
which the amendmonts received the vole of a majority of the Grand Lodge, and
now a11ait the constitutional vote of two-thirds thereof at the next Annual Communication.

Adopted Ootober, A. L. 5880.

19. No Lodge in this jurisdiction shall hereafter receive an application for
affiliation until the applicant shall have proved, to the satisfaction of the Master
of such Lodge, that he is a Master Mason.
20. No Mason under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge shall participate
Maeonically in any so-~.alled Masonic funeral service or ceremonial, other than
that prescribed by this Grand Lodge and conducted by a Lodge of Master Masons.
